events.title: Campaigners claim minister attempting to undermine 'Holiday Hunger Bill'
events.summary: Paul Givan has now proposed amendments which would give him discretion to decide when the payments would take effect Campaigners have accused the education minister of attempting to undermine a proposed Stormont law which would help poorer families with the cost of food. The Democratic Unionist Party's (DUP) Paul Givan has been consistently critical of the legislation which is being brought forward by Sinn Féin assembly member Danny Baker. Givan has warned it would immediately cost his department £20m a year at a time when it is already struggling to balance its budget. The Holiday Meals Payment Bill , external would create a new payment for families whose children receive free school meals which would be made during school holidays to help with the cost of food. The matter is due to be discussed in the assembly on Monday. Givan has now proposed amendments which would give him the power to delay implementation. He will need support from other parties for the amendments to be accepted. It is not clear if he will get that support, although the Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) has expressed reservations about the proposal. The payment would be made during school holidays to help with the cost of food As it is based on school meals, the cost of the scheme would be on the Department of Education. It is modelled on the School Holiday Food Grant scheme introduced during the pandemic, which paid qualifying families £27 per child every fortnight. In April, Givan warned MLAs that his department did not have funding for the scheme, so they would be voting to cut education spending if they supported it. He has now proposed amendments which would give him discretion to decide when the payments would take effect. A coalition of campaign groups, including the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC) and Save the Children, say the amendments would mean "no guarantees about when, if ever, payments might begin". They added: "We are calling on all political parties and all MLAs to reject the amendments tabled by the education minister and support the bill as it currently stands." events.title: Nobel memorial prize in economics to be awarded in Stockholm
events.summary: The Nobel memorial prize in economics is the last to be announced this year STOCKHOLM -- The Nobel memorial prize in economics, the final award in this year's cycle, will be announced Monday by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm. Last year, three researchers who study business innovation won for explaining how new products and inventions promote economic growth and human welfare, even as they leave older companies in the dust. The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. The central bank established it in 1968 as a memorial to Nobel, the 19th-century Swedish businessman and chemist who invented dynamite and established the five Nobel Prizes. Nobel purists stress that the economics prize is technically not a Nobel Prize, but it is always presented together with the others on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death in 1896. Nobel honors were announced last week in medicine, physics, chemistry, literature and peace. The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization. events.title: MAS introduces enhanced safeguards around public events by financial institutions
events.summary: Under the enhanced safeguards, financial institutions are expected to conduct public prospecting activities only within designated areas at commercial premises. SINGAPORE – The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) on Oct 12 announced more safeguards around public prospecting activities by financial institutions. This comes as these activities, including roadshows, allow financial institutions and their representatives to engage consumers and market financial products and services in public places, and may cause “concerns” when conducted inappropriately. Such inappropriate conduct includes instances when consumers are subjected to unsolicited or “persistent solicitation”, said the authority. Under the enhanced safeguards, financial institutions are expected to conduct public prospecting activities only within designated areas at commercial premises, and appoint “suitably qualified individuals” to oversee their representatives’ conduct at such events. Representatives must clearly inform consumers at the outset that they intend to market financial products or services, and obtain consumers’ consent before proceeding with the engagement. Street canvassing and door-to-door prospecting will also remain prohibited. The enhanced safeguards follow a public consultation by the authority on proposals to strengthen standards of conduct in this area. Lim Tuang Lee, assistant managing director for capital markets at MAS, said consumers should not feel “pressured or caught off guard” when approached about financial products and services. He added that the enhanced safeguards assist in ensuring that consumers are treated “fairly and professionally”, while allowing financial institutions to continue engaging consumers through appropriate channels. MAS will issue the updated guidelines in 2027, and financial institutions will be given a nine-month transition period to implement the enhanced safeguards thereafter. THE BUSINESS TIMES

events.title: New report highlights 'unacceptable' levels of poverty in the NT
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Territorians 'in crisis' as report shines light on skyrocketing cost of living over past decade Four generations of Shirley Napurrula Miller's family in Central Australia are supporting each other to try to make ends meet. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) New data has revealed the rising cost of essentials is making it harder for people to meet their basic needs in the Northern Territory compared to a decade ago. The report by the NT Council of Social Service examines the changes in the cost of living between 2016 and 2026 across key spending areas of housing, utilities, transport and food. The community sector peak body is recommending federal government welfare payments be increased along with the remote area allowance for people in isolated areas. For an Alice Springs grandmother who receives a disability pension, the struggle to afford groceries between pay cheques is constant, with the cost of food "too high". Shirley Napurrula Miller is among the nearly 50 per cent of the Northern Territory's population who experienced food insecurity because of rising prices in 2025, according to a new report. "Sometimes I can't buy groceries, or meat, or anything," she said. Shirley Napurrula Miller says she struggles to afford the basics for herself and her family. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) The report by the NT Council of Social Service (NTCOSS), released today, examines changes in the cost of living between 2016 and 2026 across key spending areas of housing, utilities, transport and food. It shows every day, across all spending areas, many Territorians are having to make impossible money decisions and weigh up what they must prioritise to live. Hunger relief charity Foodbank Australia estimates that 46 per cent of NT households experienced food insecurity in 2025, above the national average of 33 per cent, according to the NTCOSS report. The report found that while incomes have increased in real terms in the past 10 years, the cost of essentials has too. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) In remote areas, the cost of food is even more prohibitive than in urban centres such as Darwin and Alice Springs, where prices have also risen substantially. "In 2023, the average cost of a healthy food basket was 40 per cent more in remote stores than in a supermarket," the report states. The 10-year comparison report found that while incomes have increased in real terms, the cost of essentials has too, making it harder for everyone — especially those on low incomes — to meet basic needs. Power costs have risen 18 per cent and those on prepaid plans, predominantly First Nations people in urban and remote public housing, are having their electricity cut off more frequently, with an average of 2,284 more disconnections per month last year compared to 2019 to 2020. The report found there were 103,648 involuntary self-disconnections in major centres in the NT last year. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) Further compounding cost pressures for those already on the poverty line, the report states the prepaid electricity price is higher than for standard postpaid billing to account for customers not paying a fixed daily charge. According to the report, there were 103,648 involuntary self-disconnections in major centres in the NT last year. "Affordability challenges are a key driver of such disconnections," the report states. Ms Miller said she had faced disconnection many times and Aboriginal families often lent on each other to share their limited incomes and keep the power on, particularly in the heat over summer. Linda Lechleitner says her electricity bill alone is more than her Centrelink payment. ( ABC News: Xavier Martin ) Her daughter, Linda Lechleitner, who lives between Alice Springs and a remote Aboriginal homeland near the community of Papunya, about a 3-hour drive away, said she worried about electricity costs amid a heating climate. "It's more than the government payment that they give you, the Centrelink payment doesn't carry people through fortnightly," she said. "Every little dollar counts … it's not carrying through to the next fortnight or the next week, they're having to borrow money from family and then pay that back. The report reveals rents have skyrocketed 55 per cent over the past decade. Meanwhile, the NT's social housing stock only increased by 4 per cent between 2017 and 2025, while social housing applications increased by 37 per cent over the same period. The report shows transport costs have also shot up, with an 80-litre tank of diesel now costing $28 more in Darwin and an extra $88 in Alice Springs.

events.title: AI less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says in warning over safety
events.summary: Brad Smith adds to calls for tougher rules governing AI, including ‘kill switches’ and legal obligation to victims of rogue agents Artificial intelligence is less regulated than milk and washing machines, the president of Microsoft has said, as the tech industry warns over the safety of AI. Brad Smith said there should be more safety rules to govern the technology including a legal obligation to a “victim” if their system was breached by rogue AI agents. He told the BBC: “Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.” There are growing calls from experts, politicians and regulators for tougher rules to control AI, as well as warnings from Anthropic, Google DeepMind and OpenAI that the pace of the technology’s development should slow. Smith said AI could be both a “tool and a weapon” that should be regulated urgently. Companies needed “emergency brakes”, also known as “kill switches”, to pause or slow down AI if it grew out of control, he told the BBC. Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is a shareholder in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI, is led by chief executive Satya Nadella. On Saturday, Nadella also called for AI models to have an “emergency brake”. He wrote: “We can’t treat super intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions. “We must build contained systems whose behaviour we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.” His and Smith’s comments came as Britain’s AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, prepared to call on firms developing frontier AI to do more to make sure it is safe. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning In a speech on Monday, Narayan is expected to say companies building AI models should do more to deal with risk and build better safeguards. He will also say the UK government is preparing to legislate to increase oversight of AI, according to reports. Experts have said enemy states could also steal unreleased, powerful AI models. Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK’s AI Security Institute, said that AI companies did “not have security that would prevent an adversarial country from stealing the models”. Meanwhile, cases of rogue AI behaviour continue to come to light. Last week, Anthropic revealed that when it was testing a version of its Claude model, the AI contacted police and falsely claimed it could help solve a murder .

events.title: UK inflation pressures hit three-year high; Nobel prize for economics awarded today – business live
events.summary: Introduction: UK business inflation pressures hits three-year high; Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets, and the world economy. Having missed out on the Nobel Peace Prize , again, Donald Trump is unlikely to trouble the scorers in Stockholm today when the economics equivalent is handed out. Instead, Trump’s Middle Eastern conflict is proving – to no-one’s surprise – that high energy prices fuel inflation, and that geopolitical instability hurts growth. Just this morning, a new report shows that UK businesses are facing the sharpest inflation pressures in three years, due to rising energy, fuel and raw material costs. Accountancy and advisory firm BDO has reported that its inflation index rose to 103.65 in September, up from 102.18 in August and its highest reading since June 2023. These elevated costs and weakening demand are putting renewed pressure on firms ahead of the Autumn Budget, BDO warns. Their report has also found that output fell across UK manufacturing and services last month as domestic demand softened. Scott Knight , head of growth at BDO , says: “Businesses head into this Budget with one clear message: no surprises. Cost pressures continue to squeeze margins, hiring intentions are low and growth is starting to plateau. Firms are not looking for grand interventions, but they do need certainty. Right now, concerns about further downside risks outweigh expectations of positive change.” The oil price has dropped slightly this morning, though, after Trump declared that Ukraine and Russia have agreed to halt attacks on each other’s energy facilities following the US diesel-supply deal with Moscow announced on Friday night. Brent crude had been down around 2% a few hours ago – but it’s now just 0.25% lower at $104.46 a barrel, a fairly small move really. Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com , explains why: A highly contentious US deal with Russia to allow the export of more diesel to ease pressure in the market for the critical industrial fuel helped slightly with optics. But the true impact is piecemeal, especially as Middle East refining remains heavily compromised and Ukrainian forces strategically strike Russian refineries. From 10.45am BST: Nobel Prize for economics announced 2pm BST: Russia’s trade balance for August 18m ago EU sets cap on imports of hybrid EVs from China 1h ago IFS warns UK faces £35bn budget shortfall 2h ago Who might win the Nobel prize for economics today? 2h ago Introduction: UK business inflation pressures hits three-year high; EU sets cap on imports of hybrid EVs from China Newsflash: The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electrical vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, senior officials have confirmed in Brussels. Exports of hybrids have been soaring in the last two years with about 800,000 battery and plug in hybrids expected to be sold this year. The EU expects that the quota will halve China’s market share, which currently stands at 6%, in a four-year agreement made in Beijing last week. Recruitment firm Hays are suffering this morning after reporting a drop in fee income over the last three months. Hays , which earns revenue by successfully placing a candidate into a job opening, says there was “ongoing fragility in Northern Europe”. Mark Dearnley , Hays ’ chief executive officer, says: In line with our expectations, the decline in Group net fees eased to 3% in Q1 driven by good Temp & Contracting growth in several of our countries. Perm activity remains mixed with sustained strong growth in North America but ongoing fragility in Northern Europe . Our medium term targets can be achieved through our own actions and we were pleased to make continued good progress with our structural cost and productivity initiatives during the quarter.” Stocks have opened higher in London this morning, where the FTSE 100 share index is up 53 points, or +0.5%, at 10,604 points. Banks are leading the risers, with HSBC up 2.1% and Standard Chartered 1.8% higher. The Fight Inequality Alliance is calling on finance ministers attending the IMF/World Bank meeting in Bangkok to consider debt cancellation measures to help the Global South. They insist that “the era of austerity is over”, and demand an end to the lending rules that force governments to pay creditors before they pay for hospitals, schools and food. FIA General Secretary Jenny Ricks said: “The IMF and World Bank are legacy institutions still writing the economic rules for the rest of the world. Their austerity programmes force governments to cut funding from hospitals and schools while every dollar sent to creditors is a dollar taken from a classroom, a clinic or a family’s food budget. Cancel the debt, tax the super-rich, and stop making ordinary people pay for a crisis they didn’t create. “Bangkok will deliver more of the same. The era of the IMF and World Bank is over.

events.title: AI is less regulated than milk, says Microsoft president
events.summary: Microsoft boss: 'If a company builds AI agents and they break loose, there should be a legal obligation to tell the victim' Published 12 October 2026, 00:07 BST Milk and washing machines are currently more regulated than AI, the president of Microsoft has said. Brad Smith said there needed to be global safety rules in place, including a legal obligation to tell a "victim" if their system is breached by a rogue AI agent as well as deciding when outside evaluators should sign off on an AI product before it is released. His comments put him at odds with President Donald Trump, who said the sector should regulate itself so US firms don't lose out to Chinese rivals. But Smith said: "Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection." Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector said they believed the technology is a threat to humanity. The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown , but Trump has pushed against this. Speaking to the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast, Smith called AI both a "tool and a weapon" that urgently needed to be regulated. "Let's get started today," he said. He said firms need "emergency brakes" – often known in the industry as 'kill switches' – to pause or slowdown AI if it got out of control in some way. He also said there should be a legal requirement for firms to write "incident reports" and tell victims if the technology goes rogue. He also suggested that independent government evaluators should vet new AI technology. "We know how to do this for other products," Smith said. "We should build on that knowledge and think about how to apply it to AI." Smith said the UK was best placed to drive forward these global rules for AI because of its AI Security Institute , external , launched during former prime minister Rishi Sunak's government as the AI Safety Institute. "In the world of technology, in the tech sector, most people that I know would say, if you ask them, name the country that is the leader in having this technical capability, they would say, it's very simple. It's the United Kingdom. They are the best." Smith's views are very different to those of his president, who believes the US should be going full-steam ahead on AI. Trump has repeatedly said that "whoever wins AI, wins". However, Smith does not believe the US government would be as opposed to UK-led AI regulations as Trump's comments make it seem, suggesting the US would be more accepting of the UK making standards than the EU. "In Washington DC, people don't look at the UK and they don't look at London the way they look at Brussels – that's a strength," he said. "When you look at AI agents that have escaped human control, when you look at models that are so powerful that they're putting the world's cybersecurity at risk. I would say: The moment has arrived. "Let's speak calmly, maybe even softly, but firmly, and start to bring people together. I hope that's the role we can play as a company. I hope that's the role the UK can play as a country." Big Boss Interview: Microsoft's Brad Smith The president of the tech giant calls for global rules on AI, and says the UK is in the "best position" to lead the charge. At the end of last month, Trump hosted the leaders of US tech giants OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, SpaceX, Meta, and Google at the White House where the executives signed a "morally binding" document . The companies agreed to work with "independent auditors" to assess whether their AI systems are working as intended and make sure they do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways". Smith said he applauds the statement and Microsoft is "happy to sign it". "It's a good step, it's a necessary step... But I don't think it's sufficient any longer." He added that the challenge for any "self-regulatory regime" is that "the good companies will do what you want". "It's the companies that are not as responsible that you need to worry about." events.title: Healey faces £35bn Budget challenge to meet spending pledges, says think tank
events.summary: Published 12 October 2026, 00:04 BST Chancellor John Healey faces having to find £35bn to avoid cuts to public spending while meeting defence promises in his first Budget on 28 October, an influential think tank has warned. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said that if the government wants to increase defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030 and lift health spending without squeezing other departments, it will need a "top-up" of billions of pounds. Higher inflation, caused by the Iran war, could eat into what the government hoped to spend on public services, meaning Healey will have to choose between spending cuts, tax rises, or a mixture of both, the IFS warned. The IFS urged the government to ensure its spending plans are credible, as opposed to proposing unrealistic future cuts to make the Budget add up. The government is under growing pressure to show financial markets that it has a tight grip on finances as the cost of borrowing rises. The IFS cautioned Healey about making any spending announcements in the 28 October Budget speech he has no intention of honouring. "A 'steady-as-she-goes' Budget is not an option available to the chancellor," said IFS director Helen Miller. "Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments' spending plans off course. "Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the Budget a work of fiction," she added. Speaking ahead of the annual International Monetary Fund meeting this week, Healey said: "The consequences of conflict in the Middle East and Europe are hitting countries worldwide, leading to higher prices at the pumps and more expensive mortgages at home. "But Britain and our allies can face up to these challenges together." He said his Budget "will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience" and give people "breathing space". Miller told the BBC's Today programme that Healey has inherited spending plans for government departments where spending growth would slow in the coming years. "[It] already looked likely that he would have to make spending cuts just to live within those," she said. "Now, along comes the Middle East war, inflation goes up and those spending plans look very tight indeed." Added to that, the chancellor has said he wants to get defence spending up to 3% of national income. Under Keir Starmer's leadership, Healey resigned as defence secretar y in June in a battle with the Treasury over military spending. Miller said: "You put all that together, if he wanted to do all of that within current spending plans he's looking at having to cut some other services by something like £35bn." The chancellor does not have to address spending totals in this Budget, and may choose to leave such decisions until future events - for example, next year's Spring Statement or Spending Review - by which time the outlook for the economy could look very different. But the IFS warned not addressing it would cast doubt on the credibility of the government's plans. Previous chancellors have relied on a similar strategy of pencilling in unrealistic future spending plans to ensure that they meet the fiscal rules on the day - only to change the plans further down the line. Miller said Healey's focus on fiscal discipline was a "good first start but what he needs to do is not just say he's going to cut borrowing in coming years but actually deliver on those plans." The US-Israel war against Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine have together helped drive up energy prices around the world. These higher costs have been passed to customers via higher prices on shelves and at the pumps. The wars have also contributed to a rise in the cost of UK government debt interest payments, adding to the pressure on Healey. Although higher inflation will boost tax revenues, it will also eat into the value of departments' cash budgets, the IFS said. Like other analysts, the IFS thinks recent turbulence on bond markets and higher inflation will add around £10bn to forecasts for the government's borrowing costs in 2029-30. However, it still expects the government to meet its self-imposed fiscal rules - that it will only borrow for investment projects by the financial year 2029-30 and also be reducing debt as a percentage of GDP - not least as inflation pushes up tax revenues. But it expects those rules to be met by a smaller buffer - known as "headroom" - of around £20bn. That is less than the £24bn buffer predicted at the time of the Spring Statement by the official forecaster, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR). Recent indications have been that the markets would be comfortable with that degree of reduced headroom. The IFS also expects any "breathing space" help for households to be temporary and limited in scale. However, the IFS warns that in such a volatile environment, its forecasts are exceptionally uncertain.

events.title: Alvarez vs M’billi boxing bout to go ahead in Saudi Arabia despite attacks
events.summary: Mexican boxer tells Turki Al-Sheikh he ‘fears nothing’ and will face M’billi in Riyadh on October 31 ‘no matter what’. The world title fight featuring Saul “Canelo” ‌‌Alvarez and Christian M’billi will go ahead this month in Saudi Arabia despite attacks on the country’s airports, which have killed at least 14 people in Riyadh in two days, Saudi sports promoter Turki Al-Sheikh confirms. Alvarez vs M’billi is scheduled for October 31 in the Saudi capital, which has repeatedly come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis, but Al-Sheikh sought to allay the doubts over the bout on Sunday. One person was killed and 11 were injured on Sunday when a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA). A Houthi strike on the same airport on Saturday killed 13 people and injured more than 300, making it the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The Houthis claimed responsibility for all four strikes on Saudi airports before Sunday’s attack, which has yet to be claimed by any group. Alvarez, who has held multiple world titles across several weight classes, will face WBC super-middleweight champion M’billi in a highly anticipated bout. “Canelo reached out ⁠⁠and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens,” Al-Sheikh, chairman of Saudi Arabia’s General Entertainment Authority, wrote in a social media post. “He [Alvarez] fears nothing.” The ‌‌Mexican boxer, a former two-time undisputed super-middleweight champion, has not fought since he was ‌‌beaten ‌‌by American Terence Crawford in September 2025.

events.title: AI investment boom offsets energy shock to keep global growth at 3%, IMF chief says
events.summary: Strong investment ⁠in AI infrastructure is keeping global growth at about 3 per cent, yielding major ​benefits for many Asian economies that supply the hardware, such as Thailand, International Monetary Fund managing director Kristalina Georgieva said on Monday. The artificial ⁠intelligence investment boom was already delivering a “demand shock, an investment shock” that could boost growth in advanced Asian economies by a half to one full percentage point, and emerging Asian economies by 0.2 to 0.8 percentage point, she said. “AI, love it, hate it. It's already here,” Ms Georgieva said. “That ⁠shift into higher gear is what is keeping the world economy growing at around 3 per cent, despite the fact we are ​being dragged down ⁠by the energy supply shock,” she told ‌hundreds of participants on the first day of a week-long series of meetings of the IMF and World Bank in the ​Thai capital. The IMF in July forecast global growth at 3 per cent in 2026. It will release an updated outlook on Tuesday. About 18,000 people are expected to attend the meetings this week, including finance officials from the IMF's 191 members. Several ministers will skip the meeting to focus on domestic priorities, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Spanish Finance Minister Arcadi Espana, sources said. Profound consequences Ms Georgieva said AI amounted to a “slow-moving tsunami” that would have profound consequences for jobs, growth, education and even how governments generate revenue through taxation, given the expected shift from labour to capital. The IMF estimates that AI could lead to 40 per cent of jobs being augmented, downgraded or eliminated, over time, she said. An initial study showed that 10 per cent of jobs in the US already required AI skills. While routine, repetitive jobs were shrinking, low-paying jobs were increasing in two lower-paying sectors, construction and data centres. “It is a transformative technology . It so completely changes how we work, how we live,” she said, noting that an AI assistant now gave her a ​30-second message about her schedule each day. The US, China and India are the most important ‌producers in the AI supply chain, but many of ⁠the firms building the needed infrastructure are in Asia , Ms Georgieva ​said, referring to Thailand, host of this year's annual meetings. Impact on entry-level jobs World Bank President Ajay Banga, who ​has made jobs ‌a central focus of his presidency, said the development bank was focused on leveraging “small AI”, which is not dependent on large language models, to generate ⁠enormous productivity gains for farmers, healthcare systems, educators and others in emerging markets. Singapore's President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, speaking at the same event, ⁠said governments should address how AI was reducing job opportunities for graduates. “There is a particular problem that we have to address very soon … and that is that, the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand,” he said. Mr Shanmugaratnam said the world should also guard against AI resulting in a “new divergence” in growth and job creation between ​developing and advanced economies. “AI is going to widen the divergence if we are too passive about it,” he said. “So we've got to do everything we can to first use AI to create good jobs and to create jobs that can be done well by human beings, can allow them to ride up a career ladder despite AI.”

events.title: Human judgment and intentional outcomes are vital in AI use: DBS, TikTok CEOs
events.summary: DBS Bank CEO Tan Su Shan during the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference at Suntec Convention and Exhibition Centre on Oct 12. SINGAPORE – Applying artificial intelligence is not enough – it has to be harnessed towards intentional business and work outcomes, said DBS chief executive Tan Su Shan on Oct 12. Human judgment is also vital in AI usage, said TikTok CEO Chew Shou Zi. The CEOs were speaking separately at the inaugural DBS Asia Future Forward Conference at the Suntec Singapore Convention and Exhibition Centre. Organised by DBS, the new flagship event brings together global leaders across technology, business and investment to examine the forces shaping the region’s future. In this first edition, the focus was on artificial intelligence (AI) and how such technology is transforming industries, business models and the nature of work. Tan spoke about Asia’s emergence as a region and how it has proven that AI can be brought to everyday use cases, from enterprises to solving health issues and supporting finance. “I think Asia’s proven and shown that we are able to use AI for good business outcomes and good human outcomes - whether it’s to help the elderly at home, whether it’s to redesign workflows,” she said during her opening address. She added that simply applying AI is not good enough. “We call that AI lipstick. That’s not going to work,” Tan said. “What we have to do is we really have to rethink our workflows and our work processes so that we can truly unlock our potential. So just adding AI in it might help marginally, but it’s not going to change the way we work.” She made these remarks in conjunction with the release of a DBS report on AI outcomes. The report noted that as AI capability becomes more widely available, technical advantage becomes harder to sustain. “Competitive advantage increasingly depends on identifying important problems, earning the trust required for adoption and connecting intelligence to real-world outcomes,” it said. The report said that businesses can start with the intended outcome. “Redesign workflows, partnerships and operating systems around that outcome, then demonstrate that it improves organisational performance and delivers measurable value for customers,” it said. It added that for Asia, the challenge is to turn regional strengths into shared advantage. Tan also said in her speech that countries need to be better connected with one another, and mentioned agreements such as the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) signed by 15 Asia-Pacific countries, and the Future of Investment and Trade (FIT) Partnership, which was co-convened by New Zealand, Singapore, Switzerland and the United Arab Emirates. Better connections have to be made, even while countries become increasingly protectionist, Tan said. She noted that AI depends on everyone trading with one another, because each country has its own niche area. For instance, Taiwan has the semiconductor foundries, South Korea has the memory components, and the raw materials come from China and South-east Asia. “So if we don’t cooperate, we will continue to have blockages in our AI supply chain. Even if we want sovereignty, you need to have some trade cooperation,” Tan added. “So stay connected, but keep your sovereignty with your models or data. We have sovereignty, but we also stay connected.” She added that AI has created both visions of a dystopian future where technology takes over, or a utopia where AI helps to solve many issues. “What we need now is for humans to exercise good judgment, good wisdom, good creativity to ensure that this AI journey that we take together as a human race will take us up the right path,” Tan said. Chew said during a panel discussion that human judgment is also important in AI. He brought up the “paperclip example”, which suggests that if a machine is asked to produce more paperclips, it ends up doing only that one thing at the expense of everything else. “My view is that in the next two to three years, we’re going to have a real scientific breakthrough: physics, biotech, chemistry, material science, because of AI,” he said. TikTok CEO Chew Shou Zi speaking at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference at Suntec Convention and Exhibition Centre on Oct 12. “It’s very, very, very possible. And if that happens, then you know the question will be: How do you align the models? How do you align the machines to be doing things that is obvious to us as human beings?” he said. events.title: If Netanyahu goes, does anything really change for Palestinians?
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Analysts say opposition victory in October 27 polls may bring only marginal change and no fundamental shift on Gaza or West Bank. Four rival Israeli political movements have agreed to work together in a bid to unseat Israel’s longest serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. The factions – the Yashar party, the Democrats, the Yisrael Beytenu party and the Together alliance – span different parts of Israel’s political spectrum but say they are united in their goal to “preserve and strengthen Israel as a Jewish and democratic state”. list 1 of 3 Israel election double standard: Arab leader forced out, far right cleared list 2 of 3 Israeli barrier cuts off water to West Bank Palestinians before elections list 3 of 3 Israel could’ve ended Gaza war, freed captives sooner: Israel ex-negotiator The opposition grouping is in a close battle with a pro-Netanyahu coalition heading into the October 27 elections , recent polling indicated, although neither side appeared on track to win a parliamentary majority. The election comes as Israel faces a series of domestic crises that are tearing at its social fabric, including questions over political accountability for alleged corruption and security failures , disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service and efforts to exclude Arab parties from political life . The country also faces growing backlash abroad , including from allies, over its continuing attacks on Gaza and Lebanon as well as settlements, which are illegal under international law, and settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank. Analysts said the combination makes the upcoming elections among the most consequential in Israel’s history but even an opposition victory may bring only marginal change for Palestinians suffering record levels of settler violence and mass displacement. While the opposition alliance has taken Netanyahu to task personally, there is little daylight between them when it comes to Israel’s foundational policies in Gaza and the West Bank. “Palestinians should not expect a fundamental change in Israeli policy if the Netanyahu bloc loses power,” said analyst Samer Jaber, a doctoral researcher specialising in political economy at Royal Holloway, University of London. “The major political blocs share core positions on the Palestinian question, including support for the existing settlement structure, while the state institutions that formulate and implement policy would remain unchanged,” he added. What is the anti-Netanyahu coalition? The leaders of the four major Jewish-led opposition movements gathered on September 26 and signed a declaration promising not to attack each other in the run-up to the elections and to collaborate in forming a government after the vote. In addition to Yair Lapid, who leads the official opposition in Israel’s Knesset, the meeting included Gadi Eisenkot, who heads the Yashar party; Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together alliance , cofounded by Lapid; Avigdor Lieberman, who heads Yisrael Beiteinu; and Yair Golan, who leads the Democrats. The declaration does not set out an official leader although Eisenkot is viewed as the opposition’s most likely candidate for prime minister. In a joint statement, the figures said defeating the current government was their “shared highest objective”. Of the four opposition parties, Yashar is projected to be the strongest. A recent poll by Israel’s Channel 12 suggested Yashar would win 23 seats in parliament, the most of any party and more than the 21 seats projected for Netanyahu’s Likud. Trailing is the Together alliance, projected to win 13 seats, followed by Yisrael Beiteinu and the Democrats, each projected to win nine. That would give the opposition a combined 54 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, seven short of a majority. Netanyahu’s alliance, which includes several ultra-Orthodox and far-right parties, is projected to win 49 seats. Arab-led parties, representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population, are projected to win 13 seats, but most leaders of the Jewish-led opposition bloc have ruled out joining forces with them. Roi Zur, an assistant professor at the University of Essex who leads a research project on Israeli parties’ political ideology and policy, said the anti-Netanyahu coalition has a chance to win if turnout is on its side, noting that several parties that do not “strictly oppose” the prime minister could fall below the 3.25 percent threshold to enter the Knesset, shaking up the balance. “If these parties waste enough right-wing votes, the opposition might translate their support into power,” Zur told Al Jazeera. “But this might not be enough.” Even if the opposition alliance manages to find a way to oust Netanyahu, it would likely be weak and incapable – or unwilling – to overhaul Israeli policy in the West Bank and Gaza, analysts said.

events.title: China’s domestic car sales downturn continues, exports retain momentum
events.summary: Chery and Leapmotor vehicles at a Chinese auto show in Buenos Aires on Oct 2. BEIJING - China’s domestic car sales extended their decline for a 12th successive month, while exports remained a key growth driver as automakers looked overseas to cushion the impact of a sluggish home market. Passenger vehicle sales fell 28.1% from a year earlier to 1.63 million units in September, worsening from a 23.7% decline in August, data from the China Passenger Car Association showed on Monday. Annual car exports jumped 73.2% to 923,000 vehicles last month, versus a 77.5% rise in August. Sales of battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids at home slid 16.7% from the year before to 1.08 million units, compared with a 10.1% fall in August. The segment’s export growth quickened to 163.5% from August’s 154.7%. Any curbs on plug-in hybrid exports are unlikely to significantly affect overall new energy vehicle exports, given the dominant role of pure EVs, said Cui Dongshu, secretary-general at CPCA. China and the EU have reached a deal that could halve Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the bloc over four years, EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic said on Oct 9, though volume limits and terms for shipments above those quotas remain unclear. Shrinking domestic sales reflect broader economic weakness, with subdued consumer spending and a prolonged property downturn weighing on demand. Regulators have shifted focus from growth to safety and value, proposing rules that would curb rushed vehicle launches lacking sufficient validation. REUTERS

events.title: Startup Funding: Q3 2026
events.summary: AI dominated funding in the third quarter of 2026, with two inference companies each announcing $1 billion in funding. But with the data center buildout driving insatiable demand for memory, investors also rewarded startups with alternatives to costly, capacity-limited HBM. Some are building on commodity DRAM or holding models in on-chip SRAM, while others stack memory directly onto compute. Data movement at all levels of the stack remains a critical bottleneck, too. Interconnect technologies, networking chips, and photonics were the most active areas of the quarter, with startups tackling the problem with diverse approaches ranging from manufacturing-ready co-packaged optics, millimeter-wave RF signals over plastic waveguides, and ferroelectric glass modulators to optical couplers printed directly onto chips and coherent DSPs designed specifically for AI optics. Nearly $7.5 billion of the quarter’s total was directed to just 22 startups that raised $100 million or more, including eight that saw investors return within roughly a year, some more than doubling the previous round. Plus, agentic EDA and AI-generated analog layout, small chip fabs, diamond-based defect inspection, large-area nanoimprint lithography, and memory-safe microcontrollers feature in this look at 80 companies that collectively raised over $8.5 billion in Q3 2026. Rowe Price , Union Group , and Valor Equity Partners . Xsight Labs designs fully programmable data processing units (DPUs) and Ethernet switches for hyperscale, edge, and AI data center networks. Built on open standards, its DPU runs native Linux, DPDK, and SONiC and uses 64 Arm Neoverse N2 cores that sit directly in the data path to process millions of connections per second at full 800 Gbps line rate. The company’s 12.8 Tbps Ethernet switch operates at deterministic, sub-700ns latency under 200W. Funds will be used to accelerate the company’s roadmap, add support for emerging Ultra Ethernet Consortium standards, hire, and scale manufacturing. Founded in 2017, it is based in Tel Aviv, Israel. Celero Communications raised $275.0M in Series C funding led by Atreides Management , Valor Equity Partners , and CapitalG , with participation from Sutter Hill Ventures and Maverick Silicon . Celero develops coherent DSPs for AI optical interconnects. Rather than adapting a long-haul coherent design, the company built a DSP architecture optimized for low power and low latency, paired with new analog circuitry connecting the DSP to the optical system that it says is designed to scale to higher bandwidth over multiple generations. The architecture targets scale-up, scale-out, and scale-across connectivity from 1.6T to next-gen 3.2T. Celero has validated 2nm coherent DSP silicon, including the DSP processing and analog technology. Funds will go to accelerating the product roadmap, R&D, and production readiness. Founded in 2024, it is based in Irvine, California, USA, and has raised $415M to date. Cornelis raised $205.0M in funding . Cornelis builds scale-out networking for AI and HPC, spanning SuperNICs, switches, and open-source software built around its own switch silicon. Its 400 Gb/s system uses credit-based flow control and fine-grained adaptive routing, which the company says makes the fabric lossless and congestion-free. The company is sampling an 800G SuperNIC that supports Omni-Path, RoCEv2, and Ultra Ethernet concurrently. Cornelis is extending into scale-up networking with programmable in-fabric compute built on UALink and ESUN, an approach it says lets the network offload collective operations. Funds will be used to scale production. Founded in 2020 as a spin-out of Intel’s high-performance interconnect business, it is based in Wayne, Pennsylvania, USA. Eliyan raised $145.0M in Series C funding led by Seligman Ventures , with participation from Cisco Investments , Lumentum , and other new and existing investors. Eliyan develops die-to-die, chip-to-chip, and rack-to-rack PHY and chiplet interconnect technology designed for AI systems with advanced package-level integration, multi-package scale-up architectures, memory expansion, and emerging high-bandwidth infrastructure fabrics. Available for both standard and advanced packaging, the protocol-agnostic PHY supports BoW and UCIe as well as simultaneous bidirectional signaling, which transmits and receives on the same wire at once to double bandwidth per interface. For die-to-memory applications, the company says its PHY delivers the bandwidth requirements for HBM on standard organic packaging with 90um and above bump pitch. Funds will be used to develop next-generation interconnect products, scale manufacturing, and expand into electro-optical interconnects. Founded in 2021, it is based in Santa Clara, California, USA. Delos Data raised over $100.0M in funding from Matrix Partners , Playground Global , Socratic Partners , Capricorn Investment Group , Matter Venture Partners , IAG Capital Partners , and others. Delos Data builds a reference architecture for composing AI inference clusters from mixed hardware, models, and topologies, with a data interface between every endpoint. The interface silicon comes in three multi-protocol form factors: a 30+ Tbps I/O chiplet for GPUs, XPUs, and accelerators; 10+ Tbps near-packaged optics; and a 400+ Gbps card for CPUs, flash, and memory. Sitting between each endpoint and the network, it can detect failures first and manage recovery in hardware. A disaggregated scale-up server is planned to sample at the end of 2026. events.title: Nearly 70 million kids now have a Trump Account—but parents have to claim it first. Here’s who gets the $1,000
events.summary: The Trump administration says nearly every child in America now has a Trump Account. Whether the money in those accounts ever adds up to much is a different question. The Treasury Department announced Oct. 1 that it had finished automatically enrolling eligible children in the tax-advantaged investment accounts, creating accounts for more than 60 million kids who didn’t already have one. Combined with the families who signed up on their own, that brings the total to nearly 70 million accounts, according to the White House . “Today, I’m pleased to announce that every single eligible minor child in America has now been automatically enrolled in a Trump Account,” President Donald Trump said at an Oval Office event on Oct. 7. But having an account doesn’t mean it’s ready to use. A parent or guardian still has to claim it through the official Trump Accounts app before they can manage it, accept contributions from family and friends, or collect the government’s $1,000 seed deposit for eligible children. The switch to automatic enrollment followed slow uptake. Before the change, Treasury had processed about 5.6 million sign-up forms, less than a tenth of the roughly 73.4 million children eligible, InvestmentNews reported . Fortune previously reported that some families who signed up early were still waiting on their promised $1,000 . Where the money is coming from Since the program launched on July 4, more than $4.5 billion has been deposited into Trump Accounts, including $1.3 billion in government seed contributions, more than $600 million from family and friends, and $2.6 billion in philanthropic gifts, according to the White House. Spread across nearly 70 million accounts, that averages out to about $64 per child. Much of the philanthropic money comes from Michael and Susan Dell’s $6.25 billion pledge, which provides $250 to up to 25 million children age 10 and under who live in ZIP codes with median household incomes below $150,000. More than 70 companies have also signed on to contribute to employees’ children’s accounts, the White House said, following early commitments from firms like JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America . The administration has pitched the accounts as a path to serious wealth. The calculator on TrumpAccounts.gov projects that a lone $1,000 seed could grow to $243,000 by age 55, and that an account receiving the $5,000 annual maximum could reach $13 million. Those numbers assume the S&P 500 returns more than 10% a year without interruption for 55 years. Financial planners who spoke with Fortune put more conservative estimates at roughly $1.5 million to $2 million by 55 for a maxed-out account, assuming a 7% return. Stock gifts, with strings attached Most money in Trump Accounts goes into low-cost index funds . But Treasury said in July it would also accept large philanthropic donations of publicly traded stock, and the IRS released a rule on Sept. 30 setting the procedures. Qualifying stock is transferred to Treasury and allocated to eligible children according to donor instructions and Treasury guidance. “By accepting contributions of publicly traded stock, Treasury is creating a practical pathway for large-scale private giving to support the next generation,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a July statement . The rules are narrow. Stock donations can come from companies or charities set up by stockholders, not from relatives, and must be spread across at least 5,000 accounts in a qualified geographic area, according to Yahoo Finance . The shares must be held for at least five years before they can be sold. SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell is among the first to use the option, pledging one share each to more than 2 million children’s accounts. Single-stock gifts can give children a stake in corporate growth, but they also concentrate risk. “A child could, hypothetically, receive $10,000 of Company X stock and suddenly at least 67% of the minor’s portfolio is concentrated in Company X,” U.S. Bank wealth management advisor Jonathan Lee told Yahoo Finance. Who benefits most Critics argue the program’s biggest winners will be families who can afford to contribute. “The program may be open to every child, but its benefits will flow overwhelmingly to families with the means to contribute thousands of dollars a year,” Stanford economists Neale Mahoney and Adam Shaw wrote in Time last December. Researchers at The New School reached a similar conclusion in an analysis for Fortune , based on 15 years of 529 college savings data. The White House counters that about 80% of Trump Accounts are linked to families earning less than $200,000 a year. Who is eligible and how to claim an account Every child under 18 with a valid Social Security number now has an account. The government’s one-time $1,000 seed contribution, however, is limited to U.S. citizen children born between Jan. 1, 2025, and Dec. 31, 2028, and the account must be claimed for the child to receive it. Parents and guardians can claim accounts through the Trump Accounts app for iOS and Android; more information is available at TrumpAccounts.gov. Once an account is claimed, family and friends can contribute up to $5,000 a year combined, while employers can add up to $2,500 annually. The government’s $1,000 seed and certain contributions from state and local governments and nonprofits don’t count toward the $5,000 cap. When a child turns 18, the account essentially becomes a traditional IRA. Withdrawals are taxed as ordinary income, and early withdrawals may face penalties unless they’re used for qualifying expenses such as education or a first home, so families should review the tax rules before deciding how to use the money. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: The IEA wants to empty its oil reserves faster. A federal watchdog says the US isn’t ready for what comes next
events.summary: Governments are tapping their emergency oil faster than ever, and the room to keep doing so is shrinking. On Oct. 7, member governments of the International Energy Agency backed speeding up the oil stock releases they pledged under the agency’s March 2026 Collective Action, aiming to finish them as soon as possible. They also agreed to prioritize diesel, given how tight that market has become. According to Reuters , JPMorgan analysts read the move as an acceleration of barrels already promised, not a fresh intervention. The March action was historic on its own. In response to the Iran war and the disruption of tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, IEA members agreed to make 400 million barrels of oil available to the market . It was only the sixth collective action since the agency’s founding in 1974, and by far the largest. Seven months later, the buffer is visibly thinner. IEA governments still hold roughly 1.1 billion barrels of publicly held emergency stocks, including more than 200 million barrels of diesel, the agency says. In March, that figure was more than 1.2 billion barrels . Including company inventories, Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser estimated this week that more than 1 billion barrels have been pulled from stockpiles worldwide. The G7 steps in The IEA’s move followed an Oct. 2 videoconference of G7 leaders convened by French President Emmanuel Macron. In a joint statement , leaders said they had agreed on coordinated measures to “stabilize immediate energy supplies, shield households and businesses from price shocks.” The core of the plan is a coordinated release of 100 million barrels through the IEA over four months, with a large share of diesel front-loaded into the first 20 days. The G7 also pledged to stagger refinery maintenance so plants don’t go offline at the same time. Members said they would push refiners to run harder where feasible and encourage countries with significant refining capacity to boost diesel output. They also reaffirmed that they would not restrict energy exports among themselves. Diesel is the pressure point. Damage to refineries and disrupted shipping from the wars in Iran and Ukraine have pushed diesel to record highs in many markets , feeding directly into trucking, farming, and freight costs. On Sunday, IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote to member governments ahead of the agency’s Oct. 15 Governing Board meeting. He urged all of them, including those that have already completed their pledged releases, to consider whether more diesel needs to come out of storage. America’s reserve is running low and getting old In the U.S., the strain is showing in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The Trump administration began a 172 million-barrel emergency release in March as its share of the IEA effort. The SPR has since fallen to about 284 million barrels, its lowest level since 1982 , and is on track to drop to roughly 243 million once the final barrels are delivered. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has warned that drawing the reserve down too far could damage the salt caverns where the oil is stored. That is a sharp reversal from the administration’s earlier pledge to refill the SPR “right to the top.” A report from the Government Accountability Office, published in May and released publicly in June , suggests the problems run deeper than inventory levels. GAO found that DOE has released more than 500 million barrels of crude from the SPR since 1985, more than half for emergencies such as wars. Nearly 70% of all releases occurred between 2014 and 2025. Before this year, the largest drawdown on record was the 180 million-barrel emergency sale in 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine. That pace has collided with aging infrastructure. GAO found that investment in the reserve isn’t keeping up with its needs, leaving a growing maintenance backlog. DOE itself has warned that aging equipment will increasingly limit the SPR’s ability to carry out fill or drawdown orders. The bigger gap, GAO argues, is strategic. DOE hasn’t completed a long-term review of the SPR since 2016, and Congress has never set a target size. “Without an updated long-term plan or target size for the SPR, DOE and Congress are making operational and investment decisions amidst uncertainty about what the SPR is capable of at present, what it should be capable of in the future to meet changing U.S. needs and obligations, and what investments and other actions may be required to bridge any gaps,” the report states. GAO urged Congress to require DOE to complete long-term SPR plans on a set timeline. It also recommended that DOE reassess the technical criteria governing how fast the reserve can be drawn down and refilled. DOE concurred with the recommendations. What happens next Under IEA rules, member countries must hold oil stocks equivalent to at least 90 days of net imports . Net exporters are exempt. Governments have wide latitude in how they meet that obligation, using some mix of government-held reserves, dedicated stockholding agencies, and stocks that industry is required to keep. The harder question is how and when those stocks get rebuilt. The G7 asked the IEA to deliver a follow-up report within 20 days with recommendations to improve future responses, including how to replenish stocks. IEA governments will review the situation again at the Oct. 15 Governing Board meeting. Refilling won’t be cheap or quick. Analysts have noted that governments rebuilding their reserves after the war, possibly to levels above where they stood before it, would create a new layer of oil demand on top of normal consumption. That could keep prices elevated long after the shooting stops. For now, governments are leaning on a cushion they’ve already worn thin. As the IEA put it, it stands ready to release more “if and when required.” The question is how much is left to give. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: European, Chinese automakers launch product blitz at Paris car show in fight for market share
events.summary: The DS F3VER concept car, by DS Automobiles, at a Stellantis NV presentation ahead of the Paris Motor Show in Meudon, France on Oct 11. PARIS - European and Chinese automakers were expected to unveil as many as 60 new models at the Paris car show on Oct 12, as the fight for car buyers’ attention on the continent continues to intensify. This year’s show comes just days after the European Union announced a deal with China that could cut Chinese imports of hybrid vehicles to the bloc by more than half, though it did not provide details on how the agreement will be implemented. Around 20 Chinese brands are attending this year’s show, including BYD and Chery, double their presence at the last Paris car show in 2024 as they face a gruelling EV price war and falling sales at home. Chinese brands have gained share rapidly in Europe in the last three years. According to a client note issued by Jefferies on Oct 11, the EU-China deal could hit BYD, Chery and state-owned SAIC’s MG brand hardest as between them they accounted for 90% of Chinese brand hybrid sales in the EU in the first eight months of 2026. Speaking at an event late on Oct 11, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume welcomed progress in EU-China trade talks, adding: “Europe must still ensure a level playing field in its own markets.” “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe too,” Blume added, at a venue festooned with blue EU flags. As part of its bid to regain lost market share in Europe, world No. 4 automaker Stellantis alone is launching six new models across its European brands at the show and unveiling nine concept cars, a remarkable turnaround after years of maintaining a low-key presence at shows on the continent. During a high-profile event on Oct 11, Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa promised attendees they would “witness the reinvention of a European icon,” with an affordable retro electric version of the iconic Citroen 2CV aimed at fending off Chinese competition. “Our great brands never stand still,” Filosa said. Like other Western car shows, Paris had been in decline until Chinese automakers started showing up in Europe in force four years ago. Alongside automakers like BYD and Chery, this year’s show will feature new Chinese brands like Aito, while state-owned automaker Changan will launch two new brands - Nevo and Avatr. The EU imposed tariffs on Chinese-made fully electric vehicles in October 2024. The European Commission is also working on legislation that would include “Made in Europe” provisions mandating minimum local content in EVs to gain access to large parts of the EU’s car market. Major Chinese automakers have been looking for European production ahead of “Made in Europe”, often in partnership with legacy automakers. In July, China’s Geely Auto said it will produce electric SUVs at a Ford Motor factory in Spain. Speaking at an event on a floating gallery on the River Seine on Oct 11, Geely Auto CEO Alex Nan emphasised the automaker’s deepening partnership with French automaker Renault and the company’s “commitment to Europe”. Car sales in China, the world’s largest car market, fell 20% in the first half of 2026, increasing the pressure on Chinese automakers to grow sales overseas. As the US market is effectively closed to China’s auto industry, Europe is the top priority for its automakers. “If they drop exports in Europe, they die because they can’t make the money elsewhere,” said Francois Roudier, secretary general of the International Organisation of Motor Vehicle Manufacturers. events.title: McKinsey strips partner of leadership role over LinkedIn posts
events.summary: The decision came after an internal review sparked by Chris Bradley’s LinkedIn comments on a book that discusses the “glass cliff” for women. McKinsey & Co removed a senior partner from his leadership role at the firm’s research arm after he posted online comments questioning the uphill battle female executives face in the workplace. Chris Bradley, one of a handful of directors at the McKinsey Global Institute, its high-profile business and economic research unit, was removed from that role, the consulting firm said in a statement on Oct 11. He remains a senior partner at the firm and is based in Australia. The unusual decision came after an internal review sparked by Bradley’s LinkedIn back-and-forth in September with one of the authors of a new book discussing the workplace “glass cliff” for women. The comments were deleted, and McKinsey previously distanced itself from Bradley’s remarks. “Following our conduct review process, we have removed the partner from his leadership roles, including at the McKinsey Global Institute. His public comments fell well short of the standards we expect at our firm,” McKinsey spokesman Taylor Burns said in an e-mailed statement. Bradley also served as a leader on some internal committees, Burns said. Bradley could not be reached immediately for comment outside of normal business hours. The term “glass cliff” was coined by academics to describe the phenomenon in which female leaders are more likely to be offered CEO jobs at struggling companies. Proponents of the theory say research shows that women are more likely to get an opportunity to be CEO when a company is in crisis or turnaround mode. Bradley called the glass cliff “a very convenient way to always be a victim in the rain” in the deleted posts and generally questioned whether the concept even exists. McKinsey has long sought to advance the conversation about challenges women face in the workplace. The company has published a Women in the Workplace study, compiled with Sheryl Sandberg’s LeanIn advocacy group, for more than a decade. It surveys about 9,500 employees from 124 organisations; participants consistently report that women leaders face stronger resistance than men and are more likely to have their judgment questioned. A 2020 report from McKinsey about women working in healthcare even references the term “glass cliff” when outlining hurdles cited by women of colour. Over the past decade, women CEOs of Russell 3000 companies left after an average tenure of 6.2 years versus 8.9 years for men, according to Exechange, a researcher that tracks corporate leadership changes and scores them on the likelihood that the exit was forced or voluntary. In examining the reasons for CEO departures over the same period, the research firm found that women were more likely than men to be forced out. Just one in 10 S&P 500 companies is led by a female CEO. BLOOMBERG

events.title: AI may change the price of your Big Mac and groceries — what this means for shoppers
events.summary: Supermarkets and fast food giants are increasingly using artificial intelligence to digitize their operations. Some have been accused of using so-called "dynamic pricing" to set rapid real-time changes in prices that could dramatically affect shoppers' experiences. Experts told CNBC that this could raise the risk of shoppers facing more individualized prices. Fast-food giants and supermarkets are rolling out a range of AI tools that could affect the prices shoppers pay, but experts warn the spread of data-driven tools could make personalized pricing easier to deploy. Just this week, a federal antitrust lawsuit filed against McDonald's alleged the fast food giant uses an AI-powered "pricing engine" to set menu prices across U.S. locations and overcharge customers for Big Macs and fries. McDonald's has denied that it's using AI to determine what individual customers are willing to pay and said it provides its franchisees with "tools, resources, research and recommendations to help them make informed decisions." Even so, food businesses globally are increasingly digitizing operations with AI. Earlier this year, American grocery chain Kroger said it's using an AI platform called FlashFood to mark down perishables nearing the end of their shelf life and marketing them to shoppers via an app. Meanwhile, electronic shelf labels (ESLs), which display prices on digital screens, are becoming increasingly popular at supermarkets like Kroger, Walmart , and Amazon Fresh. Whole Foods Market spokesperson Rachel Malish said the supermarket chain "does not use dynamic pricing" in a statement to CNBC. Malish said that digital shelf labels "simplify the price tag change process for our employees [and] reduce paper waste from traditional tags." The technology is also gaining traction among U.K. supermarkets such as Tesco , Morrisons, and Asda. Morrisons declined to comment to CNBC on its ESLs . The British Retail Consortium's director of food & sustainability, Andrew Opie, has said that supermarkets have "no intention to use dynamic or surge pricing in their stores," and that digital pricing is instead a way of updating and checking prices quickly. More recently, global financial platform Revolut trialed facial recognition checkout in select coffee shops, allowing customers to pay with just a picture at checkout. The technology relies on a pre-existing selfie ID that Revolut customers submit as part of standard security checks for comparison, but no additional information is collected. CNBC reached out to Tesco and Asda for comment on the use of AI tools but did not receive a response. As AI use becomes normalized among retailers, experts warn that this could lead to more dynamic pricing, which refers to frequent, rapid real-time changes in prices that could dramatically affect shoppers' experiences. "Dynamic pricing means changing prices in response to changing market conditions, such as demand, timing, capacity or competitors' prices," Miroslava Marinova, a senior lecturer of commercial law at the University of East London, told CNBC. "It is not new. Airlines, hotels, and ride-hailing services have used it for years." Bank of England economists Clare Lombardelli and Rupal Patel said in April that more sophisticated technology is leading to prices changing more frequently and also becoming more individualized, which could see more firms charging "as close to the maximum price a consumer is willing to pay for a good or service," which they defined as "perfect price discrimination." These conditions could make it harder for statisticians to "measure and interpret" month-to-month inflation data, as the consumer price index is based on a representative sample of prices for shoppers. "That works well when prices mostly move slowly and uniformly. But when prices shift continually – and differently for each shopper – the idea of a 'representative' price becomes strained," the BOE economists added. While dynamic pricing has been in play for a long time, the BOE economists and Marinova noted that AI tools such as ESLs and facial recognition checkout are changing the amount of information that companies can collect on consumers, from transaction histories to browsing behavior, location, and purchasing patterns. On Wednesday, U.K. supermarket chain Sainsbury's released "SmartLists," an AI feature that helps customers create shopping lists and find products just by uploading pictures of what they need or by typing out meal ideas. CNBC reached out to Sainsbury's for comment but did not hear back immediately. "This is also why the traditional distinction between dynamic and personalised pricing is becoming less clear in practice," Marinova explained. "Dynamic pricing responds primarily to market conditions, whereas personalised pricing uses information about the consumer to estimate willingness to pay.

events.title: UK van drivers face extra £2.5bn in diesel costs this year, figures show
events.summary: Calls for planned fuel duty rise to be scrapped as analysis finds average fuel bill could hit £1,965, up from £1,294 Millions of British van drivers face a combined £2.5bn cost to cover the rising price of diesel this year, according to figures, fuelling calls for the government to scrap its planned fuel duty rise. The owners of diesel vans and pickups can expect to collectively spend almost £8.5bn at the pump this year, according to analysis for the Guardian, after diesel prices climbed to record highs due to a global fuel shortage caused by disruption to refineries in the Middle East and Russia. The estimated fuel costs, calculated by analysts at Moneysupermarket, is significantly above the £5.95bn spent last year, raising concerns that the price of food and goods transported by road could rise sharply as retailers pass on increased logistics costs. The comparison site warned last week that the average fuel bill for a van driver could reach £1,965 this year, up from £1,294 for the average van in 2025 based on typical mileage and fuel consumption. The number of vans on British roads has grown significantly in recent years fuelled by the boom in online shopping, home deliveries and the rising number of self-employed people working in trades . Although the adoption of electric vans has begun to increase, about 95% of light commercial vehicles are still powered by diesel. The average pump price climbed to a above £2 a litre for the first time this month, up over 40% since late February, when the US-Israel war on Iran began disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf, leading to cost increases across the economy. The rising cost burden has led to calls for government help in the upcoming budget, including abandoning plans to raise fuel duty from next year. The planned increase – postponed from September – will add 3p a litre in duty from 1 January, and another 2p from 1 March, in “a hammer blow” for costs, according to the Road Haulage Association (RHA). Richard Smith, the RHA’s managing director, said: “Many of our members run on margins of around 2%. Surging diesel prices are impacting firms across the country, with some spending many thousands extra every week on fuel. “Adding [fuel duty rises] on top of today’s fuel prices would be a hammer blow for many firms that move goods and the households that buy them. A fuel duty hike is a food price hike.” Data from the motoring group RAC showed that, despite a recent dip in the cost of diesel, the price remains about 57p a litre higher than before the US-Iran conflict while petrol remains 42p higher. This means households are paying £31 and £23 more respectively every time they fill up a family sized car, according to the group. The fuel duty rise “will only make prices at the pump even more expensive,” according to Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC. “As things stand, this year is still set to be the second most expensive year on record for drivers,” Williams said. “The government has the power to take some of the sting out of higher fuel costs, either by extending and increasing the fuel duty cut or reducing VAT as they’ve done with domestic electricity.” Smith added that the RHA was calling on the chancellor to bring in a 15p a litre rebate for British van, coach and haulage operators after Spain, France and Italy offered similar help for commercial vehicle businesses. “It’s time we caught up,” he said. On Friday, the US president, Donald Trump, attempted to ease pressure at the pump for US drivers by announcing a deal for Russian deal, in a move which infuriated the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy . The government was contact for comment.
