events.title: Drivers forced to use parking apps can pay up to 40% more
events.summary: Council car parks have switched away from ticket machines to cut costs, leading to extra fees for users Drivers are unwittingly paying up to 40% more to park as more councils switch to app-only payments and force customers to pick up the tab. Many councils across England have removed pay and display machines and replaced them with app payments, including a number in London. Most local authorities encourage drivers to pay by app to beat queues, while apps are often the only way to pay when ticket machines are out of order. However, many car park signs fail to mention that app payments may incur an additional service fee. Parking apps save councils money by removing the cost of installing and maintaining ticket machines, but while a few pay the app providers directly for their services, many leave drivers to foot some or all of the bill through “convenience fees” or “service fees”. These typically range from 10p to 30p, but they are not included in the advertised parking tariffs in car parks, even when an app is the only payment option, and they are often not strongly flagged within the apps. Of the parking apps tested by the Guardian, none clearly displayed the service fee until the payment stage, and even then, some required customers to click on an information symbol to find out why the price had increased. These surcharges can push up the cost of an hour’s parking slot dramatically. In Harrogate, North Yorkshire, drivers who park in the town centre and pay by app are hit with a mandatory 30p service charge – a 38% rise on an 80p tariff. Meanwhile, the price of two hours at the council’s Christleton Road car park in Chester soars by 40% when the 20p convenience fee is added to the 50p tariff. Extra fees are added if drivers agree to receive booking confirmation and expiry alerts. They are typically between 10 and 30p per text. According to the Advertising Standards Authority, quoted prices must include all mandatory fees for a contract to be valid. Drivers enter a contract with a council as soon as they accept the car park’s terms and conditions and park their vehicle. However, few realise that they enter a separate contract with the app provider if they choose to pay online. App fees, therefore, may not legally have to be displayed on parking council signs. Because service fees are agreed between local authorities and individual app providers, and since they can vary depending on location, drivers have no way of predicting what they will be charged. The Guardian tested the apps by booking an hour’s parking at car parks around the country. RingGo’s convenience fee added an extra 20p to the £2 tariff at Kings Yard in Lancaster. Drivers have to click on a small “see prices” link above the prominent “Next” button when they have chosen their location to see the charge. It is mentioned again on the payment page, but only when the “i” symbol beside the final price is clicked. PayByPhone charged a 15p service fee on top of the £5.10 parking tariff at Dudley Street car park in Birmingham. The existence of the charge was not explained until the payment page and was hidden behind the Apple Pay button. Customers have to scroll down to the end of the page to see it. Customers using JustPark have to click on a tiny pale grey “i” symbol beside the final price at the end of the booking process to discover its transaction fee. This added 12p to a £3.50 parking charge at Charmouth Road car park in Lyme Regis, Dorset. MiPermit listed its 10p convenience fee above the final price at the end of the booking. This was levied on top of the £1.90 parking charge in Littlehampton, West Sussex. RingGo said the fee funded the service it provided and that it was up to the councils it worked with whether or not to display it on car park signs. “In line with existing regulations, wherever pricing information is shown in the RingGo app, we also display any additional fees,” said Adam Dolphin at its parent company Arrive. JustPark said mandatory fees were included in the price quoted during payment. “Nothing is added at the payment stage,” said a spokesperson. “The ‘i’ icon simply shows how that all-in price is made up, for drivers who want the detail.” PayByPhone said its pricing was transparent. “The pricing elements related to parking, SMS options and service fees are presented before payment confirmation,” said a spokesperson. “Applicable pricing information – whether fees, parking rates or options – is available on the website and in the app.” MiPermit was contacted for a comment. The Local Government Association, which represents councils, said it was up to app providers to ensure their fees were clear and upfront. The Department for Transport said parking tariffs and surcharges were a matter for councils. “Drivers should be able to see clearly what they will be charged before they pay for parking,” a spokesperson said.

events.title: Father was asked for DNA test to get a passport for his daughter
events.summary: New post-Brexit rules mean that dual nationals cannot enter the UK unless they have a British passport My teenage daughter is unable to see her grandparents because of the UK’s new requirement for dual nationals to hold a UK passport. I’m a UK citizen, married to a French national, and we live in France. Our two older children have both French and UK passports. Our third child was born while we were living in Zimbabwe and only has a French passport. I began her application for a British passport in February. I had to submit photos of my wife when pregnant, family photos from the birth to the present day, hospital records and official translations of French marriage and birth certificates. During an official interview I was asked about my job, commute and the layout of my house, but very little about my relationship with my daughter. I was then told that there was insufficient evidence to prove my paternity and was invited to consider a DNA test, which will cost £600 and take yet more time. We need to visit my elderly father who is unwell in the UK but cannot risk it in case our daughter is denied boarding. Your daughter is a victim of new rules that came into force in February and effectively deny entry to the UK to dual national Britons who do not have a British passport. Foreign nationals can enter freely on passports issued by their country of residence, but expats cannot unless they stump up £589 for a certificate of entitlement. The law has caused chaos, with children being stranded abroad or arbitrarily denied a passport granted to their siblings. Since the UK government is not accepting that your daughter is a UK national, you asked if she could travel on her French passport. No one could answer the question. As a result, you face Christmas apart from your parents. Home Office rules state that officials must consider a passport application on the “balance of probability” if an applicant refuses a DNA test. They must also explain why an application is refused. You have never been told why your copious proofs of paternity have been deemed inadequate. The Home Office will not comment on individual cases, but it did tell me that additional evidence, such as the layout of a home, may be requested to add “credible authenticity”. Soon afterwards, you were informed that the application had been accepted after all, despite no new paperwork having been sought since April. I can only assume that press scrutiny prompted the realisation that your domestic floorplan is credibly authentic. We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. events.title: Oil falls after Trump declares 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine
events.summary: President Donald Trump said that Russia and Ukraine will not be targeting each other's energy facilities. Al Jazeera reported that Iran was ready to provide assistance to help with the start of dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis. Oil prices are likely to remain volatile in the near term amid concerns over the Middle East conflict and the impact of Hurricane Isaias. Oil prices fell Monday on optimism about improved supplies after President Donald Trump said that Russia and Ukraine will not be targeting each other's energy facilities, while Iran reached out to Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks against the kingdom. Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery dropped 0.77% to $103.91 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for November declined 1.26% to $90.69 per barrel. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump said in a social media statement Sunday stateside. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a social media post that "Ukraine supports the ceasefire, and it is important that Russia support it as well." Prospects of more Russian energy hitting markets after a deal with the U.S. have also risen after Trump said Friday that Moscow will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under a deal he struck with Putin during a phone call. According to the Saudi state news agency , Iran's Minister of Foreign Affairs Abbas Araghchi made a phone call to Saudi Arabia's Minister of Foreign Affairs Faisal bin Farhan bin Abdullah, to discuss about the region's recent escalation of events as well as the efforts to address it. Al Jazeera reported Araghchi had said Iran was ready to provide assistance to help with the start of dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis. Oil prices are expected to remain volatile in the near term as the U.S.-Iran conflict continues, while the impact of Hurricane Isaias on U.S. energy producers could also hurt supplies . "The pressure on oil prices could remain on the upside as Hurricane Isaias strengthened to Category 3 with 120mph winds as it approached the US Gulf Coast, forcing energy producers to curtail offshore output," UOB said in a note on Monday. "Separately, Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport on Sat which killed 12 people and injured over 300, have materially elevated Middle East risk premia," UOB added.

events.title: Countries warn against travel to Saudi Arabia following Houthi attacks
events.summary: US, Australia, Canada, Japan, South Korea and New Zealand among countries urging citizens to avoid travel to Kingdom. Several countries have warned their citizens against travel to Saudi Arabia following a series of Houthi attacks on airports in the kingdom. On Monday, Australia and New Zealand became the latest to issue advisories against travelling to the kingdom, following similar warnings from the United States, Canada, the UK, South Korea, and Japan. list 1 of 4 Iran’s FM urges diplomacy in call with Saudi counterpart list 2 of 4 UK PM Andy Burnham says it is ‘clear’ Russia interfered in 2016 Brexit vote list 3 of 4 Bridge washed away by torrent of water in Nepal list 4 of 4 Saudi Arabia says 1 dead, 11 injured in latest attack on Riyadh airport Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said Australians should avoid King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and “reconsider” travel to other Saudi airports. New Zealand’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade urged citizens not to travel to the Saudi capital’s main gateway and the provinces of Najran, Jazan and Asir for any reason, and to avoid “non-essential” travel to Saudi Arabia as a whole. The US embassy in Riyadh on Sunday advised US citizens to reconsider travel to the kingdom, citing the threat of attacks by Iran and the Iranian-backed Houthis. Global Affairs Canada issued an advisory against non-essential travel to any part of Saudi Arabia. South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs recommended that its citizens in Saudi Arabia leave unless they are on essential business and advised anyone planning to travel to the kingdom to cancel their trip. The UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office urged citizens to avoid travel to Jeddah and Dammam, and to all airports apart from Medina International Airport, except for essential reasons. The warnings come as Saudi Arabia reels from five attacks on its airports in less than a week. One person was killed and 11 others were injured on Sunday when a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA). A Houthi strike on the same airport on Saturday killed 13 people and injured more than 300 others, marking the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The Houthis claimed responsibility for all four strikes on Saudi airports before Sunday’s attack, which has yet to be claimed by any group. King Khalid international airport and King Fahd international airport in Dammam remain closed following the attacks, causing significant disruption to aviation across the Middle East. The attacks have also disrupted flights to and from King Abdulaziz International Airport in Jeddah. More than 150 flights were cancelled and 374 flights were delayed at the Jeddah airport on Sunday, according to the flight tracking website Flightradar24. Brendan Sobie, an independent analyst and consultant in Singapore, said it was too early to predict the ramifications of the attacks for aviation across the region and beyond. “As has been the case with the Iran war and the impact from that crisis on the UAE, Kuwait and Bahrain, the impact of this latest crisis really depends on how long it lasts, how long Riyadh airport remains closed, and how long and to what extent are the restrictions once it reopens,” Sobie told Al Jazeera.

Weiss Eubanks/NBCUniversal via Getty Images Kelly Clarkson said a Brooklyn toy shop gave her the "Pretty Woman" treatment. Here's how the dispute between Clarkson and the store unfolded. A publicist said a celebrity pile-on can hurt a small business before people know the full story. A Brooklyn toy shop has found itself at the center of a celebrity internet drama after Kelly Clarkson said she received the " Pretty Woman " treatment when she inquired about a $15,000 item in the store. In an X post on Saturday, the singer said she had a negative experience at Art of Play, a toy store in New York City . "Just drove all the way to Brooklyn to check out this store I thought looked really rad and had a few things in mind to buy and literally was looked at as if I couldn't afford it and was told he could find something comparable for me," Clarkson wrote in her post, adding that the store "just lost a huge sale." events.title: IFS: budget will be ‘work of fiction’ without clear plan to cover UK’s £35bn spending pressures
events.summary: Thinktank’s influential pre-budget report urges key decisions to be made now and not put off until next year John Healey has been warned by Britain’s leading tax and spending experts that his budget risks being a “work of fiction” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures. As the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade. Against a febrile backdrop in the bond market, the thinktank warned Healey that failure to address the issue at his 28 October budget risked leaving the impression that Labour was setting unrealistic spending plans. Helen Miller, the director of the IFS, said: “Simply pencilling in implicit cuts that he has no intention of delivering would make the budget a work of fiction.” Her comment echoes a criticism levelled at Jeremy Hunt , the former Conservative chancellor, who before the 2024 general election was accused by the then head of the Office for Budget Responsibility of setting unrealistic spending plans. Publishing its influential “green budget” report, which analyses the public finances before Healey’s speech to the Commons, it called on the chancellor to avoid announcing a “steady as she goes” budget that delayed decisions until next year’s spending review. “If John Healey sets out spending envelopes for public services that he would not be willing to live within, his plan for meeting the fiscal rules will not be credible,” it said. Last week, the governor of the Bank of England, Andrew Bailey, said fiscal policy “must be credible and be seen as such by financial markets”. The following day, the Times quoted a government source as saying: “Andrew Bailey needs to focus on doing his job.” Miller said the Treasury adopting an assumption that “everything can be kicked forward” to next year’s spending review risked undermining the chancellor’s credibility. “We would be better served by a chancellor who hopes for the best, but plans for the worst, rather than sets out plans that either say, ‘I hope it’ll be fine and some money will come in’, or ‘I’ll get a plan in a year’s time’.” Attention before the budget has largely focused on the hit to the chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s main fiscal rule to balance day-to-day public spending with revenues in 2029-30. With the war in the Middle East fuelling a dramatic sell-off in the market for government debt, higher borrowing costs are expected to erase a significant chunk of the £24bn buffer left by the former chancellor Rachel Reeves at the spring statement. Leading economists have predicted the market moves since the start of the war in February could wipe out about half of the headroom, adding to nerves in the Treasury over the risk of a market backlash. The IFS said that although the surge in debt interest costs could add £10bn to borrowing in 2029-30, the exchequer would benefit from higher inflation boosting tax revenue – meaning Healey could see headroom cut by only £4bn. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning However, it warned against focusing on this buffer because the inflation shock rippling from the Middle East would also dramatically hit the government’s plan for funding public services. Higher inflation squeezes public spending power, forcing the government to choose between accepting real-term cuts and finding efficiency savings or topping up departmental budgets either by raising taxes or allowing an increase in borrowing. The IFS said a choice to leave spending totals unchanged at the budget would implicitly mean allowing the quality or quantity of public services to fall. However, it said compensating for the inflation shock, and funding Healey’s pledge to raise defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, would require tax rises or benefit cuts of about £35bn. “Choosing to stay the course with the inherited tax and spending plans would mean allowing inflation to blow departments’ spending plans off course,” Miller said. “It would be a choice to tolerate chunky cuts to the quantity or quality of some public services – cuts that would be larger if defence spending was increased within existing totals.” She said Healey would not need to make detailed plans for the next spending review period at the budget but merely set out overall spending envelopes that he would be prepared to live within. A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “The chancellor is fully focused on his priorities to boost business, help with the cost of living and support people in every postcode, underpinned by fiscal discipline and a commitment to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.

events.title: Why some have no choice but to pay costly oil prices
events.summary: Many heating oil customers are having to buy early in preparation for the colder months As the temperature drops, some of us will start putting the heating on but for the one-and-a-half million people across the UK that are not on the mains gas network - and who are relying instead on heating oil - that decision may give them pause. The vast majority of those people live in rural locations. The heating oil market is unregulated, unlike gas and electricity, so any changes in the global price quickly gets passed on to customers . Tensions in the Middle East and the ongoing war in Ukraine are two issues currently both affecting supply which is causing prices to rise. Author shares how books have 'magical way' of reaching you when struggling Published 1 day ago Accessible playground to 'allow all children to play' Published 17 hours ago 'What terminal cancer has taught me about life' Published 2 days ago Until March this year, the price was quite stable at about 60p per litre (ppl) but when the war in Iran started in March, it jumped to a high of 134ppl . After a dip in the past few months, it is rising once again and it currently stands at 111ppl, according to price comparison site Boiler Juice. The BBC has spoken to a number of business and homeowners across the West about how that rise is affecting them. Peter Mason lives in Minety, in north Wiltshire, where most homes rely on heating oil. "I'm getting toward the end of the tank and need to top up for winter... it will be over £550," he said. Mason said that last year "it was about £300 to fill up - it is horrendous". He said: "The price goes up and down. It can vary plus or minus £50 but it has never been as high as it is today. "It means I'll have to eek out what I spent my money on. I'm retired, its not like I can change jobs. "I have to be really careful and pull money out of savings." Most tanks hold 500 litres of oil and would cost about £550 to fill currently Dylan Williams owns van-driving business Van & I of Monmouth, Wales and regularly operates in the Forest of Dean, Stroud and South Gloucestershire. The 51-year-old said he was currently paying more for fuel than he ever had in the three years of running his business. He said he had had to put the prices of his services up to offset the rise. At the start of the year he would pay between £120 and £130 for a full tank, he said, but that had now gone up to £160. "It's ever increasing, ever worrying - keeping an eye on the news, keeping an eye on the diesel prices," he said. "I mean I've got fuel cards... you don't pay the pump prices, you pay the fuel card prices but it doesn't make much a difference these days. Tristan Holland (pictured with Mel Holland) runs a small team of community care workers Yvette Farrell, volunteer director for Dean Forest Kitchen, which cook fresh meals every day and delivers them to clients within the Forest of Dean, said they might have to increase prices as there's "not going to be much choice in the future". She said: "It's impacted us a lot because we work on a not-for-profit scenario so there is not a lot of wiggle room when it comes to increase in any expenses. "So the cost of fuel is really, really hitting the business hard and we're having to do our best to still keep going to our clients who are spread across a very rural area with no public transport. "But we have to take these meals to them because... they will not have somebody coming to see them during the day because they're so isolated." Tristan Holland, company director at TLC Support Service, manages a small team of community care workers who travel around Wotton-under-Edge and Dursley. Staff use their own vehicles and the company pays mileage at 55p per business mile. He said: "We had an increase in our fees back at the start of the year, just kind of taking into account all the extras that were coming in this year but even that does make it tight. "Everything has risen - the cost of the fuel, the training, even the uniforms that we purchased. "Everything has gone up and so we try to keep our services as affordable as we possibly can but there has to be a profit or else we just can't carry on going." The Iran war has disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil and prices can rise or fall based on the words and actions of key political figures. It is thought prices could come down if there is a peace deal between the US and Iran. For people who rely on heating oil, it means feeling helpless. Richard Willan, who runs the Nadder Oil Buying Club in Wiltshire where more than 1,000 residents buy in bulk together to get a better price, said rural residents were increasingly vulnerable as the colder months set in. "We are watching to see what happens with (Donald) Trump in the mid-term elections in America, that might change things again," he said. The Competitions and Markets Authority (CMA) said heating oil customers in remote areas were too vulnerable to price shocks.

events.title: Documents falsified to evade tax on Abramovich's wealth, BBC finds
events.summary: Watch: The documents that were falsified to allow Roman Abramovich to evade tax The world's biggest accountancy firm helped in falsifying documents to hide Roman Abramovich's wealth and evade tax, BBC Panorama has found. Accounts signed off by Deloitte in Cyprus meant assets such as superyachts, mansions and private jets worth $672m (£508m) vanished from Abramovich's company accounts. Deloitte also appears to have advised on a scheme to evade a huge tax bill on the oligarch's wealth through the falsification of documents. Barrister Andrew Mitchell KC, an expert in financial services law, said Panorama's evidence showed the scheme was "straightforward" tax evasion and "it couldn't be more blatant". Roman Abramovich's lawyers said he denies that he evaded tax or concealed his fortune. They said Panorama provided no evidence he knew about, authorised or directed the falsification of any document and said it was legitimate to rely on advice from professionals. Deloitte Cyprus said it "acts in compliance with applicable laws". The findings are being revealed following a joint investigation between BBC Panorama and the Bureau of Investigative Journalism. For nearly two decades, Roman Abramovich was the most famous Russian oligarch in the UK, welcomed in London where he bought Chelsea Football Club in 2003 and bankrolled the club's most successful period. But after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he was sanctioned by the UK government as an associate of President Vladimir Putin and forced to sell the club. Abramovich has been reported to be living in Turkey, a safe haven for him because it did not apply sanctions. In the Channel Island of Jersey, £5.4bn of his assets remain frozen and a criminal investigation has been going on for four years. The oligarch's lawyers told the BBC he denies the allegations in the Jersey investigation and says it was "undertaken for political purposes". Our investigation has uncovered new evidence about the way Abramovich's business empire has been run. It also raises serious questions about the integrity of some of his professional advisers. Chateau de la Croe (top left) in the south of France, Fyning Hill in Sussex and two superyachts vanished from company accounts The evidence is contained in a leak that includes thousands of documents about the oligarch's finances and the operations of a network of offshore companies administered from Cyprus - which used to be a tax haven popular with Russians - between 1995 and 2022. The BBC and media partners including the Guardian, Paper Trail Media, the Organised Crime and Corruption Reporting Project, and the Cyprus Investigative Reporting Network - as well as the Bureau of Investigative Journalism , external - have been reporting on the leaked files since 2023 as part of the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists' Cyprus Confidential , external investigation. In 2022, Panorama also reported on how Abramovich had made his fortune from a corrupt deal to buy a Russian state-owned oil company in the 1990s, selling it back to the government a decade later for billions in profit. He has previously said allegations of corruption in the deal are false. The profits from Abramovich's oil deals in Russia were funnelled into a web of offshore companies. They were administered from Cyprus by a corporate services firm called MeritServus, in Limassol, the island's second-largest city. Until 2005, Deloitte - now the biggest of the "big four" firms which dominate the accounting industry - owned MeritServus. After they split, the two companies worked closely together with Abramovich's associates to manage his global fortune. The leaked documents from MeritServus reveal some of their practices. Panorama - Roman Abramovich: How He Hid His Fortune He was the Russian oligarch who brought his wealth to the UK. But what’s the truth about Roman Abramovich’s fortune? Panorama investigates the documents that were falsified to hide his wealth and evade tax. Watch now on BBC iPlayer or on BBC One at 20:00 BST on Monday 12 October. Our first example of backdated paperwork comes in 2006, after a new law in Cyprus meant that company accounts had to be made public. The new transparency law threatened to expose the secrets of Abramovich's vast wealth. Deloitte Cyprus had prepared draft accounts for 2003 - but had not yet finalised them - for his Cypriot company Amiscan Investments. The accounts detailed $672m of luxury property. A mansion in West Sussex, a luxury flat in London and an estate in the south of France were all included - plus helicopters, private jets and a small fleet of boats the oligarch owned at the time, including the $147.5m Pelorus. Deloitte in Cyprus appears to have advised Abramovich's company on a scheme to evade tax To keep them secret, Abramovich's associates and Meritservus decided to rewrite history.

events.title: Roman Abramovich aides falsified paperwork to disguise assets and dodge tax, records suggest
events.summary: Accountancy firm Deloitte Cyprus among those that appear to have backdated records outlining the Russian billionaire’s assets A ides of Roman Abramovich – including staff at the global accountancy firm Deloitte – falsified paperwork mapping the oligarch’s sprawling offshore business empire, records suggest, helping his businesses dodge tax and disguise assets. New analysis of leaked corporate records uncovers what appears to have been a long-running and carefully orchestrated strategy of backdating documents. The Russian billionaire’s closest aide, London-based Eugene Tenenbaum, appears to have been involved in the backdating and may also have given false evidence to the UK high court during a potentially costly lawsuit, the papers indicate. Abramovich’s personal and financial affairs are now restricted, owing to sanctions imposed by the UK and EU in response to Russia’s war on Ukraine. But the documents raise questions about how Abramovich was able to shield his financial affairs from the authorities for more than a decade, with the apparent assistance of apparatchiks and blue-chip advisers. The findings are based on the Cyprus Confidential leak , more than 500,000 documents, first released to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ) and analysed by organisations including the Guardian, the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC. The digital paper trail charts the reorganisation of billions of pounds that the former Chelsea FC owner obtained via the controversial acquisition of oilfields in the frozen wastes of Siberia, amid the break-up of the Soviet Union. From 1999 until at least 2013, a cadre of aides and accountants tasked with shifting the funds between offshore jurisdictions deployed tactics that experts say may have constituted fraud and tax evasion. This, it seems, involved backdating documents to create a convenient paper trail showing that agreements and transactions had taken place years earlier. Lawyers for Abramovich denied any wrongdoing and said he relied on the advice of his advisers and Deloitte Cyprus. Tenenbaum denied any wrongdoing and said he also relied on the specialist advice given by Deloitte Cyprus. Deloitte Cyprus said that it “acts in compliance with all applicable laws” and that it could no longer access the relevant material because of the time that has elapsed. A crown jewel in Russia’s rich seam of natural resources, Sibneft’s oilfields fell into Abramovich’s hands during the chaotic post-Soviet privatisation era. The famously shrewd entrepreneur obtained the business for roughly $250m, reportedly spending as little as $19m of his own money. By the time he sold the last of his shares to Gazprom in 2005, Abramovich had raised $16bn, money he ploughed into investments, mansions, superyachts and Chelsea FC. One Cyprus-based company, Kravin Investments, was among several early vehicles through which that cash flowed. Kravin received a $3bn windfall in May 2003, of which it retained about $2bn. The money sat in Kravin’s bank account or was loaned to other companies, accruing interest that was, in theory, taxable in Cyprus. But Abramovich’s aides soon began devising plans to “eliminate” a tax liability that one financial adviser warned could be “very large”, records suggest. The gatekeeper to Abramovich’s fortune was Demetris Ioannides, who was the chair of Deloitte Cyprus before spinning out his own business Meritservus. That firm became Abramovich’s go-to financial advisory, serving him for nearly 20 years, before it was sanctioned by the UK in 2023 , along with Ioannides, for its role helping Russian oligarch hide their wealth. “It will be necessary to change the [Kravin’s] financial statements and the accounting records accordingly for 2003 and 2004,” Ioannides wrote in August 2005 email, citing discussions with Deloitte Cyprus partners and erstwhile colleagues Antonis Taliotis and Nicos Charalambous. The following month, in an email copying in staff at Meritservus and Abramovich’s investment vehicle, Millhouse, Taliotis appeared to agree. “Certain changes will have to be made to the accounts […]” he wrote. Millhouse and Meritservus duly began producing paperwork showing that Kravin was simply holding and investing the Sibneft billions as a trustee for another business, the British Virgin Islands-based Kelvedon Worldwide. Documents detailing this supposed fact, including correspondence and trust agreements, were given dates between March and December 2003, despite being created at least two years later. The result was simple: although the billions had sat in Kravin’s accounts for years, it now appeared that the money had never really been Kravin’s at all. Deloitte Cyprus, apparently aware of the deception, duly signed off the accounts. History had effectively been rewritten, analysis of the documents suggests, disappearing $2bn from Kravin’s balance sheet – and with it any tax liability.

events.title: ‘If nothing is done, it’s almost inevitable’: Ukraine’s Yuriy Ryzhenkov on why steelmaking is on the brink of collapse as Russian bombing intensifies
events.summary: Yuriy Ryzhenkov is that rare individual—a chief executive who has led his firm of 33,700 people during a never-ending war. He is the chief executive of the largest steelmaker in Ukraine, Metinvest. More than 8,000 of his employees are fighting Russian forces. Factories are under constant bombardment. Hundreds of Metinvest colleagues have been killed. Amid the flames and destruction, Ryzhenkov says that this period of the war is as tough as anything the company has seen since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four years ago.  “The blockade of the seaports is more severe now than it was in 2022,” Ryzhenkov, who became CEO in 2013, tells me. “We’ve been hit numerous times. Our facilities have been hit over the last four and a half years, and even though we were restoring them after every hit, you lose. You get weaker with every such attack.  “In wartime you cannot afford to restore to the original state. You do the best you can to continue operating and that best is never the ideal. Unfortunately, it was one of the most severe campaigns for bombing in August and September this year. We had to stop both of our steel mills.  “We lost 14 people at our steel mills, which was probably the largest loss since 2023 in a single bombing. That’s where we are.”  Metinvest factories are under constant bombardment and hundreds of Metinvest colleagues have been killed. Giulio PISCITELLI / AFP via Getty Images Now there is another threat to the future of steelmaking in Ukraine, and it doesn’t come from the East, but from the European Union. In July, new tariffs were applied to all EU steel imports in an effort to protect the continent’s industry from cheaper foreign competition. The key steel tariff-rate quota for Ukraine from July 2026 was cut by 60%, and is expected to reduce steel imports from Ukraine to the EU by 1.3 million metric tons per year, according to the GMK Center , a Ukrainian think tank.  Read more: He manages one of the most successful soccer clubs in the world and is the elite leader every CEO wants to talk to. So why has Mikel Arteta decided to go public on having his own DNA mapped? “If you compare the quotas that were allocated to Ukraine this year to what was supplied last year, it’s minus 60% and that’s at the time when the ports were already closed, and we literally have no other alternative,” Ryzhenkov says.  “When the invasion happened, the EU pretty much realized that for Ukraine the only available market is actually the EU with the blockade of ports. They abolished any restrictions for the steel to be supplied there, which was, in my view, the correct answer.  “In wartime you cannot afford to restore to the original state. You do the best you can to continue operating and that best is never the ideal” Yuriy Ryzhenkov, CEO of Fortune 500 europe company, Metinvest “And then suddenly, in the first half of this year, we got these quotas where we were pretty much dumped with all the other countries [outside the EU], and the fact that we had exceptional circumstances in terms of logistics, in terms of energy supply, in terms of personnel availability, they were not taken into account, in my view, at all.  “It was too harsh, given the circumstances.”  Negotiations continue and the EU has said it is aware that Ukraine is a unique case. But the pincer movement—the armed invasion from the East, and tariffs from the West—is leaving steelmaking in Ukraine in a perilous position. Between 2021 and 2025, steel production in Ukraine fell from 21 million metric tons to 7.4 million metric tons, the value of exports fell from $22 billion to $6 billion, and tax revenues dropped from $3.5 billion to $870 million. Russia’s constant attacks on factories, energy supply systems and the railways means that steel supply to the Ukrainian armed forces is also being degraded.  “There is pretty much no future without a market to which you can sell,” Ryzhenkov says. “With the continuing disruptions, it’s very difficult to make a steel business economically viable. [This] is typically a business where you have to have 90% plus capacity utilization to be profitable, even in normal times, and where you have to develop your markets with long-term commitments, and in today’s circumstances, that’s just not possible.”  I ask whether we could be witnessing the end of steelmaking in Ukraine?  “Well, if nothing is done, it’s almost inevitable,” he says. “If Ukraine is not allowed to participate in the European market fully, and at the same time the circumstances preclude any significant investments, then I mean everything comes to an end eventually.”  Ryzhenkov comes from a long line of steelmakers. His grandmother was a coal plant chemical engineer closely aligned to steel making, and his mother, father, and uncle all work in the sector. That family history does bring with it a high level of determination to continue despite the losses and the constant threats of more attacks.  “To be honest, that’s the only choice we have, right?” he tells me. “Well, not the only choice. I mean, obviously, you can slam the door and walk out, but we have more than 35,000 people working for us with their families. We have 8,500 of our employees in the Ukrainian armed forces, which also rely on us. So, I mean, why would you slam the door if you can still try to do something to carry on? I just don’t find a reason for myself to do that.”  This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: China sanctions Paraguay, Belize ministers over Taiwan ties
events.summary: Chinese foreign ministry cites national sovereignty and Taiwan separatist activities as reasons behind the measures. China has sanctioned Paraguay’s communications minister and Belize’s foreign minister over ties to Taiwan. The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs made the announcement on Monday, citing the safeguarding of China’s national sovereignty and opposition to Taiwan separatist activities as the reasons behind the measures, which went into effect the same day. list 1 of 3 Taiwan president says defence spending boost aims to ‘deter war’ list 2 of 3 What the Iran war has done to the world’s energy supply, in charts list 3 of 3 North Korea fires multiple ballistic missiles towards the sea The measures against Paraguay’s Communications Minister Gustavo Villate and Belize’s Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca include the freezing of their assets in China and the denial of entry visas to Hong Kong and Macau. The sanctions also prohibit Chinese organisations and individuals from engaging in transactions, cooperation or other activities with the ministers. The Foreign Ministry said that “certain anti-China politicians” who are “driven by self-interest” have pushed their nations to maintain diplomatic relations with Taiwan. Beijing said the ministers had “taken a series of egregious actions and statements”, which are “damaging China’s core interests”. Paraguay and Belize are two of 12 countries that maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan. China views Taiwan as its territory, a view the island’s government strongly rejects. The measures come two days after Taiwan’s National Day celebration. In a National Day speech outside the Presidential Office on Saturday, Taiwan President William Lai Ching-te said the island “cherishes peace” and will “not give up our freedom”. China’s Taiwan Affairs Office condemned Lai’s speech, saying it “disregards facts, ⁠distorts the truth, misleads the public, and reveals ulterior motives”. In January, Chinese President Xi Jinping pledged to achieve the “reunification” of China and Taiwan, calling the goal “unstoppable”. Paraguay’s Communications Minister Villate marked Taiwan’s National Day with a social media post, saying: “Paraguay reaffirms its relationship of friendship and cooperation, based on shared values and principles: the self-determination of peoples, human rights and democracy.” The Belize embassy in Taiwan also posted a message on its Facebook celebrating the 37th anniversary of their diplomatic relations. “Together, we look forward to a future of growth, opportunity, and lasting friendship,” the embassy wrote. Last month, Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung visited Belize. His ministry said the two sides had agreed to deepen ties. Taiwan’s other allies in the Americas include Guatemala and Haiti. It also has formal diplomatic ties with three Caribbean islands. The United States does not have ⁠formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but Washington is bound by law to provide the island with the means to ‌defend itself. Earlier this month, the US delivered two fighter jets to Taiwan as the island seeks to build its defence capabilities to deter a feared attack from China .

( ABC News: Jano Gibson ) South 32 is likely to make redundancies at its manganese mine on Groote Eylandt in the Northern Territory. The company is looking to cut $129 million from the business and spend about $100 million on new water infrastructure. The company says it will make changes to strengthen its long-term viability. Job losses are likely at South 32's manganese mine on Groote Eylandt in the Northern Territory as the operation battles years of flooding impacts and skyrocketing production costs. The Groote Eylandt Mining Company (GEMCO) mine has begun consultations with staff. The ABC understands it needs to cut $129 million from the business in response to costs increasing by more than 80 per cent in recent years. The island and mine site were hit hard by Tropical Cyclone Megan in March 2024, but it is understood multiple wet seasons and persistent seepage of groundwater into the pits are also responsible. Mining pits on Groote Eylandt filled with water after Cyclone Megan in 2024. ( Supplied ) A South32 spokesperson said in a statement the company would make changes to strengthen its long-term viability and was speaking to workers. "GEMCO has completed an internal review in response to a more challenging operating environment and increased cost pressures, and has begun implementing changes designed to strengthen the long-term sustainability of the business," the spokesperson said. "The review forms part of a program focused on improving structures, systems and processes and ensuring GEMCO is well positioned to operate successfully into the future. As part of this work, GEMCO has reviewed its workforce requirements and commenced consultation with employees and contractors who will potentially be impacted. Officials from two separate unions representing workers at GEMCO told the ABC they believed office staff would likely be the target of redundancies . A spokesperson for the NT branch of the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union said it was closely monitoring the situation to see if blue-collar workers were affected. Union officials were told South 32 management would provide staff with more information about the redundancies by the end of the week. According to GEMCO's enterprise bargaining agreement, the company must consult with workers before making any significant organisational changes. The bargaining agreement is due to expire at the end of 2027. The MV Anikitos was loaded with 41,000 tonnes of manganese ore when it crashed into a loading wharf on Groote Eylandt. ( Supplied ) The island's wharf was destroyed in 2024 when Tropical Cyclone Megan pushed a loaded bulk carrier into the structure during high tides . Heavy rainfall damaged the mine's pits, a critical bridge and several roads. Exports from the island did not restart until 2025. Mining is expected to conclude on the island within the next 10 years, according to the local Aboriginal land council. events.title: Sheng Siong shares fall 3% after Maybank downgrade, target price cut
events.summary: The research house also lowered its forecast for new Sheng Siong stores in 2028 from five to four. Maybank downgraded Sheng Siong to “hold” and cut its target price to $3.12, sending the shares down as much as 3% on Oct 12. The broker said Sheng Siong is now one of the region’s “most expensive food retailers” after a strong rerating, even with 8% NPAT CAGR to 2028 and a 2.5% dividend yield. Maybank also trimmed profit forecasts and warned that vouchers, competition, RTS-linked shopping and online grocery growth could weaken Sheng Siong’s future growth. SINGAPORE – Shares of Sheng Siong fell as much as 3% on Oct 12 after Maybank downgraded the supermarket chain to “hold” from “buy” and cut its target price. The counter fell as low as $2.83 in early trade on Oct 12, but pared some losses to be 1.7% down at $2.87 as at 10.10am. On Oct 9, it was the biggest decliner on the Singapore Exchange, having fallen 5.5%. The decline followed Maybank cutting Sheng Siong’s target price from $3.22 to $3.12 on Oct 9. This was due to a narrower upside that makes the supermarket chain one of the region’s “most expensive food retailers” at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of 28.4 times. This is despite a net profit after tax (NPAT) compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 8% through 2028 and a 2.5% dividend yield. Maybank analyst Hussaini Saifee said: “Within the consumer space, we prefer Food Empire, supported by its strong NPAT growth (31% CAGR), moderate valuations and 5% dividend yield.” The research house also lowered its forecast for new Sheng Siong stores in 2028 from five to four and reduced financial year 2026-2028 net profit after tax by a range of 1% to 3%. “Sheng Siong remains a high-quality operator, but its strong share price re-rating now prices in much of it,” said Saifee. “With growth normalising and slight headwinds emerging, we see limited scope for further re-rating.” While Sheng Siong has benefited from “resilient consumption”, market share gains and targeted vouchers that channelled spending directly to supermarkets, such tailwinds are weakening. Maybank said that more assistance is being provided through unrestricted goods and services tax vouchers and cash payments. The $500 tranche of CDC vouchers, originally scheduled for January 2027, was brought forward to June 2026, boosting financial year 2026 demand but raising the comparison base for FY2027. With supermarket growth already easing to low single digits, the research house expects Sheng Siong’s growth to track underlying income and population trends, rather than benefit from a repeat of the unusually favourable conditions of recent years. Sheng Siong’s capture of displaced demand from store closures at Giant and Cold Storage has also petered out, as the two competing chains have closed only one store between them. Cold Storage’s new owner, Macrovalue, which bought both chains from DFI Retail Group in 2025, has “resumed expansion” through its On The Go convenience stores. It will be rolled out progressively to all 58 Esso petrol stations across Singapore through 2026 and targets more than 100 outlets over time. Saifee said: “Although the convenience-led format does not directly replicate Sheng Siong’s full-basket proposition, it adds competition for top-up grocery purchases, convenience items and ready-to-eat meals.” Separately, Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS)-linked cross-border shopping and the gradual evolution of online grocery fulfilment could also pose headwinds for Sheng Siong. The supermarket chain appears more exposed to northern Singapore catchments than its larger competitors. About 10% of its network – nine stores – is within 5km of the RTS station, while about 27.5% – 25 stores – is within 15km. “While neither appears disruptive enough to reshape the industry in the near term, both point to a less favourable backdrop than in recent years,” said the analyst. events.title: TikTok CEO sees major scientific breakthroughs from AI within three years
events.summary: TikTok CEO Shou Zi Chew expects artificial intelligence to drive major scientific breakthroughs within the next three years. Chew said rapid advances in AI were opening up possibilities far beyond the technology's current applications. SINGAPORE — TikTok CEO Shou Zi Chew expects artificial intelligence to drive major scientific breakthroughs within the next three years, transforming a broad range of sectors. "In the next two to three years, we're going to have a real scientific breakthrough: physics, biotech, chemistry, material science, because of AI. It's very, very, very possible," Chew said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday. Chew's remarks come as ByteDance, TikTok's Chinese parent, expands its artificial intelligence research beyond consumer applications. In April, the company's Seed research team unveiled Protenix-v2 , an AI model focused on biomolecular structure prediction and design, with potential applications in drug discovery. Chew said rapid advances in AI were opening up possibilities far beyond the technology's current applications, even as questions remain over how to ensure increasingly powerful systems operate within human ethical boundaries. "If that happens, then you know the question would be: how do you align the models? How do you align the machines to be doing things that are obvious to us as human beings?" he said. Chew highlighted the accelerating pace of technological development, particularly in scientific research, arguing that the longer-term implications of AI could be far greater than currently anticipated. "The trend is very very clear. It's that we are only at the beginning of what artificial intelligence can probably do," he said. "And if you look at where the trend is, [where] the progress is, particularly in areas of science, it's really trending on a very steep curve at this moment in time." Chew explained that while the technology's immediate impact could be overstated, its longer-term potential remained underappreciated. "I think in the short term we are probably overestimating it, but in the long term we are probably underestimating it," he said. His optimism comes at a time when technology giants have been pouring billions of dollars into AI-powered scientific research. Last week, the U.S. government, Meta and Google announced their participation in a $1.8 billion initiative to develop AI models capable of predicting how cells behave, in an effort to accelerate biological research and drug discovery. TikTok's parent company, ByteDance, is also developing its own AI models and exploring opportunities to collaborate with scientists on research. "There's an effort to see how we can collaborate with a lot of scientists to make some progress in science as well," Chew added. "There's been some work that we've done in this area, and it is very exciting." He described scientific discovery as one of the most promising applications of AI, even as the technology increasingly reshapes TikTok's operations, from content creation and recommendations to search and moderation. Chew cautioned that AI's growing capabilities would require stronger safeguards, particularly as autonomous systems become more widely adopted. "I think the cybersecurity risks are quite big," he said, warning that users may grant AI agents extensive permissions without fully understanding the potential consequences. He pointed to the risks of allowing AI agents to make purchases autonomously, saying the systems could end up buying more than users intended in their eagerness to complete a task. Chew also highlighted the growing cybersecurity challenges facing companies, as increasingly sophisticated AI models make it significantly cheaper for malicious actors to carry out fraudulent activities. "So you need the right tools to now you know defend against the fast falling cost of creating problems for platforms like us, security problems for us," he emphasized.

events.title: Netanyahu demands probe into sources for award-winning Gaza film NAZA
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Documentary draws on 24 anonymous Israeli sources accusing military of killing Palestinians in Gaza using AI systems. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has called for an investigation into the anonymous sources featured in a documentary alleging that Israel’s military killed civilians in Gaza using AI-powered targeting systems. The award-winning film, NAZA, draws on testimony from 24 unnamed Israeli military whistleblowers accusing the army of using the systems to kill numerous civilians in the besieged territory. list 1 of 3 Child among eight killed by Israel on Gaza ‘ceasefire’ anniversary list 2 of 3 Hundreds of doctors demand World Medical Association suspend Israel list 3 of 3 How genocidal war on Gaza is shaping Israel’s election “I demand that the chief of general staff, the head of the Shin Bet, and the attorney general launch a comprehensive investigation into the participants in the film ‘Naza’ and prosecute them for serious information security violations, criminal libel, and harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests,” Netanyahu said on X on Saturday evening. “The film presents a false, misleading, and biased narrative that defames the State of Israel and the [Israeli military] internationally, severely damaging Israel’s standing,” he added. In a statement last month, the Israeli military said it “categorically” rejected the whistleblowers’ allegations, calling some of their assertions “absurd’ and contradictory. It insisted that the selection and approval of strikes “are made by human personnel only”, in line with the military’s guidelines. Israeli army Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir has called for legal action against the participants to be considered and ordered an investigation into suspected leaks of classified military information used in the film’s production. NAZA takes its name from the Israeli military term for civilian casualties expected in air strikes, an abbreviated form of the Hebrew phrase for “collateral damage”. The film was awarded a special jury prize at the Venice International Film Festival and received a historic 25-minute standing ovation. It has also triggered a political storm in Israel. The film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, have been accused of “treason”. Netanyahu and Culture Minister Miki Zohar have threatened to revoke their Israeli citizenship. Last week, the head of Israel’s National Public Diplomacy Directorate, Tzipi Hotovely, awarded the creators of another film, NAZA: The Real Story, certificates of recognition for countering the “blood libels” made in the original NAZA film. According to a statement from the Prime Minister’s Office, NAZA: The Real Story features testimony from soldiers refuting the original claims. In contrast, 43 Israeli rights groups defended the filmmakers of NAZA and denounced the threats being directed at them, according to Israel’s Channel 12 news. Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began on October 7, 2023, after Hamas’s armed wing, the Qassam Brigades, and other Palestinian groups attacked southern Israel, killing 1,139 people and taking about 240 captive. Since then, Israel has killed at least 74,000 Palestinians, including at least 21,000 children, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.

events.title: Kaniva wants to be known as an EV charging hub
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tesla applies to nearly double the number of chargers in Kaniva Kaniva could soon become one of the biggest EV charging sites in Australia. ( Supplied: Bale Farming ) Tesla hopes to nearly double the number of fast chargers it has in the country town of Kaniva from 10 to 18. Experts say more investment is required to ensure EV charging infrastructure keeps up with vehicle sales. Residents have until next Monday to object to the company's plans. On a long stretch of highway roughly halfway between Melbourne and Adelaide is a farming town hoping to cement its reputation as an electric vehicle (EV) charging must-see. The western Victorian farming town of Kaniva, with a population of roughly 800 people, already has 10 Tesla Superchargers behind its quaint country pub. The global tech giant has submitted plans to the local council to install another eight, and publican Bob Cane couldn't be happier. Kaniva is home to 10 EV charging sites, with plans to install another eight. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) "It's about bringing people to Kaniva, connecting them with a classic, quintessential Australian classic town," Mr Cane said. Painted sheep have adorned the streets of Kaniva since 2012. ( ABC News: Martin Boulton ) Kaniva currently markets itself as the first and last highway town in Victoria, the gateway to the Wimmera Mallee Silo Art Trail and the "home of Sheep Art". Mr Cane said the chargers were invigorating the town and adding another string to its economy. "When they plug in their car, what are they going to do? [They will] go for a walk into town, get a coffee, grab a hamburger," he said. Bob Cane is hoping the new Supercharger stations will be up and running before Christmas. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) The Windmill Cafe owner Jemma Hill said the chargers had been a boon for the town. "They [travellers] stop, they come over, they grab their lunch and their coffee, they come into town," she said. "It's creating extra foot traffic within the town, which is fantastic, makes it feel very alive." Jemma Hill says the current EV chargers have helped her business. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) The existing chargers are a lifesaver for some travellers already tackling the trek between Melbourne and Adelaide. "We do this trip a few times a year … If we didn't have this, we couldn't get [to Melbourne]," Tom Beresford said. Kaniva is home to about 800 people. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) West Wimmera Shire Council deputy mayor Helen Hobbs said the site, which has been open for about nine months, had already made a difference in the town. "That has actually given people like the bakery confidence to invest," Cr Hobbs said. "To have a brand new bakery with seating for 100 people, it's beyond anything I could have imagined." Helen Hobbs says the EV chargers have brought outside investment into the town. ( ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya ) EV sales doubled in the first half of 2026 compared with the same period last year, according to the Electric Vehicle Council of Australia. The council's Aman Gaur attributed the jump to cheaper EVs, rising fuel costs and improved charging networks. "We're now up to 4,200 charging locations across Australia and over 11,000 connectors," Mr Gaur said. "Charging stations have definitely been increasing in Victoria and the number of connectors has also been following suit." Ampol this month paid $225 million to buy Evie, one of the country's largest charging networks. Milad Haghani says if EV demand continues to grow at the same pace, charging infrastructure will have to catch up. ( ABC News: Patrick Stone ) University of Melbourne associate professor of urban resilience and mobility Milad Haghani said charging infrastructure would have a serious job keeping up if the EV sales boom continued. "It's hard to predict whether or not the spike in demand that we have observed this year is going to be sustainable," he said. "But if even a fraction of this demand continues into the future, that means that the infrastructure has some catching up to do." Public chargers have rarely had queues, he said, but that could change as more people buy EVs. The West Wimmera Shire Council has published Tesla's planning application online while it assesses the proposal. The application says the upgrade would cost $250,000 and that the existing 10-stall site, open for about nine months, has exceeded the company's expectations. A traffic report filed with the application says 10 to 20 EVs charge at the site each day, with holidays a natural peak period. Residents have until next Monday to lodge an objection to Tesla's plans.

events.title: NutryFarm shareholders seek CEO’s removal as company pivots from durians to data centres
events.summary: The dispute comes as NutryFarm seeks to rebuild its business and resume trading on the SGX mainboard after more than four years of suspension since April 2022. The dispute adds pressure to NutryFarm as it tries to restart trading on the SGX mainboard after years of suspension. The company says it is reviewing the allegations and seeking legal advice. NutryFarm is shifting from durians to data centres and AI services. Its restructuring could turn creditors into major shareholders, but it may also dilute existing holders and deepen the control fight. SINGAPORE – Shareholders seeking to remove NutryFarm International chief executive Niu Liming have challenged his right to vote on behalf of a major shareholder, complicating matters at the former durian distributor as it tries to rebuild its business around data centres and artificial intelligence services. NutryFarm said on Oct 11 that it had received a letter the previous day objecting to the validity of proxy votes granted by shareholder Jia Lijie to Niu, including any conflict of interest arising from the arrangement. The letter concerns votes that Niu allegedly intends to exercise at a special general meeting. The announcement did not identify the specific meeting. This follows an Oct 9 request from shareholders identifying themselves as Tianci International, Chen Meng, Lee Bee Li, Lim Hean Nerng, Gao Huazhu, Ang Poh Guan and Wu Jiansheng, who claim to hold at least 10% of NutryFarm’s paid-up capital, to convene a special general meeting. At the meeting, the shareholders want to remove Niu as a director and from his other appointments within the group, elect shareholder Charlie In to the board, and ask directors to consider appointing In as CEO. In, identified as In Nanny (sic) Sing Charlie in the Oct 9 filing, is chairman of corporate advisory firm Raffles Financial Group. His biography lists experience in investments, restructuring, capital raising and helping Chinese companies list overseas. According to media reports, his connection to NutryFarm dates back to March 2021, when Raffles Financial invested $5 million in exchange for 10 million NutryFarm shares through a married deal with a substantial shareholder. Charlie In is chairman of corporate advisory firm Raffles Financial Group. PHOTO: RAFFLES FINANCIAL GROUP LIMITED In a separate demand letter on Oct 9, the same shareholders demanded Niu’s immediate removal from all executive positions, his exclusion from board discussions and voting on the matter. NutryFarm said it was reviewing the allegations in the demand letter, and seeking legal advice on the other two letters. However, its announcement did not detail the allegations or explain the reasons for the removal demand. The dispute comes as NutryFarm seeks to rebuild its business and resume trading on the Singapore Exchange mainboard after trading was suspended in April 2022 , more than four years ago. NutryFarm was placed under judicial management in June 2022 and discharged from the arrangement in February 2026, returning control of the company to its board. Its restructuring involves creditors who could become major shareholders by exchanging loans for shares, and lenders with security over its new AI business. According to NutryFarm’s 2024 annual report, Jia held 21.7 million NutryFarm shares, or 15.78%, making her the largest shareholder of the company. Niu directly owned just 360,000 shares, or 0.26%. However, the report lists him as having a deemed interest in Jia’s shares and a further 13.3 million shares belonging to Cheng Meng through a share pledge arrangement. Together with his own shares, these amounted to a 25.72% direct and deemed interest in NutryFarm. Niu’s involvement in NutryFarm began before he became its executive director and CEO. He has an ownership interest in Corpbond IV, the creditor that applied to the High Court to place the company under judicial management in June 2022 . Judicial management puts a distressed company under an appointed manager to try to rescue the business or achieve a better outcome for creditors. According to NutryFarm’s 2022 annual report, Niu was appointed executive director and CEO on Dec 19, 2022, when the company was under judicial management. Niu Liming’s involvement in NutryFarm began before he became its executive director and CEO. At its annual general meeting on Dec 5, 2025, In asked Niu about the difficulties the company faced during judicial management, the prospects of the new AI business and his suitability to continue as executive director. Niu said he had been NutryFarm’s largest creditor when he initiated judicial management over a company with no cash and difficulties retaining control of overseas subsidiaries. He said he lent the company another $1 million in December 2022 to support operations and cover the judicial manager’s fees. NutryFarm previously operated nutrition and health food businesses and expanded into durian distribution.

events.title: My cofounder and I were rivals at hackathons. At 21, I've put college on hold to build a startup with him.
events.summary: Raymond Loong Ng put his college plans on hold to build a startup in San Francisco. Provided by Raymond Loong Ng. At 21, Raymond Loong Ng put college on hold after his startup raised $250,000 from VC firm Afore Capital. He and his cofounder spent two months in a program in San Francisco, working on their startup. A subsequent investment brought their total funding to $1 million, and they're now back in Singapore awaiting O-1 visas. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Raymond Loong Ng, 21, the cofounder of Makeable, a San Francisco-based startup. It's been edited for length and clarity. I was born in Vietnam and moved to Singapore when I was 9. As a kid, I always had some kind of side hustle . In school, I sold toys, snacks, in-game currency, and sneakers to my classmates — anything that might earn me a little extra pocket money. When I was 16, I did an internship at an auditing firm, where I had the chance to speak with a lot of business owners. I began to see technology as a tool that could help me advance in the business world. I ended up getting a diploma in applied AI and analytics at a polytechnic after finishing secondary school. I was never the best at math or coding, but it offered me a way to turn my ideas into actual projects. Have you relocated abroad for career opportunities, retirement, or lower living costs? We want to hear from you. Fill out this short form to share your story. I always saw myself as the connector: I could spot a problem, form a vision, attract resources, then bring in my smartest classmates to make things happen. That was how I began building projects of my own. I built an AI tool that helps ex-offenders build résumés and find jobs. I also started a community of young AI builders that runs workshops for students across Singapore. From rivals to cofounders In school, the projects we built often felt theoretical. Participating in hackathons gave me the chance to build solutions under real-world market constraints. Although we had crossed paths earlier through a separate scholarship program, hackathons were also how I got to know the person who would later become my cofounder better. Ng and his cofounder started out on rival hackathon teams before deciding to work together. Provided by Raymond Loong Ng. We competed as rivals on different teams, but would often find ourselves among the only people still working at 2 or 3 a.m. Eventually, we decided we wanted to be on the same team. We started entering competitions together in late 2023 and went on a winning streak. We soon realized that full software solutions were becoming harder to differentiate in hackathons as AI tools and models advanced. We ventured into hardware because it gave AI a way to be deployed in the real world. At a medical technology hackathon in 2025, we built a device to help paralyzed patients communicate through brainwaves and eye blinks. That became our startup, Neural Drive. The product caught the attention of a local hospital and is set to undergo a clinical trial there. At the same time, I was trying to find my way to the US. I grew up fascinated by the people and stories of Silicon Valley . My favorite films were "Jobs" and "The Social Network," and they made me feel that if I wanted to build something that could change the world, I had to be there. While serving my two years of mandatory military service, I applied to several US colleges but was rejected by all. I ended up being accepted into the computer science program at the National University of Singapore, but I still wanted to go to the States. I kept reaching out to venture capital firms in the US, and Neural Drive eventually caught the attention of Afore Capital in June. In June, Afore Capital made a $250,000 pre-seed investment in Neural Drive. My cofounder and I then joined its two-month Founders-in-Residence program in San Francisco . Ng and his cofounder spent two months in San Francisco as part of Afore Capital's founders-in-residence program. Provided by Raymond Loong Ng. The timing was tricky. College was due to begin in August, so I had to defer my enrollment before classes started. My cofounder had to request a leave of absence from school, too. It wasn't an easy decision, but we took a bet on ourselves. I found a city that moved as fast as I did I had visited Shenzhen in China before and expected Silicon Valley to look even more futuristic. Instead, I was surprised by how ordinary it looked. Because we were scrimping on rent, we moved into a hacker house in San Francisco's Tenderloin neighborhood. Those two months in San Francisco were intense, but incredibly rewarding. We were often working until 4 a.m., but we made as much progress as we would have in two years in Singapore. The sheer density of talent inspired us: "What are you working on?" felt like the way people said hello. It was a city full of workaholics. I thought: This is my kind of place. Ng said he enjoyed the fast-paced lifestyle in Silicon Valley. Provided by Raymond Loong Ng. We went through several pivots before landing on Makeable, our startup that lets people build a physical product from an idea. All they have to do is describe their idea in a prompt. Makeable can generate everything from the 3D model to the electronics and code, then sends users a kit they can put together themselves, like Lego. In our final week of the program, Afore Capital made a follow-on investment, bringing our total funding to date to $1 million. We flew back to Singapore to apply for our O-1 visas . While we're home, we're still working. The plan is to return to San Francisco for the next few years and keep building our company. I probably have to extend my leave of absence. If it doesn't work out, I'll go back to school. I want to keep that option open. But honestly, I hope I don't have to. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: UAE Property: 'Can my tenant legally list my apartment as a holiday rental without my consent?'
events.summary: Question: I own an apartment in Dubai Marina, which I've rented to the same tenant for two years. A neighbour recently contacted me because different people appear to be entering the apartment every few days with suitcases. I checked one of the holiday rental websites and, to my surprise, found what appears to be my apartment being advertised for short-term stays . I never agreed to this and my tenancy contract says the property is for residential use by the tenant. The tenant is paying the rent on time, so financially, I haven't lost anything, but I'm uncomfortable with strangers continually using a property I'm responsible for. Can a tenant legally do this without my permission, and could I as the owner face problems if something happens? Ahmed, Abu Dhabi Answer: I wouldn't ignore this simply because the rent continues to arrive on time. There's an important distinction between a tenant occasionally having friends or family stay and somebody commercially offering another person's property as short-term accommodation. Dubai's holiday-home sector is regulated, and properties being used for this purpose need to comply with the relevant licensing and registration requirements. Separately, your tenancy agreement determines what your tenant is permitted to do with the apartment. Subletting in Dubai is not illegal; however, the landlord must be informed and agree to the subleasing. Since you were not informed, his actions are illegal and he cannot simply decide to turn your property into his own short-term rental business. Before taking any action I suggest you document what you've discovered. Save screenshots of the advertisement, including photographs that clearly identify your apartment and keep any messages from neighbours or building management. I would then write to the tenant and ask for an explanation rather than immediately making accusations. I'd also establish whether the apartment has actually been registered as a holiday home and, if so, how this was done without your knowledge. There's another practical concern: short-term occupation can mean considerably more wear and tear than a conventional tenancy, as well as possible issues with access cards, building security and insurance. For landlords, this is a useful reminder that receiving the rent doesn't necessarily mean everything is fine with the property. Sensible asset management means knowing how your investment is actually being used. Q: My former partner and I bought a villa in Dubai several years ago in both our names. We have now separated. I want to sell the property so we can both move on financially, but my ex refuses. He says that because he owns half of the villa I cannot force him to sell his share. Neither of us can realistically afford to buy the other person out, and there is still a mortgage on the property. What happens when two people jointly own a Dubai property but one wants to sell and the other simply refuses? Are we effectively stuck owning it together indefinitely? Emma, Dubai A: This is unfortunately one of the complications of joint property ownership that people rarely think about when they're happily buying together. You cannot ordinarily sell your former partner's ownership interest simply because you want the whole property sold. Equally, however, joint ownership doesn't necessarily mean two people must remain financially tied together indefinitely. The first thing I'd establish is exactly how ownership is recorded on the title deed and the respective ownership percentages. Then have the property independently valued. Once you know the realistic selling price, deduct the outstanding mortgage and likely selling costs so both parties can see what equity would actually be available. Sometimes having a real number on the table makes negotiations considerably easier. Possible solutions include one party refinancing and purchasing the other's interest, an agreed sale on the open market or another mutually acceptable transfer arrangement, subject of course to the lender and Dubai Land Department requirements. I'd also check who has been paying the mortgage , service charges and other property expenses since the separation because those contributions may need to be considered when the financial position is ultimately resolved. If agreement genuinely cannot be reached, this moves beyond estate agency advice. You should speak to a Dubai lawyer experienced in property and co-ownership disputes about the legal mechanisms available to bring the joint ownership to an end. The wider lesson for unmarried couples, friends and relatives buying together is simple: discuss the break-up before the purchase. A written co-ownership agreement setting out what happens if one person wants to sell can prevent an enormous amount of difficulty later.
