events.title: Judge orders Trump administration to immediately stop taxpayer-funded TV ads
events.summary: A New York federal judge ordered the Trump administration to immediately stop airing government-funded ads criticized as propaganda and aimed at influencing the midterm election. The temporary restraining order by Judge Jennifer Rochon also bars the Department of Homeland Security from spending any more of the $20 million set aside for the TV ad campaign. President Donald Trump said on Oct. 5 he would pay for the ads going forward. The White House said the president would not reimburse the federal government for the cost of the already aired ads. A federal judge in New York ordered the Trump administration Sunday night to immediately stop airing controversial government-funded television ads featuring President Donald Trump that critics call political propaganda intended to influence the November midterm election. The temporary restraining order by Judge Jennifer Rochon in Manhattan federal court also bars the Department of Homeland Security from spending any more of the $20 million allocated for the ad campaign. About $19 million of that allocation has already been spent on the ads. The order came a day after the Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office, which is defending the Trump administration in a lawsuit challenging the ads, told Rochon that the ads would not continue being aired past Sunday. Rochon's order, which lasts 14 days unless extended, directs the Trump administration to cancel all scheduled ads, including those due to air on Sunday evening. The ads have included the caption "Paid for by the U.S. Government" since they began being aired. The Manhattan U.S. Attorney's Office declined to comment. The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment. The money for the ads came from a large appropriation by Congress for immigration enforcement. Russian lab worker dies amid plague reports — here's what we know Trump's nemesis in Europe: Why Spain's Sanchez is calling a snap election Trump tells South Korea to sign on to Alaska LNG deal or 'I'll just charge them more' The coalition of plaintiffs that sued to block the ads told Rochon earlier Sunday that she should issue the TRO despite the claim by the U.S. Attorney's Office that the ads would not continue past Sunday. "Defendants admit that appropriated funds were used to pay for political ads and do not dispute that this use of taxpayer money is unlawful," the plaintiffs said in a court filing Sunday. "Instead, much of Defendants' opposition boils down to a single premise: it is too late for the Court to act. That is not because Defendants have stopped airing the ads," the plaintiffs said. "Indeed, Defendants assert — boldly, given their failure to defend the ads on the merits — that ads will continue to air today, including during evening programming that will attract millions of viewers." Rochon agreed, saying in her order that the TRO request was not rendered moot by the U.S. Attorney's statement that the ads would stop Sunday. The judge also rejected an argument by the Justice Department that the coalition lacked legal standing to challenge the ads. Rochon said the coalition has shown it was likely to win the lawsuit, that it would suffer irreparable harm if the TRO was not granted, and that "an injunction serves the public interest." In addition to the other actions, the judge ordered the Trump administration not to enter into any new agreement or expand existing ones for the ads. And she stayed a purchase order for the ads between U.S. Customs and Border Protection and a contractor, Lepugh Inc., doing business as LMD Agency Inc. Rochon said she would soon issue a full opinion explaining her ruling. The coalition, which filed its lawsuit on Oct. 7, includes the advocacy group Common Cause and the Service Employees International Union Local 32BJ, which is headquartered in New York City. A separate lawsuit challenging the ads was filed that same day by the Democratic National Committee. The ads, which have been airing for weeks, drew criticism from Democrats who said they appear designed to help Trump's fellow Republicans in November's election, which will determine which political party controls both chambers of Congress. In its lawsuit, the coalition described one ad, titled "The Country He Loves," as featuring "rapid cuts of photos and videos of President Trump mixed in with text touting what the President views as his accomplishments in office," which includes "Largest Tax Cuts in History;" "Reigniting American Manufacturing;" and "Defend Law and Order and Police." "Between those messages, the screen repeatedly flashes the words "AMERICA WILL NEVER BE A COMMUNIST COUNTRY," the civil complaint noted. Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., wrote White House chief of staff Susie Wiles on Sept. 24, a day after that ad first aired.

events.title: The extra stripe that's landed Australian retailer White Fox in court
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Adidas sues White Fox Boutique over its trademark three-stripe design A pair of Adidas shorts with its trademark three-stripe design next to White Fox Boutique shorts with four stripes. ( Supplied ) German sportswear brand Adidas has accused Australian fashion retailer White Fox Boutique of infringing its trademark three-stripe design with garments featuring four stripes. Legal experts say the case could test the trademark registration. The matter is set down for hearing in early 2027. When is a stripe not a stripe? According to sportswear brand Adidas, when it is part of its trademark. The global sportswear giant is suing Australian online fashion retailer White Fox Boutique for selling items allegedly "deceptively similar" to its three-stripe logo, in a case experts say could test the trademark's registration. The German-based brand has filed a trademark infringement claim against the Sydney-based company, popular with teenagers, in the Federal Court of Australia. According to court documents, Adidas accuses White Fox of replicating its trademark across multiple clothing items and advertising content that feature four parallel stripes of equal width in a colour contrasting with the colour of the clothing. Adidas claims this design is "deceptively similar" to its three-stripe trademark, which it has used in Australia for more than 65 years and globally for more than 75 years. White Fox is defending the case, which will play out in court hearings next year. A White Fox Boutique advertisement seen on the back of a bus. ( Supplied ) According to the documents, White Fox Boutique has promoted and supplied clothing with four parallel stripes on it since March this year, including advertisements on buses, bus stops and on social media. Adidas said it asked White Fox to remove the garments from sale in March and to stop using the four-stripe design, which White Fox declined to do. Adidas further claimed White Fox used genuine Adidas shoes, in the same colours as its clothing, in some promotional material, which it said took advantage of the brand's reputation and may lead consumers to draw an association between the two companies. An Instagram post advertising a White Fox Boutique outfit paired with genuine Adidas shoes. ( Supplied ) It alleges White Fox's actions are likely to cause damage to its reputation. In court on Friday, White Fox's barrister Ed Heerey KC said the online fashion retailer would argue the four stripes emblazoned on the label's clothing were simply decorative rather than a trademark. He highlighted similar items bearing the four stripes from other brands, including fast-fashion labels Princess Polly, Glassons and Shein. Intellectual property law expert Muhammad Abbas said this case was not just about a fourth stripe. "Adding a stripe is neither a complete answer to a trademark claim nor automatically an infringement," Dr Abbas, a Queensland University of Technology lecturer, said. He explained a 2023 High Court decision considered the impression a notional buyer, "allowing for imperfect recollection", would have of the registered trademark, compared to the impression created by the sign used. The three-stripe design dates back to the brand's foundation in 1949, but was not trademarked until 1952 after Adidas discovered a Finnish brand Karhu had trademarked the same logo. Founder Adolf Dassler struck a deal and traded two bottles of whiskey and the equivalent of 1,600 euros ($AUD2,500) for the logo, which it has extensively protected ever since. In 2013, it successfully sued Pacific Brands over its use of a four-stripe design on some of its Dunlop and Grosby shoe designs, with the court ruling that three of the 12 designs in question were "deceptively similar". However, University of Technology Sydney School of Law senior lecturer Sarah Hook said challenges overseas had led to Adidas losing its trademark registration in some jurisdictions. In the US, Adidas unsuccessfully took high-end designer Thom Browne to court over a four-stripe design. Thom Browne wore socks with the four-stripe design to court in New York. ( Reuters: Eduardo Munoz ) Thom Browne then challenged the trademark registration in the UK, and the High Court ultimately ruled the trademark was invalid. Fashion designer Thom Browne emerges from a New York courthouse victorious over sportswear giant Adidas. University of Melbourne intellectual property law studies director Benjamin Hopper said distinctiveness was a core doctrine of trademark law, meaning it had to be distinguishable from other goods or services from other traders in the same marketplace.

events.title: Judge halts Trump administration's taxpayer-funded ads
events.summary: A federal judge on Sunday ordered the Trump administration to immediately halt taxpayer-funded ads featuring President Trump. Why it matters: The ruling temporarily blocks the ads weeks before November's midterm elections as multiple lawsuits challenging the Trump administration's use of taxpayer money play out in court. Sunday's ruling stems from a suit filed in the Southern District of New York by Washington, D.C.-based watchdog Common Cause, non-profit Democracy Forward and other plaintiffs. A similar lawsuit , filed by the Democratic National Committee, was filed in D.C. federal court earlier this month. The big picture: The Trump administration maintains that the ads are public service announcements and that previous Republican and Democratic administrations have used taxpayer-funded advertising to promote government policies. Trump pledged to pay for the ads himself after both lawsuits were filed, though the White House told Axios there were no plans to reimburse the government for millions already spent on the ads. Driving the news: The plaintiffs in the New York lawsuit allege that the Trump administration exceeded congressional authorization and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda. In a brief order , U.S. District Judge Jennifer Rochon found that a motion filed by the coalition was "not moot." She found they had "demonstrated that they are likely to succeed on the merits, will suffer irreparable harm in the absence of an injunction, the balance of the equities tips in their favor, and an injunction serves the public interest," according to the order. The suit names the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought, and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles as defendants. What they're saying: The coalition said in a statement emailed by Democracy Forward it was "pleased the court acted swiftly to prevent more taxpayer dollars from being used for such blatantly unlawful political propaganda." The statement added, "There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda." Representatives for the White House and DHS did not immediately respond to Axios' Sunday evening request for comment. What's next: A hearing is scheduled for Oct. 13 to discuss next steps in the case. Editor's note: This story was updated with a statement from the plaintiffs.

events.title: Saudi Arabia says 1 dead, 11 injured in latest attack on Riyadh airport
events.summary: Sunday’s strike on King Khalid International airport kills a Pakistani national. A projectile has struck Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International airport, killing one person and injuring 11, according to the country’s civil aviation authority. The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) identified the deceased in Sunday’s attack as a Pakistani resident and said the injured were transferred to several hospitals for medical care. list 1 of 3 Yemeni government’s military says its forces advancing against Houthis list 2 of 3 Why are Houthi missiles breaking through Saudi Arabia’s air defences? list 3 of 3 Iran’s FM urges diplomacy in call with Saudi counterpart The strike on terminals 3 and 4, which serve domestic flights, occurred a day after a Houthi missile hit the airport, killing 12 people and wounding more than 300, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died on Sunday due to injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, bringing the death toll to 13. Following Sunday’s attack, GACA said damage assessments and safety inspections of the airport were under way. A witness on board a taxiing aircraft at the airport told the Reuters news agency that a projectile struck the tarmac next to several parked planes at about 8:30pm (17:30 GMT) on Sunday, causing a fire. The witness said the aircraft returned to the gate, where the passengers disembarked and were told to leave. The Riyadh airport has been struck four times in the past five days. Houthi attacks on King Khalid airport on Thursday killed at least three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, according to GACA. The airport has been closed since Saturday’s attack, which was the deadliest in the country since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the strikes before Sunday’s. The airport attacks have escalated the war in Yemen and threaten to draw in the US military. US President Donald Trump says he is weighing whether to join the fight against the Houthis. The escalation puts further pressure on global oil supplies and prices, as well as on commercial shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait off the Yemeni coast, a crucial alternative waterway to the Strait of Hormuz. Trump had said he intends to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, who is seeking help against the Houthis, but there were no signs on Sunday that the US president had followed up on his claim. There are fears that US intervention could prompt the Houthis to halt shipping through Bab al-Mandeb, further restricting the flow of oil out of the Gulf. The rebels seized key areas along the strait last month. The Saudi-led coalition, backing forces loyal to Yemen’s internationally recognised government, has been trying to seize them back.

events.summary: The claim marks the first time a UK prime minister has publicly acknowledged Russia’s interference in the vote to leave the EU. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is “clear” that Russia interfered in the country’s 2016 Brexit vote, warning French and German voters of the same threat. “I asked the question coming to Downing Street: Was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? And I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was,” Burnham said in an interview with The Rest Is Politics podcast released on Sunday. list 1 of 3 UK Greens leader seeks rule change after party declares Zionism is racism list 2 of 3 Photos: Thousands march across Europe to demand end to Israel’s war on Gaza list 3 of 3 Has Israel shut the UK consulate in East Jerusalem – or downgraded it? Burnham’s comments mark the first time a UK prime minister has publicly acknowledged that Russia interfered in the UK’s vote to leave the European Union. Burnham did not provide evidence for or details on the claim. He said that “these things are important now to put clearly on the record, and, I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.” Burnham said he spoke with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz about possible links between Russia and the far-right Alternative for Germany party when the two leaders met last week in Berlin. In his address to the United Nations General Assembly in September, Burnham also condemned Russia’s attempt to interfere in the UK’s 2019 general election. According to a 2020 report by Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee, the UK government had failed to ask for a deep assessment of Russia’s interference in the 2016 referendum. The report did confirm that Russia had meddled in the 2014 Scottish independence referendum , however. Russia has repeatedly denied meddling in Western democracies or interfering in another country’s elections or referendums, casting the UK as being gripped by “anti-Russian hysteria”. Last month, Burnham argued that the UK should reconsider options for a future relationship with the EU, including rejoining the bloc, reigniting the decisive debate more than a decade after the historic vote. He said that the UK’s departure from the bloc had failed to fulfil Brexit supporters’ pledge of “taking back control”, and instead has made the UK weaker economically and on immigration.

events.title: Beyond AI: How HKICC 2026 Develops Judgement, Resilience and Global Leadership
events.summary: As technology transforms how business problems are analysed and solved, the HKUST International Case Competition 2026 challenges students to develop the human capabilities that remain essential to leadership. [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] AI can generate an answer in seconds. Knowing which answer to trust—and how to act on it—still requires human judgement. The HKUST International Case Competition (HKICC) 2026 put that distinction to the test, bringing together twelve elite undergraduate teams from leading business schools around the world to navigate ambiguity, defend complex decisions and work across cultures under pressure. The University of British Columbia Sauder School of Business emerged as champion after a week of competition focused on the innovation and application of artificial intelligence. As businesses navigate technological disruption and growing complexity, future leaders must look beyond fast answers. They must use technology to strengthen analysis while retaining responsibility for context, trade-offs and long-term value. Supported by HSBC for the fourth consecutive year, HKICC brings together high-performing teams from universities across Australia, Canada, Hong Kong SAR, Hungary, the Netherlands, Singapore, South Korea, Spain, Thailand, and the United States. Participants tackle real-world business challenges while collaborating across cultures and perspectives. “At HSBC, we are committed to nurturing the next generation of business leaders,” said Mr. David GRIMME, Chief Operating Officer, Asia and Middle East, HSBC. “HKICC is an exceptional platform for talented students to tackle real-world business challenges while sharpening strategic judgement, strengthening creative problem-solving, and building collaboration skills.” Turning AI-Enabled Analysis into Decisions Business challenges rarely have a single correct answer. Leaders must still evaluate assumptions, weigh risks and make decisions under uncertainty. Leaders must decide which assumptions to test, which risks to accept and where limited resources can have the greatest impact. At HKICC, participants developed practical strategies related to the innovation and application of artificial intelligence. Working within tight timelines, teams adjusted their strategies as new information emerged and defended their reasoning before experienced industry judges. Liron SAEDI of the University of Southern California Marshall School of Business, who received the Best Presenter Award, said: "AI can help with the research behind a case, but at the end of the day, we are the ones recommending and implementing the solutions.” While participants spent much of the week analysing cases, their learning also extended beyond the competition room. A highlight of this year's programme was the HSBC Student Engagement Event, where participants engaged directly with senior leaders and gained insights into leadership and career development. After a week of intense competition, the University of British Columbia Sauder School of Business emerged as Champion of HKICC 2026. The University of Southern California Marshall School of Business and the National University of Singapore secured the first and second Runner-up titles respectively. UBC Sauder also received the Outstanding Business Concept Award for its innovative and compelling solution. Beyond the case analyses and final presentations, participants practised the behaviours that effective teamwork requires: managing time, testing assumptions and ensuring different perspectives were heard. Anjana SRINIVASAN, Chief Administrative Officer Asia & Middle East and COO Asia International Markets at HSBC, who served as one of the final judges, said: "Great teamwork is more than simply sharing the work. It means listening as much as contributing, challenging ideas respectfully, and ensuring every voice is heard and valued. The ability to collaborate across different perspectives while working under pressure is a skill that will serve these students well throughout their studies and careers.” For participants, those principles were tested in practice. Boin KANG from the National University of Singapore said: "It's really about time management, working under pressure, stress-testing our knowledge and rationale, and explaining our thinking to one another." Together, these experiences required teams to move beyond dividing tasks. They had to challenge ideas constructively, reconcile different viewpoints and maintain a coherent recommendation under pressure. The Capabilities Future Leaders Will Need Through HKICC, HKUST Business School and HSBC share a commitment to developing leaders who can navigate uncertainty, adapt to change and work across cultures and markets.

events.title: Why China is importing a record amount of gold — and what it means for prices
events.summary: Central-bank diversification and a weak property and stock market are driving China’s institutional and retail gold buying. The gold rush would help put a floor under bullion prices, even as the buoyant U.S. yields kept a lid on demand for the non-yielding precious metal. China's gold reserves still remain well below the U.S. stockpiles. China's central bank has bought gold for 23 straight months, and the country is importing more of the precious metal than ever. That buying spree reflects Beijing's push to cut its dependence on the dollar, and Chinese households' lack of safe alternatives, with analysts expecting sustained demand for the bullion in a struggling economy. The People's Bank of China added about 23 tonnes in September, its biggest monthly purchase in almost three years, according to State Administration of Foreign Exchange data, extending the longest purchasing streak since at least 2015 . Chinese households and companies are turning to gold as a safe haven. The country spent a record $158.8 billion, importing more than 1,000 tonnes in the first eight months of 2026, customs data show. That exceeds the $96.5 billion and 886 tonnes imported in all of 2025. Consumer gold imports in China hit a record in the first eight months of this year, according to Aakash Doshi, head of gold strategy at State Street Investment Management. The surging premiums in China's onshore prices indicate "stronger winter seasonal demand," Doshi said. The accumulation of the metal comes as gold prices have fallen. They pulled back more than 8% in September to about $4,176 an ounce, after in January hitting a record above $5,500 . Doshi forecasts gold prices to rise to $4,750 to $5,500 per troy ounce by the end of the first quarter in 2027, buoyed by robust demand. The PBOC's main motive is political, according to Carsten Menke, an analyst at Julius Baer Group, pointing to "the weaponization of the U.S. dollar and the related desire to be less dependent on U.S. Treasuries as a reserve asset." Western governments froze Russia's central bank assets after its 2022 invasion of Ukraine, underscoring how foreign-held reserves can be restricted at times of geopolitical friction, while gold in a country's own vaults remains insulated. China has offloaded holdings of Treasurys, which reached an 18-year low of $618 billion in July, according to U.S. Treasury data, as Beijing continued to diversify its foreign-exchange reserves . Chinese demand is also being fueled by gold's reputation as a safe haven. Consumers in the country, nervous about the shaky economy, are loading up on gold jewelry, bars and coins. Domestic investors have few alternatives with the real estate market, once the main store of household wealth, locked in a multiyear slump. The benchmark CSI 300 index is down around 8% this year, versus the S&P 500's 13% gain. Returns from bank deposits and bonds have declined amid tepid borrowing demand. China's one-year government bond yield fell to around 1.2%, against about 4.46% in the U.S . "The opportunity cost of holding gold is also much lower in China than in many Western markets," said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank. Adding to the momentum of the unprecedented buying is Beijing's plan to build a deeper domestic gold market, prompting it to replenish inventories, said Menke. He estimated that the central bank bought around 190 tonnes this year by end-August, including 110 tonnes that were unreported. China's demand for gold has helped bullion withstand pressures that would have caused a deeper fall in prices, as buoyant U.S. yields kept a lid on demand for the non-yielding precious metal. The price of gold usually goes down when interest rates go up. "Chinese buying has become an important source of structural support for gold prices," Ewa Manthey, commodities strategist at ING Bank. Central banks buy for the long term and are far less sensitive to price than retail investors, Manthey added. Echoing that view, Carsten pointed out that gold prices have stayed above their levels in summer, even though interest rate expectations and bond yields have risen more sharply. The Federal Reserve has indicated another interest rate hike on the cards for 2026. The world's fifth-largest gold holder owned 2,387 tonnes as of August, according to the World Gold Council , less than a third of the that held by the U.S. Any renewed confidence in China's property and equities could blunt demand for gold, as well as a weaker yuan that makes gold pricier at home or higher interest rates that make deposits more attractive, Hansen said. The larger shift would come if central banks lost interest in diversifying reserves and geopolitical tensions eased, Hansen said, adding that "neither appears particularly imminent."

events.title: Fox stays positive on data centers even as public backlash grows
events.summary: The News Despite increasingly critical media coverage of AI and the spread of data centers across the US, one news network has been painting a more positive picture. More than half of the references to data centers on Fox News over the last two years would have left viewers with a favorable impression, compared to less than 10% on CNN and 5% on MS NOW, according to a new Semafor analysis of mentions of data centers on each network. The mentions were pulled from closed captions preserved by the Internet Archive, which keeps a digital, searchable library of recorded TV news. A pair of AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI scored each reference on its content, with the network’s name removed. Mentions of data centers have, predictably, shot up across all three networks in recent months as political backlash against AI swells and the data centers themselves have become a salient issue ahead of the midterms. But Fox’s opinion and morning shows, including, , and leaned on the promise of AI, economic investment and the race with China, skewing Fox’s coverage more favorably, the analysis showed. The network’s news shows were more measured. In an Aug. 23 monologue that at one point featured a chyron reading “The case for data centers,” Fox host Brian Kilmeade acknowledged “real concerns,” but argued that “saying no to data centers nationwide also means saying no to the tax dollars that can flow into a community. … If Americans don’t build the infrastructure to meet the demand, somebody else will.” On CNN and MS NOW, the criticism focused as much on the facilities’ political toxicity as on harms like power bills or water use, casting them as unpopular with voters and a liability for politicians who back them heading into the midterms. Data centers “are driving up energy costs, sucking up water supplies, wiping out rather than creating jobs,” MS NOW’s Katy Tur said in May. “Politicians beware.” Polling shows that across demographic groups, Americans hold increasingly negative views of data centers: More than half of Americans say data centers are mostly bad for the environment , Pew Research Center found last month, compared with 39% in January. Fox News did not comment for this story. Max’s view The pro-data center programming on Fox News comes as the right tries to define its positions in an AI-fueled, post-Donald Trump future. Fox’s favorable data center coverage mirrors Trump’s position on their growth and the need for AI companies to help fuel the US economy. “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in August. “If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame.” But anger about data centers and the rapid advancement of AI represents a faultline within the MAGA coalition that swept Trump back into office. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., have questioned some data centers in their states, while Texas Gov. Greg Abbott seems to have flipped from supporting data centers to looking to slow their growth in his state amid a tougher-than-expected reelection campaign. Some on the right I have talked to in the last several months worry that Fox News, which Trump watches religiously, and other pro-data center voices are encouraging the president to take positions that are broadly unpopular with his rural and suburban base. “The Big Tech oligarchs, the guys driving AI, did a terrible job,” Steve Bannon, a staunchly anti-AI Trump ally, told the Daily Signal in September. “They came in to try to muscle local communities, and particularly since President Trump’s strongest base is in exurban and rural communities, that’s where they were really the ugliest, and they haven’t made their case, and they particularly haven’t made their case at the local level about the economics of this, and the energy of this, and the water of this, and the manifestation of what these things are going to be used for.” Room for Disagreement Not all of Fox’s data center coverage has been rosy; its tenor grew slightly less favorable in 2026 compared to last year. “It’s taxing our system way too much on water, agriculture land, or electricity. We’re gonna implode,” the Texas agriculture commissioner said in an interview on a weekend Fox show in August. “We just can’t do it. There’s not enough.

events.title: Hack reveals Netanyahu campaign's media ties
events.summary: The News Hacked messages from an adviser to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are providing a glimpse of his aides’ close ties to the media. The incumbent prime minister’s reelection campaign has been repeatedly rocked by hacked and leaked documents, part of broad attempts to destabilize a wildly divisive leader both inside and outside his country ahead of Oct. 27 elections. The latest breach comes from the WhatsApp account of Netanyahu aide Jonatan Urich, who appears to have exposed sensitive information through a vibe-coded media-monitoring app. Haaretz reported Sunday that it had “verified” the leak. The messages include conversations between Urich and Amit Segal, a central media figure who is chief political analyst for Channel 12 News, the country’s leading broadcaster, and host of the program , an analogue of the US show of that name. In the exchanges, Segal offers advice about the campaign’s videos and its messaging: Netanyahu’s management of the aftermath of the October 7 attack is his core political advantage, he suggests. Segal mentions he offered the same advice to Netanyahu’s campaign spokeswoman. In another message, Urich shares a speech Netanyahu is planning to give. Segal declined to discuss the messages on the record. Urich, who is also enmeshed in a scandal over payments from Qatar, didn’t respond to an inquiry, but in a lawyers’ statement posted to X confirmed that he had been hacked and threatened legal consequences against anyone who published the content of the leaks. Israel’s Privacy Protection Law prohibits republishing content obtained through illegal means. Ben’s view Hacks and leaks are challenging to cover. The most important story in most hacks — including this one — is the hack itself; this is part of the broad internationalization of the Israeli political campaign, in which actors across the region and in the US line up for and, mostly against, the leader who led his country’s response to the October 7 attacks. But Israeli commentators also professed shock, if not surprise, Sunday at how closely aligned the journalist and spin doctor appeared to be. Segal is a center-right figure broadly aligned with Netanyahu — but he’s also a top journalist who appears on international platforms, like the American political figure Dan Senor’s widely-followed podcast, as an independent analyst. One Israeli journalist compared Segal’s role in Israel to that of Fox News host Bret Baier, who maintains journalistic independence despite working for a right-wing platform. The messages put a dent in Segal’s version of that image, and offer a glimpse at parts of an Israeli media that has grown very close to its prime minister. Room for Disagreement Segal addressed the controversy on News 12, describing the messages as part of a “very delicate tango between the journalist and the subject of their coverage.” He added that “any people I’ve covered over the years gave me drafts of speeches, saying, ‘This will be our campaign, what are your thoughts?’” Notable The region’s politics have been buffeted — and illuminated — repeatedly by aggressive cyber campaigns for years. Semafor reported in 2023 on extensive, leaked Iranian government communications that revealed Iranian attempts to influence US politics.

events.title: Hurricane Isaias leaves trail of destruction across the US Gulf Coast
events.summary: Crews rally for massive cleanup efforts in Florida and Alabama as weakened Isaias leaves hundreds of thousands in the dark. Residents across the southeastern United States have begun cleanup efforts after Hurricane Isaias , the first Atlantic tropical cyclone of the 2026 season, slammed ashore near Destin, Florida, on Friday. As of midafternoon Sunday, roughly 356,000 customers remain without power in southern Alabama and the northwestern region of Florida, according to data from PowerOutage.com, an independent tracking website. At its peak, the storm knocked out power to nearly 800,000 homes and businesses across the Gulf Coast. Sarah Gatewood, a spokesperson for the utility company Florida Power and Light (FPL), announced that workers from across Florida and more than two dozen other states had mobilised to restore power. At least four deaths have been linked to Isais after it made landfall as a Category 2 storm on the five-tier Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale. The tempest churned northward into Alabama on Saturday with fierce tropical-storm-force winds before weakening into a post-tropical cyclone and tracking further north towards the Appalachians. Though its power is waning , the storm continues to endanger the mid-Atlantic region with the potential for flash flooding. According to the National Weather Service (NWS), surface observations indicate that Isaias now has maximum sustained winds of 160 km/h (100 mph) and an estimated minimum central pressure of 28.88 inches, or 978 millibars. Across Florida and Alabama, residents have reported damage from the storm’s high-velocity winds. A Rest and Relax Inn in the resort city of Pensacola, Florida, saw its roof sheared off during the hurricane, and a boathouse was flattened in Destin. The immediate struggle for basic necessities was most stark in Pensacola, the westernmost part of the Florida Panhandle, where the storm downed power grids and caused widespread structural damage. Hundreds of cars lined the block around a United Cajun Navy distribution site, a volunteer disaster relief organisation, on Saturday morning. Pensacola’s Mayor DC Reeves warned of critical drinking water shortages following the storm, which affected drinking wells and water infrastructure. Residents, he said, remain under an advisory to boil tap water before use. “We are winding down day three of storm response and recovery operations, and we remain focused on public safety, clearing debris, and restoring critical infrastructure and services,” Reeves said on social media. Isaias also forced the indefinite closure of Pensacola International airport, Florida’s 10th-largest airfield, due to severe damage. Fallen trees and power lines continue to make travel hazardous in Houston County, Alabama, which remains under an emergency flash flood warning, according to state emergency officials. “Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice,” the agency posted on X.

events.title: ABC News offers contradictory explanation for vanishing Anduril story
events.summary: The News When ABC News removed a story about Donald Trump’s sons from its website without explanation on Thursday, an unnamed company source told media reporters the article had been published “prematurely.” Nathan Lee, the investigative reporter who wrote the original piece , used the same language in emails to Powerus and Anduril, two of the companies at the center of the piece. But emails between ABC News and its subjects, provided to Semafor, show the network seeking to downplay its errors by misrepresenting its own processes. On Oct. 7, ABC News published an investigation into a new $6.6 billion deal between defense contractor Anduril and the US Navy to build a new high-tech submarine shipyard in Maryland. The piece largely focused on the financial ties between President Donald Trump’s son and defense companies, noting that Donald Trump Jr. is a partner at investment firm 1789 Capital, which “claimed a major stake in Anduril in June 2025 from a $2.5 billion investment into the company.” After the piece was published, a spokesperson for Anduril reached out to Lee with several urgent requests for correction. The company — which had not responded to ABC News’ inquiries prior to its publication, according to an Anduril source — wanted the network to clarify connections between Anduril and 1789, noting that the firm had invested $50 million in Anduril’s latest round, a small percentage of the $2.5 billion total. “Today, 1789 owns approximately 0.13% of Anduril and has no major investor rights. Any suggestion that 1789 financed the round or holds significant ownership, governance position or ‘major stake’ in Anduril is inaccurate,” Anduril’s spokesperson wrote to Lee, according to emails obtained by Semafor. After the story was published on Wednesday, Lee told Anduril that the network was slightly tweaking the language in its piece, but it was otherwise standing by its story. “I have spoken to my editors and we have updated the story for accuracy,” Lee said in a note. “We had pulled the ‘major stake’ language from previous reporting. 1789 Capital did claim a stake from the $2.5 billion investment your company received, so we are standing by our language to that extent.” Anduril’s PR team was not satisfied, and continued to press the network to clarify its story, saying that the piece misstated 1789 Capital’s investment in Anduril’s fundraising round. “It’s still not clear. I read your text and it reads as if they invested the full $2.5b. Would be much more accurate to list their actual investment of $50m and even more accurate to share that they own less than a percentage point in Anduril,” a spokesperson wrote. In another email later Wednesday afternoon, Lee said ABC News’ editors had reviewed the language and were standing by the piece. “Apologies, but my editors said we are standing by the language. I’ll make sure to reach out to both of you directly for any future stories,” Lee said. But by Thursday, the network had changed its mind. The network removed the piece without explanation, and Peter Charalambous, an ABC News producer in New York, reached out to Anduril and Powerus, a drone contractor mentioned in the story, saying the story had been “published prematurely and removed from our website.” On Friday evening, ABC News republished a new version of the story re-reported by Charalambous, now without a byline . An editor’s note did not include language that the initial piece was published early. “Editor’s Note: CORRECTION: A version of this story published on Oct. 7 contained errors in the description of certain company investments, government contracts and event chronologies. After subsequent reporting, this version contains corrected information and additional context regarding some of those investments, contracts and events.” A network source told Semafor: “We always review every situation in a thorough and thoughtful manner and will not be providing further comment at this time.” The source also noted that it was extremely rare for ABC News to remove a story. Status reported Sunday that the article was mentioned during the network’s regular 9 am editorial call the day it was published, “suggesting at least some staffers were aware of its publication,” and it “circulated it through its usual email distribution without raising any immediate alarms.” Max’s view ABC News’ suggestion that its initial story was published prematurely is familiar spin to anyone who has dealt with crisis PR. It minimized the company’s mistakes and made the situation seem like an accident. But at a time when distrust in the news media continues to rise, deflections like this can damage the credibility of mainstream, nonpartisan American journalism. Tellingly, the network seemed to know the difference in its official response, acknowledging that the original piece contained errors. Brett Velicovich, co-founder of Powerus, another company mentioned in ABC News’ initial piece, complained that the network’s handling of the story reinforced his frustration with much of the media coverage of his company and the president’s administration. “It’s destroying the integrity of what reporting is all about,” Velicovich said. “The damage is already done.” The Trump family’s mix of business and governing, unprecedented in recent history, is an important reporting target, as journalists attempt to understand how companies and countries are attempting to influence policy by investing in Trump businesses or bringing the Trumps on as partners themselves. But ABC News’ decision to remove its story without explanation while misleadingly telegraphing that it was simply published on accident gave the president’s son and many on the right another opening to criticize mainstream news outlets. If more and more people continue to believe that news organizations are willing to mislead or fail to take full accountability for mistakes, will they listen when outlets have legitimate stories? Room for Disagreement Remove the numbers, and the most basic version of the story — the Pentagon is paying very large sums to a defense contractor in which the president’s sons have invested, and whose co-founder, Palmer Luckey, is a high-dollar Trump donor — is correct . It also follows a pattern congressional Democrats have promised to investigate should they retake power after the midterms.

events.title: Ceuta or Sebta? Why one city has two names and a disputed status
events.summary: Felipe VI’s first visit to Ceuta and Melilla as king brings Spain’s territorial dispute with Morocco back into focus. Spain’s King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia are due to visit Ceuta on October 13 and Melilla the following day, in Felipe’s first visit to either city as king since he ascended the throne in 2014. The trip comes after a major migration crisis at the Ceuta border in July and as the long-running dispute between Spain and Morocco over the two cities on the North African coast remains unresolved. Spain considers Ceuta and Melilla part of its territory, while Morocco regards both cities and several smaller Spanish-held territories in North Africa as part of its own territory. The city that sits on the southern side of the Strait of Gibraltar also has different names in Spanish and Arabic. In Spain, it is Ceuta. In Arabic, it is Sabta, commonly written as Sebta in Latin script. So why does the same city have two names? And how did a city on the North African coast come under Spanish sovereignty? Where does the name Ceuta come from? The name is much older than either modern Spain or Morocco. The city was known as Sabta in Arabic. Spain’s Ministry of Culture identifies Sabta with present-day Ceuta and traces its history through successive periods of Idrisid, Umayyad, Taifa, Almoravid, Almohad and Marinid rule. The Spanish form, Ceuta, developed from earlier forms of the name. Sabta and Ceuta are different linguistic forms of the same city. Ceuta passed through several political and dynastic systems in the Maghreb and al-Andalus. Under the Idrisid dynasty, the city was in the hands of the Banu Isam before being taken by the Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Rahman III in 931, bringing it into the political sphere of al-Andalus. In the 11th century, Ceuta became linked to the Taifa of Malaga. It later came under the Almoravids and Almohads. From the beginning of the 14th century, it became part of the Marinid sphere with periods when other local dynasties held power. By the early 15th century, Ceuta was under Muslim rule. On August 21, 1415, Portuguese forces led by King John I captured Ceuta. The Portuguese conquest brought an end to more than seven centuries of Muslim rule in Ceuta. Ceuta’s own cultural heritage authority dates Muslim rule from 709 to the Portuguese conquest in 1415. Ceuta remained Portuguese for more than two centuries. Portugal and Spain were then ruled by the same monarchy from 1580 to 1640. When Portugal restored its independence in 1640, Ceuta remained under the Spanish monarchy rather than returning to Portuguese rule. The 1668 Treaty of Lisbon, which formally recognised Portuguese independence, left Ceuta in Spanish hands. That is how Ceuta came under Spanish sovereignty. Morocco’s argument is rooted in the city’s history and geography. Ceuta lies on the North African coast, surrounded by Morocco on its landward side. Morocco has claimed Ceuta and Melilla since gaining independence in 1956 and regards the two cities as occupied Moroccan territories. Under Spanish law, Ceuta is an autonomous city. Its Statute of Autonomy describes Ceuta as an integral part of the Spanish nation and gives the city its own system of self-government. The dispute, therefore, is not about who administers Ceuta. Spain does. It is about sovereignty. Morocco says Ceuta should form part of Moroccan territory. Spain says its sovereignty over the city is established and Ceuta is part of Spain. Neither side has accepted the other’s position. Why doesn’t history settle the dispute? Because the two sides interpret that history differently. Morocco points to Ceuta’s long history within Muslim political systems in the Maghreb and its location on the North African coast. Spain points to centuries of Portuguese and Spanish control and to Ceuta’s present constitutional status as part of Spain. The historical record does not provide a simple answer to a modern sovereignty dispute. The political systems that ruled Ceuta before 1415 were not nation-states with today’s borders, and the city’s current status is based on centuries of subsequent Portuguese and Spanish rule. Morocco’s territorial claim dates from the period after independence in 1956, but Spain has continued to exercise sovereignty over Ceuta. Sebta, or Sabta, is the Arabic name for Ceuta and predates the modern sovereignty dispute. In Morocco, Sebta is the Arabic name used for the city while Ceuta is the established Spanish form. The choice of name can have political resonance because Morocco disputes Spanish sovereignty over the city. But using Sebta is not automatically a political statement. It is also simply the Arabic name. Melilla’s history is different from Ceuta’s. Spanish forces took control of Melilla in 1497 when it was incorporated into the Crown of Castile. Ceuta, by contrast, was first Portuguese before remaining under the Spanish monarchy after Portugal regained its independence.

events.title: Hong Kong must ease listing rules to attract more angel funds and start-ups: HKEIA
events.summary: Hong Kong could learn from the US market, where streamlined regulations foster a thriving ecosystem of angel funds and start-ups, an industry body says Hong Kong would need to ease its listing rules and transaction requirements to attract more angel funds and become a hub for start-ups to go global, according to a leading industry body in the city. The city has only around 100 active angel funds – private investment vehicles targeting very early-stage innovative enterprises. This was far fewer than Shenzhen, which had about 400 such institutions, according to Samson Tam Wai-ho, honorary chairman of the Hong Kong Electronic Industries Association (HKEIA). Besides Shenzhen, Shanghai and the United States also had many active angel funds, helping them become start-up hubs, Tam told the South China Morning Post in an interview. “Lack of angel funds and early-stage investors for start-ups is the weakest part of the capital market ecosystem in Hong Kong for us to attract start-up founders to come here,” Tam said.

events.title: Amazon in talks to buy AI start-up Decart for around US$7 billion: Report
events.summary: Decart was valued at nearly US$4 billion (S$5 billion) in May, the Wall Street Journal report said. Amazon is in talks to buy AI startup Decart for about US$7 billion, the Wall Street Journal reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Decart makes the Lucy model for live video editing and Oasis for robotics and self-driving tests. It was valued at nearly US$4 billion in May. A deal could happen soon, but it is not certain. Reuters could not verify the report, and Amazon and Decart did not comment. Amazon is in talks to acquire artificial intelligence start-up Decart in a deal that could be valued at around US$7 billion (S$8.96 billion), the Wall Street Journal reported on Oct 11, citing sources familiar with the matter. Decart’s Lucy model, backed by Nvidia, can edit live video in real time, according to the company’s website. Decart has also developed Oasis, a model that generates simulated environments to train and test robotics and autonomous driving systems. The Journal reported that Decart was valued at nearly US$4 billion in May, the Journal report said, citing PitchBook data. Amazon declined to comment outside regular business hours, while Decart did not respond to requests for comment. A deal could happen soon if talks do not fall apart or another suitor does not emerge, the report said. In September, Anthropic decided not to pursue an acquisition of Decart after conducting due diligence, Bloomberg News reported. It had explored the deal in August for potentially US$6 billion, Bloomberg reported. Decart raised US$300 million in May in a funding round led by Radical Ventures, with Nvidia joining as a new investor. REUTERS

events.title: Oil falls on hopes Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire will boost supplies
events.summary: The attacks threaten to inject fresh volatility into a pivotal week for markets. Oil prices fell as hopes grew for a Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire and more Russian diesel supplies after Donald Trump’s announcements. Brent and WTI dropped, while ICE gasoil fell 3%, but analysts said doubts over the ceasefire may limit further price falls. Middle East conflict and tanker attacks kept Brent above US$100, while Goldman Sachs raised its Brent forecast and warned of ongoing supply risks. NEW DELHI – Oil prices slipped on Oct 12 on expectations of more Russian supplies after US President Donald Trump said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to halt attacks on each other’s energy facilities following a US diesel-supply deal with Moscow. Brent crude futures fell 11 cents, or 0.11%, to US$104.61 a barrel by 0627 GMT (2.27pm Singapore time) while US West Texas Intermediate crude was at US$91.36 a barrel, down 49 cents, or 0.53%. Both benchmarks were down more than 1% earlier in the session. ICE gasoil futures fell 3% to US$1,436 per tonne after Trump said on Oct 9 that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to US and global markets. Russia would supply another 500,000 tonnes in November and a further one million tonnes “immediately thereafter”, Trump added. The daily diesel consumption globally is forecast at close to 29 million barrels, according to the International Energy Agency. Trump also unexpectedly announced on Oct 11 that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to an energy ceasefire, but Ukrainian leader Volodymyr Zelensky said he was still waiting to see details of the energy ceasefire while Russia did not comment. The announcements eased some of the immediate supply pressure, Tim Waterer, KCM Trade chief analyst, said. “Questions remain over the validity and longevity of any such ceasefire, and without clearer evidence that it will actually hold, the extent of the pullback is likely to stay limited,” he added. IEA’s executive director Fatih Birol said on Oct 11 that all members should assess whether additional diesel releases are necessary and that countries which have not yet fully delivered pledged volumes should accelerate their remaining releases, prioritising diesel. Crude supported by Middle East conflict However, the Middle East conflict continued to support Brent crude at above US$100 a barrel. The Houthis claimed responsibility for aN Oct 10 strike on Riyadh’s international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, while the Saudi authorities reported that people were injured in a new attack on the airport on Oct 11. Trump said on Oct 10 the United States was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis in the conflict, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel launched in February. In addition, more attacks on tankers sailing through the Strait of Hormuz have been reported so far in October, threatening to dampen a recovery in Middle East crude exports seen in September. A tanker was struck by a drone in the vicinity of Sohar anchorage, Oman, while another was damaged by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, the ​United ​Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reported over the weekend. Goldman Sachs raised its Brent crude price forecast for December to US$90 a barrel, up from US$85 previously, its analysts led by Daan Struyven said in a note. “We maintain our base case that continued adaptation of Middle East supply will eventually reduce crude oil prices, while potential renewed escalation still poses significant net upside risk,” the analysts said, estimating a risk premium of just over US$20 a barrel. “We forecast WTI (West Texas Intermediate) prices, which are unusually low versus Brent because of high US-Europe shipping costs, to average US$81 in December 2026 and US$73 in 2027,” they added. In the Gulf of Mexico, energy majors Shell, Chevron and BP were seeking to redeploy personnel and restore production at their platforms after Hurricane Isaias made landfall early on Oct 10. REUTERS

events.title: Roofing scammers con homeowners out of thousands of pounds
events.summary: Scammers pretending to be legitimate workmen are charging homeowners thousands of pounds for roofing work that is not completed, done badly or not necessary, according to Citizens Advice. The consumer advice charity says one in 10 of all the scams it recorded over the past year were related to roofing, making it the most common type of scam brought to them. It can leave victims like Crystal, from the Midlands, thousands of pounds out of pocket. The 68-year-old was frightened and found it hard to sleep after a rogue builder left her roof with dislodged bricks and blocked gutters. She said she felt pressured into agreeing to having her roof re-done and paid a total of £5,500, only for the original contractor to send his son instead, who left work in the eaves incomplete. "We had heavy rain a couple of weeks after he did the job, and it ended up like a waterfall coming down the wall," she said. Her neighbour's house was also damaged. "They took the lead off my neighbour's side of the chimney, which caused bricks to fall into his attic and the rain to go into his house," she told the BBC. The experience still haunts her: "I can't sleep. I don't eat properly". In the year to August the Citizens Advice Consumer Service received 9,000 complaints about roofing work, including problems with construction, repairs and weatherproofing. Of those 2,205, or about one in four complaints, were suspected scams, up from 2,098 the year before. Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice, urged consumers to carry out thorough checks on traders before agreeing to hire them. "Scammers exploit the fact that roofs are out of sight and reach, knowing most people can't easily inspect the work themselves," she said. Victims also reported aggressive and intimidating behaviour, with three quarters of fraudsters using "doorstep" sales tactics. Citizens Advice cited the case of Charlotte, 65, who lives alone in north eastern England. Tradesmen she found online initially offered to fix her leaking gutter for £250. The two men then said there was further work that needed to be done, that would cost £2,500. "An hour later they said it was sorted, but they'd found another problem," she said. It was dark and Charlotte felt afraid. "They knew I was alone, I didn't feel like I could deal with anything that might happen after, so I paid £3,500," she said. But the next day she could see no sign of any work having been done, she said. To avoid falling victim to roofing scams, Citizens Advice suggests: Be alert: Always ask for references and for everything to be in writing. Be wary of unsolicited doorknockers and callers Gather evidence: If a trader causes problems, be sure to take photos and gather the necessary paperwork and receipts Know your rights: Traders must give you the information about your right to cancel in writing. If the job is not done with "reasonable care and skill," the Consumer Rights Act 2015 also entitles you to ask for the problem to be fixed or a refund Lord Bichard, chair of National Trading Standards, said rogue traders were "criminals deliberately preying on people in their own homes". He described roofing fraud as "particularly cruel", and said Trading Standards would pursue fraudsters through legal routes. "Victims can lose life savings in a matter of hours and be left with damaged homes, financial hardship and a profound sense of vulnerability long after the criminals have gone," he said. events.title: Debt advice that may leave you owing even more money
events.summary: An increasing number of people are missing credit card repayments as finances are stretched by rising bills, according to the Bank of England. Lenders also told the Bank they expected the number of unpaid credit card debts to keep going up this autumn. This could lead to more demand for advice on how to deal with debts – but, if you are struggling and need help, there are some traps to avoid. And it is worth remembering that impartial advice is available free of charge from debt charities. So here's what to think about. If you find yourself with money troubles, it can be tempting to seize any opportunity to get things back on track. Social media and internet search pages are full of supposed quick-fix debt solutions. Cold calls and WhatsApp messages also promise debt help. But they may well come with upfront fees, unrealistic claims about writing off debt, and pressure to make a quick decision. Suggestions on the best way to find help include: Impartial, authorised debt advice comes free. You can find a provider on the government-backed Moneyhelper website , external Check whether a firm offering debt help is authorised by the regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). You should cross-check the authorisation details they give with the FCA's register , external Anyone unhappy with the service from an authorised firm can complain and, if you are still not happy, go to the independent Financial Ombudsman Service. Alison Walters, director of consumer finance at the FCA, said: "Anyone struggling with debt deserves advice that puts their interests first. "Free, impartial debt advice is available to everyone, and no one should be pressured or misled into paying for a debt solution that may not be right for them." The FCA says that some unregulated firms collect people's details, through cold calling or online adverts, sometimes impersonating debt advice charities or debt collectors, and pass this information on to firms offering debt solutions that you pay for. A quick search online will throw up lots of businesses offering ways to clear your debt, not all of which are trustworthy, according to charities. Warning signs of unscrupulous firms include pressure tactics, such as repeated contact, often in messages and on the phone, pushing people to agree to a debt solution, the FCA says. Some people have been encouraged to change financial details on lenders' paperwork, or are "coached" in ways to respond. Sometimes people are steered towards a fee-charging debt solution, such as Individual Voluntary Arrangements (IVAs) or some debt management plans, without alternative options being properly explained or offered first. And, do you know who you are talking to? Ask them who they work for, and check if their details match the firm's official details. "Before making any decisions around how to deal with your debts, it's always worth getting full, free and impartial debt advice first, exploring all options to clear your debt in the safest and most sustainable way," said Vikki Brownridge, chief executive at debt charity StepChange. events.title: Trump faces growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia
events.summary: Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February US President Donald Trump is facing a growing backlash over plans to import diesel from Russia as the Iran war continues to impact global energy prices. Trump on Friday announced that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by several other shipments. That is despite signing legislation to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas just weeks ago. The move has been criticised by some Republican and Democratic lawmakers, who believe the deal violates US laws. As well as the initial release of 300,000 tonnes of diesel, Trump said Russia would then supply 500,000 tonnes in November and one million more after that. This would be followed by a further three million tonnes, which would be delivered "within a short period" dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine during the ongoing war between the two countries. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak confirmed these numbers to Tass, the country's state-owned news agency, saying the export volume could reach three million tonnes per month in future. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended". It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen. A group of seven senators - four Republicans and three Democrats – on Sunday said the deal violated US laws, urging Trump to "reverse course". "The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the lawmakers said. They added that Congress had "explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin's brutal war against Ukraine". The statement was signed by Republicans Susan Collins, Lisa Murkowski, Thom Tillis and John Curtis, as well as Democrats Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Ron Wyden. Trump's 'energy ceasefire' claim welcomed by Zelensky but Russia silent Published 10 hours ago Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work? Published 2 days ago Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Published 2 days ago Not everyone is opposed to the deal. Republican Thomas Massie, who has sparred with Trump a number of issues, said the US should lift sanctions on all petroleum products. Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Fox News the agreement would work through existing legal channels the US has to help bring prices down and that anyone in Congress who said it would not was wrong. Global fuel prices have soared since the US-Israel war with Iran began at the end of February, with the fighting severely disrupting supplies of crude oil - a key ingredient in petrol and diesel. The rising prices have become a key issue for Americans ahead of next month's midterms elections, which will determine if Trump's Republican Party maintains control of Congress. Polls show a majority of Americans disapprove of his handling of the economy and the war in Iran and he has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain. The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market. The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September. Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers. The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tonnes this month, it amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption. It is not only at home that Trump is facing opposition to his diesel deal with Russia. A number of international leaders have criticised it, including Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who said the US and other allies of Ukraine should focus on ramping up pressure on Russia to end the war. Meanwhile, Trump announced in Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had reached an "energy ceasefire" but did not give more details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky welcomed this but there was no response from Moscow.

In an interview on Sunday with the CBS News show Face the Nation, Mullin framed the decision as part of President Donald Trump’s hardline approach to crime. list 1 of 3 US to livestream Fort Hood shooter’s execution: Is that legal?​ list 2 of 3 ‘Barbaric’: US lawmakers condemn plan to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution list 3 of 3 Pope says death penalty ‘inadmissible’ as US plans to livestream execution “I follow President Trump. He’s a commander-in chief of the country,” Mullin said, crediting the Republican leader with “restoring America values”. Mullin also brushed aside concerns that the images of Hasan’s execution could be leveraged against the US. “I don’t see an elevated risk at this point at all because of this,” Mullin said. “I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime.” Hasan, a former US Army major, was sentenced to death in August 2013 after being convicted of shooting and killing 12 unarmed active-duty soldiers and a retired serviceman at the Fort Hood military base in Texas. The attack took place on November 5, 2009, when Hasan opened fire in a medical facility on the base where service members receive routine check-ups before deployment. The incident is considered one of the deadliest mass shootings to take place on a US military base. Another 32 people were injured in the shooting. In the process of responding to the attack, police on the military base shot Hasan, leaving him paralysed from the waist down. Critics have questioned the optics of broadcasting a firing squad killing of a man in a wheelchair. The livestreamed execution is scheduled for December 3. But Mullin dismissed those concerns, arguing that viewership is optional. “Once again, no one has to watch it if they don’t choose to,” Mullin said. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had announced plans last week to livestream the upcoming execution, triggering a wave of criticism. But Trump on Saturday suggested he may reconsider the decision. “There are two thoughts: Don’t show it and show it. Because, you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did,” Trump told reporters outside the White House. “So I’ll make a decision, ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.” Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, however, have denounced the idea of a public execution. In a Sunday morning appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, Republican Senator Thom Tillis warned that broadcasting Hasan’s death would “put at risk” US lives. “Terrorist organisations will use this as a recruiting tool. It will radicalise other people, and this is not who we are,” Tillis said. “Look, the Fort Hood shooter should be put to death, but there’s a way to deal with this that’s proper, and there’s a way to deal with this that’s more improper than I have ever observed in my life.” Tillis, whose term as senator ends in January, also directed criticism at Hegseth for what he suggested was reckless leadership. “It’s another example of why Pete Hegseth and all of his bravado needs to get the hell out of the Department of Defense, because he is a failed leader,” Tillis said. The senator was considered one of the deciding votes in Hegseth’s January 2025 confirmation vote, and he has since called his support for Hegseth’s cabinet nomination “the biggest regret” of his tenure. Other Republicans echoed Tillis’s concerns about the livestream. Senator Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, for instance, compared the public execution with something she would expect “from terrorists and dictators”. She also argued that Hasan has sought public attention, something he would receive in a broadcast execution. “It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks,” Murkowski added. Republican Representative Tom Barrett of Michigan, a former military member, issued a statement on Friday explaining that he had trained at Fort Hood a year before the attack. He also said he opposed the public execution, despite considering Hasan “evil”. “Secretary Hegseth should seriously reconsider this decision,” Barrett wrote on X . “Making a public spectacle out of an already tragic situation is unnecessary and does not serve a public interest.” Military executions are extremely rare in the US and can only be approved by the president under the Uniform Code of Military Justice.

events.title: AI scale-up PhysicsX comes to Singapore with ambition to accelerate industrial innovation
events.summary: PhysicsX CEO and co-founder Jacomo Corbo at the launch of the PhysicsX Singapore Hub at Temasek Shophouse on Oct 8. PhysicsX, led by former F1 strategist Jacomo Corbo, is using AI to replace slow engineering simulations and speed up industrial innovation. The London-based scale-up has set up its Asia-Pacific hub in Singapore, where high-value manufacturing, engineering and chip production make it a strong regional base. PhysicsX has raised about US$500 million, works with major firms like NVIDIA and Siemens, and plans to grow its Singapore team to 100 in three years. SINGAPORE – As a race strategist, Jacomo Corbo helped the Renault F1 team win back-to-back double world championships with driver Fernando Alonso in 2005 and 2006. Now he is chief executive of a scale-up that offers a winning formula to accelerate industrial innovation. Before a product is physically built – whether it is jet engine parts or a machine that makes semiconductors – engineers in manufacturing firms run computer simulations to replicate, predict and optimise the behaviour of materials, mechanical systems and factory workflows. PhysicsX develops AI models that replace these slow, traditional numerical computer simulations with high-speed AI inference, where a trained AI model applies learnt patterns to new, unseen data to generate real-world predictions, decisions or outputs. After winning customers across the Atlantic, Corbo’s London-headquartered PhysicsX is now in Singapore, establishing its Asia-Pacific hub and promising to overhaul what engineering and manufacturing look like today. Corbo co-founded PhysicsX with his former F1 colleague, Robin Tuluie, a theoretical physicist. PhysicsX’s customers span advanced manufacturing sectors that involve very complex engineering design and processes, including automotive, materials science and energy. “Aerospace and defence are our largest sectors, followed by semiconductors, where we are working mostly on the equipment manufacturing side,” Corbo said, adding that the firm is increasingly deploying into chip fabrication plants. Since its official launch in 2020, the firm has established partnerships to deploy industrial AI and advance its platform and large physics models with companies such as Leonardo Aerospace, carmaker Audi, miner Rio Tinto, tech giant NVIDIA and industrial automation firm Siemens. With many of its customers and partners already in Singapore, it made perfect sense for PhysicsX to choose the Republic as the company’s regional hub, Corbo told The Straits Times in an interview last week. For years, multinational firms have gravitated to Singapore for its strategic location and a clear-eyed policy focus. But for manufacturing firms, it has been a bit more than just that. Corbo said: “The physical constraints on the city-state have meant that Singapore’s strategy has orientated itself towards high-value manufacturing. But it’s also where high-value manufacturing is co-located with high-value engineering.” The Republic recognised early on that for supply chains to be efficient, engineering and manufacturing must co-locate. “And now it plays a linchpin role in a number of really important supply chains.” Singapore today accounts for one in 10 chips and one-fifth of global semiconductor equipment produced annually. It is also one of the world’s top 10 exporters of chemical products. It contributes 10 per cent of global aerospace maintenance, repair and overhaul output, and is home to eight of the top 10 biopharmaceutical companies conducting manufacturing or R&D activities here. And bridging the gap between research and industrial application are 14 of the world’s top 20 international engineering design firms and 10 of the top 20 engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) services providers that operate in Singapore. Hence, engineering teams in companies here can design a high-value tool or component and instantly test it on a nearby production line, closing the feedback loop between blueprint and physical asset. However, much of industrial engineering, manufacturing and goods production worldwide is run on software that has remained largely unchanged for decades. Also, even very innovative firms in advanced manufacturing have proprietary software and workflows that are fragmented across different departments and engineering teams. PhysicsX AI platform integrates with a company’s existing systems, such as computer-aided design tools, numerical solvers that solve complex engineering equations, and product lifecycle management systems which are the repositories of all their designs. “We absolutely tell our customers that, look, you don’t have to move off the tools that you use and rely on at scale. You can stay on these systems of record... and we can bring optimisation enablement and put AI at the heart of these workflows,” Corbo said.
