events.title: The movie about a Facebook whistleblower who leaked incriminating details disappoints, and ‘The Social Reckoning’ will likely lag ‘The Social Network’
events.summary: The Jessica Chastain horror  “Other Mommy”  topped the North American box office this weekend with a bigger audience than expected, while  “The Social Reckoning”  got off to a lackluster start. ‘Other Mommy’ is another win for horror “Other Mommy,” released by Universal Pictures, earned $27.5 million in its first few days in 3,365 theaters, according to studio estimates on Sunday. The movie, about a sinister supernatural creature that terrorizes a young girl who thinks it’s her mother, got dismal reviews from both critics and audiences. It also joins the ranks of “Megalopolis” and “Hereditary” with a D+ CinemaScore. But with a production budget of around $19 million, it’s also another win for the horror genre and producer Blumhouse Atomic Monster, which was behind  “Backrooms” and “Obsession.”  “Other Mommy” opened in 50 international markets as well, boosting its global debut to $45.2 million. Jim Orr, Universal’s head of domestic distribution, noted that the audience gender divide was evenly split and about 2/3 were between 18 and 34 years old. “No matter how you look at it, everybody turned out for it. It wasn’t just one particular demographic,” Orr said. “That usually is a very good sign.” ‘The Social Reckoning’ fails to connect “The Social Reckoning,” the weekend’s other big release, was not as lucky, earning an estimated $5.5 million from 2,606 North American theaters.  Aaron Sorkin  wrote and directed the film about a Facebook whistleblower who leaked incriminating documents to a Wall Street Journal reporter. Sixteen years ago, “The Social Network,” which Sorkin wrote and David Fincher directed, opened to over $22 million and went on to gross over $224 million worldwide, receiving eight Oscar nominations and winning three. A similar fate might be a stretch for “The Social Reckoning,” which stars Mikey Madison, Jeremy Allen White and Jeremy Strong and received mixed-to-negative reviews from critics. Audiences gave it a B- CinemaScore. According to reports, the Sony Pictures release cost around $30 million to produce, not accounting for marketing and promotion. Paul Dergarabedian, Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends, said October is a time when studios take chances and it doesn’t always work out. “These movies that are topical in nature, sometimes they resonate with the culture, sometimes they don’t,” said Dergarabedian. “You don’t always know what’s going to connect with audiences.” He compared “The Social Reckoning” to “Digger,” which fell 60% in  its second weekend . The overall box office is still up “The Social Reckoning” opened behind several holdovers as well. The Anne Hathaway psychological thriller  “Verity”  took second place with $11.5 million, down 64% from its opening weekend. In third place, “Resident Evil” added $8.4 million, bringing its domestic total to $138.5 million. The Brad Pitt survival thriller “Heart of the Beast” took fourth with $7.1 million. Christopher Nolan’s  “The Odyssey  ” also made an encore appearance in the top 10 in its 13th weekend in theaters where it was back in 12 IMAX 70 mm locations. It added $2 million from 560 North American theaters, bringing its domestic total just shy of $623 million. Several high-profile films opened in limited release this weekend as well. The Cannes Palme d’Or winner  “Fjord”  debuted on four screens this weekend where it made $124,000. Alex Gibney’s Elon Musk documentary  “Musk,”  which runs nearly four hours, made $68,900 from four locations. And Chris Rock’s “Misty Green” made $85,716 from six locations through Sunday. The annual domestic box office crossed the $8 billion mark on Friday and is up over 19% from last year. According to Rentrak, that’s about 8% behind 2019. Top 10 movies by domestic box office With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak: 1. “Other Mommy,” $27.5 million. 2. “Verity,” $11.5 million. 3. “Resident Evil,” $8.4 million. 4. “Heart of the Beast,” $7.1 million. 5. “The Social Reckoning,” $5.5 million. 6. “Forgotten Island,” $4.5 million. 7. “Primetime,” $4 million. 8. “Digger,” $3.2 million. 9. “Angel and the Badman,” $2.1 million. 10. “The Odyssey,” $2 million. events.title: Oil theft is on the rise in the heart of U.S. shale country—and it’s mostly carried out in targeted, organized heists
events.summary: The spike in oil prices since the Iran war began this year has attracted more thieves, and they are increasingly professional criminals. West Texas Intermediate crude is up 60% so far this year, and fuel prices have risen even more as global refining capacity has fallen due to the Mideast and Russia-Ukraine wars. While oil theft has long been a part of the industry, the problem has become prevalent enough for the Dallas Fed to ask about in its quarterly surveys. The latest one showed that nearly half of firms that are primarily focused in the Permian Basin said their operations have been impacted by theft in oil fields. By contrast, 86% of firms operating mostly outside the Permian said they were not impacted. The Permian is the heart of the oil patch and the epicenter of the shale revolution that has transformed the U.S. into an energy superpower. It stretches across the vast expanses of West Texas and southeastern New Mexico—and is dotted with drilling rigs, pipelines, trucks and other infrastructure necessities. That’s made the Permian a target-rich environment. And now that U.S. oil prices have been hovering around $100 a barrel lately, criminals can’t resist the payoff. According to the Dallas Fed survey, 32% of executives who were impacted by oil theft said it had increased slightly over the last 12 months, while 47% said it remained the same, and 22% said it decreased slightly or significantly. Nearly half of the oil executives (47%) said the most common form of theft was targeted and organized, while 42% described it as opportunistic petty theft. Still, the losses were relatively minimal, with 84% saying the financial impact of the theft was low. A year ago, the Dallas Fed asked a slightly different set of questions about theft, including what exactly was stolen: 61% said crude oil; 58% said piping, valves and wiring; 39% said equipment; 27% said tools; and 12% said construction equipment and vehicles. Theft can also be committed by other firms. In August, executives from a wastewater disposal company were charged with felony oil theft, money laundering and organized crime. It was part of an investigation dubbed Operation Black Market Basin that resulted in the seizure of more than $12 million in petroleum products, vehicles, cash and other assets, according to the Texas Railroad Commission , which regulates the industry. The investigation involved petroleum allegedly acquired and sold across Texas, New Mexico and Oklahoma, the commission added. And in April, federal prosecutors announced charges in a large-scale oil theft conspiracy in the Permian Basin to transport stolen crude oil across the New Mexico-Texas border for resale. Howard County Sheriff Stan Parker told Texas Public Radio in May that his county, which is near the Midland-Odessa oil hub, sees “probably over 1,000, 1,500 barrels of oil reported stolen every month.” “Our problem is we don’t know who’s supposed to be there and who’s not,” he added. “If I pulled up on a tank battery right now, I don’t know if you can be there or you’re not. I don’t know if you’re drawing water off of it. I don’t know if you’re pulling oil. It’s got very complicated.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Environmental watchdog to review new Kimberley gas project
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Buru Energy sends gas project for EPA approval, saying it could power northern WA by 2029 Buru Energy's proposed Rafael conventional gas project in the Canning Basin. ( Suplied: Buru Energy ) Buru Energy has referred its Rafael conventional gas project to WA's Environmental Protection Authority for assessment. Environmentalists claim it could be a "Trojan horse for fracking" — something the company rejects. Buru expects a decision from the EPA by the end of the year. The company behind a proposed gas project in Western Australia's Kimberley says it could meet the region's power demands with locally produced energy for the first time. Buru Energy referred its Rafael conventional gas project to WA's Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) for review in early October. The proposal involves developing a facility at the project site, located in the Kimberley's Canning Basin about 85 kilometres south of Derby, to process conventional gas from two co-located production wells. Conventional gas is natural gas extracted using simple drilling and pumping methods, as opposed to unconventional extraction methods like hydraulic fracturing, or fracking. Well testing underway at Buru Energy's Rafael conventional gas project. ( Supplied: Buru Energy ) Buru executive chairman David Maxwell said the Rafael project was the only proven conventional gas and liquids resource in the greater Kimberley region. "At the moment, the Kimberley relies on imported energy … from Karratha, Perth, Darwin, and Asia," he said. He said the Rafael project would improve energy security and be cost-effective, with reduced road traffic another potential benefit. Up to 300 tonnes of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) would be produced at the Rafael plant per day — the equivalent of about 16 or 17 terajoules of energy — alongside LPG and condensate. Mr Maxwell said the Kimberley used between six and 13 terajoules per day for power generation, with the amount varying based on the time of year. "We'll also supply beyond the Kimberley into, for example, the northern Pilbara. "In the case of LPG, we would be supplying in the order of a quarter to a third of the Kimberley's LPG demand." The West Australian government has banned fracking in over 98 per cent of the state, but this does not include parts of the Kimberley including the Canning Basin. Earlier this year, WA's EPA recommended a fracking proposal by Black Mountain Energy subsidiary Bennett Resources go ahead subject to conditions. The Valhalla Gas Exploration and Appraisal Program would see up to 20 exploration and appraisal wells drilled in the basin. A record 8,000 appeals were lodged against the project. Community members gather in Broome to protest the Valhalla fracking proposal. ( ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic ) When asked about the fracking proposal in Broome this month, WA Mines Minister Daniel Pastorelli said the method had drawn varied perspectives. "I understand everyone has differing views on these types of things and I respect that completely," he said. "Obviously our policy and our approach is based on science, and that is what we're doing when it comes to hydraulic fracturing." Daniel Pastorelli acknowledges fracking is a controversial topic. ( ABC News: Keane Bourke ) Environmentalists have expressed concern Buru's Rafael project, although a conventional gas project, could pave the way for fracking to occur in the future. Environs Kimberley executive director Martin Pritchard said Rafael "could be a Trojan horse for fracking". "They (Buru) might be saying right now that they're not intending on fracking, but their statements to the ASX clearly say that they want to undertake fracking in the future," he said. Buru's David Maxwell rejected the accusation. "It's got nothing to do with fracking at all," he said. "And if there was any fracking involved — and I stress there is not — that would be a separate [EPA] referral, a separate application and a separate approval process and we're not in that process at all." Buru Energy's Yulleroo 2 wellhead 60 kilometres east of Broome was fracked in 2010. ( ABC Kimberley: Ben Collins ) The company previously used the hydraulic fracturing technique at its Yulleroo gas field also in the Canning Basin, but Mr Maxwell said it no longer did so. "We do not currently practice hydraulic fracturing," he said. "In the past Buru has, but Buru has put that on the shelf, and at the moment we have no plans for fracture stimulation." Mr Pritchard said solar and batteries, rather than gas fields, were the way forward for cheaper and cleaner electricity in the Kimberley.

events.title: The paradox at the core of the AI revolution: The faster we innovate, the slower we grow
events.summary: To hear Silicon Valley tell it, artificial intelligence will usher in a glorious new era of abundance. But ask the chief financial officers of the world’s largest companies how AI is transforming their bottom line and, per McKinsey’s 2026 State of AI survey , the answer for 88% of them is: “Not so much.” We have been here before. When the iPhone launched in 2007, pundits predicted a mobile-first transformation of everything. When broadband went mass-market, Businessweek heralded a “New Economy.” When the PC colonized every desk, Robert Solow quipped that you could see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics. Over five decades, waves of digital innovation have delivered spectacular consumer adoption yet continuously declining productivity growth. I call this the Innovation Paradox: the faster we innovate, the slower we grow. Two K-shapes, one problem Technology diffusion in the digital age follows what I call a double K-shaped pattern. The first K-shape is between consumers and enterprises. Smartphone adoption reached 80% of Americans in seven years. Enterprise resource planning systems took 33 years to reach 57% of U.S. firms. Consumer AI usage has surged to 53% of U.S. adults barely three years after ChatGPT’s launch. Enterprise AI in productive deployment stands at just 10%. The second K-shape is within the enterprise space. McKinsey’s 2026 survey found that 88% of organizations use AI in at least one function, but a mere 6% qualify as “high performers” achieving more than 5% EBIT impact—unchanged from 2025. That 82-point gap is not a technology deficit. It is an organizational transformation deficit. The 6% who succeed are three times more likely to have redesigned workflows end-to-end. Only 21% of all adopters have done so. The stock market echoes this divergence: 36 S&P 500 AI companies now represent 45% of the index’s market capitalization. Over three years, the headline S&P 500 returned 76%; strip out AI stocks and the figure drops to 32%. What electrification got right Electrification and telecommunications in the early twentieth century reached consumers and enterprises at similar paces and, crucially, a similar depth. Electric motors forced factories to abandon rigid layouts for flexible, continuous-flow production. Telephones collapsed coordination costs. Organizational redesigns followed: Sloan’s multidivisional structure at General Motors, Taylor’s scientific management. Diffusion was both deep, reshaping how firms operated, and broad, cascading across vertically linked industrial sectors. Digital technologies diffused into a fundamentally different economy. Services now dominate GDP. A hospital or government agency lacks the supply-chain linkages of a steel manufacturer. The economist William Baumol identified the constraint: “stagnant” service sectors resist productivity improvement because they depend on human interaction. These Baumol sectors—healthcare, education, public administration, construction—account for roughly 50% of advanced-economy GDP and remain stubbornly resistant to technological transformation. The overhead trap Why does enterprise adoption stall? Not for want of technology, but because of accumulated organizational complexity. I have developed a cross-country metric, the Combined Overhead Ratio, capturing government spending; corporate selling, general, and administrative expenses (SG&A); and regulatory compliance costs. In the U.S., this ratio crossed a threshold of 47% of GDP around 2000. Above that threshold, GDP growth has not sustainably exceeded 2.5%—roughly half the rate achieved when overhead remained below 35% in the 1960s. Government spending has surged to 36% of GDP. Corporate SG&A has doubled since the 1980s. The Competitive Enterprise Institute estimates U.S. firms spend more than $2 trillion annually on compliance alone. My within-sector analysis of S&P 500 companies (1985–2025) shows that 73% of sector-decade observations fall into the “overhead trap”: SG&A rising while revenue growth declines. As Jack Dorsey of Block argues, corporate hierarchy is an obsolete information-routing protocol. Most companies deploying AI today are putting a faster engine in a horse-drawn carriage. AI is different—but the barriers are not AI is categorically different from prior digital waves. Previous technologies made it easier to process, transmit, or display information. AI reasons, decides, and creates. This matters because Baumol sectors are not information-scarce; they are judgment-intensive—requiring diagnosis, evaluation, and personalization, precisely the capabilities AI can augment. Yet the barriers to diffusion remain. My more than 40 years of experience as a corporate executive and private equity partner confirms a recurring pattern. At one consumer company, digitization delivered impressive online-channel growth but failed to scale across the company’s much larger offline business because independently owned distributors refused to cede customer data to an integrated platform. In healthcare, introducing digital tools to doctors is straightforward; establishing end-to-end digitization to improve clinical workflows is fraught, tangled in data governance, compliance, and the asymmetric power of medical professionals over management. These are not exceptional cases; instead, they’re representative of the many businesses in which I was personally involved. Writer’s 2026 enterprise AI survey, conducted with Workplace Intelligence across 2,400 global leaders, confirms the pattern at scale: 79% of organizations report challenges in AI adoption—a double-digit increase from 2025—and 54% of C-suite executives admit AI adoption is “ tearing their company apart .” Depth and breadth, not pace The lesson of 50 years of digital innovation is that pace of adoption matters far less than its depth and breadth. Consumer adoption of ChatGPT was the fastest of any consumer technology in recorded history. It has moved no macroeconomic needle. What matters is whether AI penetrates core operations and redesigns workflows (depth), and whether that transformation extends beyond superstar firms into the vast sectors that dominate employment and GDP (breadth). Historical evidence from electrification to digital waves supports a long adoption timeline—generally over ten years, often decades. As a technology, AI progresses faster than any predecessor. But the organizational redesign required to absorb it proceeds at the pace of human institutions: slowly, painfully, and against fierce resistance. The Innovation Paradox persists not because technology fails to advance, but because institutions fail to adapt. Society will see real impact only when AI is adopted deeply within enterprises and broadly across large economic sectors. events.title: Six senators call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan
events.summary: A bipartisan group of six senators are calling on President Donald Trump’s administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices WASHINGTON -- A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices. Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they wrote. The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there's a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan. “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said. Trump's announcement came just a few weeks after Congress passed legislation that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine. The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war. “Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.” Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president's action would be in violation of U.S. law. Energy experts say the Russia deal is unlikely to make a dent in high prices at the pump. Richard Nephew, a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Center on Global Energy Policy, noted that the total amount of diesel appears to be less than what the U.S. uses in a day. Nephew argued that Iran and Russia might benefit more than the U.S. “The Iranians are probably very excited because it shows that there’s a lot of pressure still on the U.S. And the Russians are excited because it puts a big hole in the sanctions regime,” he said. Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in Iran , which has elevated world energy prices. events.title: Buttigieg gambles on a different path for 2028
events.summary: Pete Buttigieg has been able to campaign for Democrats across the country more than many of his potential 2028 rivals this past year. One reason: He doesn't have a job. That's by choice. Buttigieg said no when top Democrats urged him to run for governor or the U.S. Senate in Michigan this year. Why it matters: That decision is a gamble for Buttigieg's presidential ambitions. He's been able to build a national network over the last two years but hasn't added to his relatively thin resume as a former mayor of South Bend, Ind., and Joe Biden's transportation secretary. Buttigieg, 44, became a national political figure without following the typical path. He ran for president in 2020 as a small-town mayor and won the Iowa caucus by offering an optimistic vision and impressing voters with his communication skills — including in hostile environments. Driving the news: In early 2025, Democratic lawmakers and strategists including New York Sen. Chuck Schumer and former Michigan Sen. Debbie Stabenow urged Buttigieg — who had moved to Michigan — to run for office in his new state. Winning such an office, they argued, would help Buttigieg build his resume for a future White House run and give him a chance to distance himself from the unpopular Biden administration. Buttigieg passed, citing both a desire to stay home more with his husband and young twins, and figuring that he could still get his message out without being in the Senate. Instead, he set about building a larger national network among Democrats — particularly with Black voters in the South, where he had struggled in the 2020 Democratic primary. Buttigieg has traveled to 37 states since he left the Biden administration, Politico reported last week. Democratic candidates in vital swing districts and states have welcomed him to campaign for them this year while resisting offers from other potential presidential candidates such as former Vice President Kamala Harris , New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. In Buttigieg, many Democrats see a surrogate who can draw attention and crowds without the degree of negative attention that other prominent Democrats attract. Buttigieg also will campaign in key races in the final weeks before the Nov. 3 election. He's scheduled to be in Michigan and Virginia — which happen to hold early contests in the 2028 presidential primary. Between the lines: Buttigieg has tried to position himself as a candidate of the next generation who also has enough experience in the executive branch to be able to deliver. He's betting that the traditional ladder of running for president — becoming a senator, governor, or vice president first — no longer applies, especially after the Trump era. What they're saying: Buttigieg "knows what no one else on the Democratic side does, which is what it's actually like to run for this office — the pacing, the pressures and imperatives," David Axelrod, a former senior aide to President Obama and an outside adviser to Buttigieg in the past, told Axios. "At a time when the party and country will be searching for youth and forward-looking vision, he has the capacity to articulate one in a powerful way," Axelrod added. Axelrod said that if Buttigieg runs, "it will be because he feels the timing is right for someone like him, and the big mission is more compelling than the statewide races on which he took a pass." A Buttigieg spokesperson said that "when Pete decided not to run for office in Michigan, he promised he would still get to work to help candidates everywhere. He's been doing just that."

events.title: Trump says he is 'going to look at' joining Saudi Arabia in the fight against Iran-backed Houthis after deadly airport strike
events.summary: President Donald Trump said he is considering joining Saudi Arabia in its retaliation against Tehran-backed Houthis in Yemen after a deadly attack on Riyadh's main airport. The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said the attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday killed 12 people and injured 309 others. U.S. military involvement in the fight against the Houthis would stretch resources in the Middle East already committed to fighting Iran, analysts said. President Donald Trump said he is considering joining Saudi Arabia in its retaliation against Tehran-backed Houthis in Yemen after a deadly attack on Riyadh's main airport, a move that could draw the U.S. further into a second front in the Iran war . "We may. We're going to look at it," Trump told reporters outside the White House on Saturday when asked if the U.S. would back Saudi Arabian strikes. "We just found out about the recent attack. So, we'll make a decision. We move very quickly." Two Saudi Arabian government officials told MS NOW that the kingdom is requesting "urgent defense support" from the U.S. following the attacks. The officials, including a senior member of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, did not want to be identified because of the matter's sensitivity. They added that the U.S. needs to intervene "as soon as possible" to help the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen fight the Houthis. The White House did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment. On Sunday, a projectile struck a passenger terminal at the Riyadh airport, one day after a missile struck the same terminal, the Associated Press reported. No immediate details were available about the latest strike on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, AP said. The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said Saturday's attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh killed 12 people and injured 309 others, the country's official Saudi Gazette media outlet reported . Colonel Turki Al-Maliki, the spokesman for the Saudi-led Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen, which has been leading the fight against the Houthis, described the attack as a "war crime." "Therefore, the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will respond decisively to this terrorist attack in accordance with the Customary International Humanitarian Law," Al-Maliki said in a post on X. It was the second deadly assault on Riyadh's airport in less than a week. Three Saudi nationals, including a pilot , were killed in attacks on the facility by Iran-backed Houthi militants on Thursday. Following Saturday's attack, the Houthis renewed their warning against using Saudi airports. "We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travellers against using ⁠Saudi ‌airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become ⁠a theatre of operations for our forces, with the exception of the airports in (the holy cities of) Mecca and Medina," the Houthis said in a post on X. Saudi Arabia, a key U.S. ally in the Middle East, intervened in Yemen's civil war between the Houthis and its internationally recognized government after the group seized the Yemeni capital Sanaa in 2014. Last month, the Trump administration approved the potential $24.3 billion sale of nearly 50 F-35 warplanes to Saudi Arabia in what was seen as a major boost for the kingdom as it faces intensifying attacks from the Houthis. The sale is under congressional review. International energy conference still on The Saudi energy ministry said a long-planned international energy conference will still take place in Riyadh on Sunday, Reuters reported. The five-day WPC Energy Congress ⁠is taking place at a convention center near King Khalid airport. State television told Reuters that more than 70 ministers, ⁠300 company executives and representatives of more than 25 international energy organizations have confirmed their attendance, though it was not clear ⁠whether the participants would attend in person or virtually. Reuters said a ministerial meeting of the International Energy Forum is also set to take place, with its plenary session to be held behind closed doors. Later this month, the kingdom is expected to host the Future Investment Initiative, sometimes referred to as "Davos in the desert." In addition to attacks on civil aviation, the Houthis have also been trying to choke off oil tanker traffic through the Bab el Mandeb strait, a key entry point to the Red Sea, as Iran has effectively done in the Strait of Hormuz to the north of the Arabian Peninsula. Earlier this month, Yemeni government forces said they reclaimed the strategic port city of Mokha from the Houthis. Energy prices have soared since the start of the Iran war, which began with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian targets on Feb. 28, putting pressure on consumers globally. The surge in domestic fuel prices has been a key issue for voters ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections.

events.title: Turning AI Ambition into Real-World Advantage
events.summary: As enterprises race to adopt AI, Amitabh Sarkar, argues that AI’s real test is on infrastructure, and durable transformation will depend on converging networks, cloud, security, governance and trust. When executives talk about artificial intelligence today, they often talk in absolutes: an existential threat, a historic opportunity, the next great productivity leap. For Amitabh Sarkar, Tata Communications’ Vice-President, Asia Pacific and Japan, the more important story lies beneath the rhetoric and inside the data centres, networks and operating models trying to empower corporate ambition to meet their targets. “In the last 20 to 30 years, technology has moved from supporting the business, to enabling the business, to increasingly becoming the business,” he says. That shift has transformed corporate technology leadership. Once, CIOs were judged largely on uptime, efficiency and cost control. Today, the question is whether an enterprise has the infrastructure to launch new digital services across markets in weeks rather than months. For Tata Communications, the evolution has also been internal. Long associated with global connectivity, the company is positioning itself as a digital infrastructure and intelligence partner. The story is no longer only about pipes and bandwidth, but about platforms, AI readiness, cybersecurity and measurable business outcomes. A decade ago, customers came to Tata Communications with a simple request: connect one location to another. “Ten or fifteen years back, the prime reason clients talked to us was: can you connect country A to country B, data centre A to data centre B?” Sarkar recalls. “Transactional connectivity and interconnected data centres are all still important, but it’s now just one part of the story.” Enterprises today operate across multiple clouds, legacy and modern applications, overlapping cybersecurity tools and fragmented data. What they need is not another layer of complexity, but a partner who can simplify and orchestrate it. Tata Communications has built its business around that shift. Today, it positions itself as a digital infrastructure and intelligence partner. Its network fabric still underpins global connectivity, but it now sits alongside cloud and edge capabilities, security services, digital platforms and customer experience tools. The aim is to help enterprises connect, secure and control complex environments end to end. The story is no longer only about pipes and bandwidth, but about platforms, AI readiness, cybersecurity and measurable business outcomes. That evolution has changed not just what the company offers, but whom it serves. “Yesterday it was just the chief network officer,” Sarkar says. “Today the buying centre has expanded to several functions - the CMO, CDO, CTO, CIO and line-of-business leaders. Decisions on customer experience don’t always sit with IT any more.” As a result, Tata Communications’ teams have moved from selling technology to selling outcomes: revenue growth, cost efficiency, customer experience, resilience and security. The question is no longer whether a network is fast, but whether the architecture can support the business model the organisation wants to build. Sarkar’s view of the future begins with a contradiction at the heart of the AI boom. Boardrooms are moving quickly, but enterprise infrastructure is often the least regarded vector in the equation. “There is a widening gap between AI ambition and AI readiness,” he says. “Boardroom ambitions have perhaps moved faster than the infrastructure required to support these ambitions.” The mistake, he argues, is treating transformation as a purchase, and buying the latest model, tool or cloud service to automatically deliver transformation. “Technology is the easy part to buy,” he says. “The harder questions are those that technology alone cannot answer. What business outcome are you actually trying to change? Can your operating model support it? Can your data move across the organisation? Will your people adopt it? And can your infrastructure scale it securely?” Many companies can build impressive AI demonstrations quickly. The challenge is turning pilots into production systems connected to real workflows, governed data and secure infrastructure. Without that foundation, AI risks becoming a boardroom showcase rather than an operating advantage. The rise of AI agents will make those questions more urgent. Sarkar believes organisations may soon manage more digital agents than human employees. “You and I walk into an office with an ID card. Agents don’t,” he says. “How do you identify, govern and securely manage them? What are they allowed to access? What actions can they take? Can we trace why they made a decision and pivot quickly if it’s not the right move?” His conclusion is clear: the real AI story is increasingly an infrastructure story, not simply one about models and GPUs. Hybrid cloud is where many of the stress fractures are already visible.

events.title: askST Jobs: I keep having to pick up a colleague’s work. How should I raise it with my boss?
events.summary: An employee’s role is to highlight the issue and its impact, while managing the colleague’s performance is ultimately the manager’s responsibility. - Workers should raise workload concerns calmly, with clear examples of extra tasks, missed deadlines and work they covered for a colleague. - Experts say to avoid blame, scorekeeping and phrases like ‘pulling their weight’; focus on the impact on the team and ask for solutions. - Managers should be asked to clarify duties, rebalance work or reset priorities, while performance issues remain the boss’s responsibility. In this series, business correspondent Timothy Goh offers practical answers to candid questions on navigating workplace challenges and getting ahead in your career. Get more tips by signing up to The Straits Times’ Headstart newsletter . How can employees raise concerns about an uneven workload without blaming a colleague? Raising a genuine workload concern is not the same as complaining, but the difference lies in how employees present it, said Michelle Koh, managing director at executive search firm The Edge Partnership. “Raise the issue when you are calm rather than in a moment of frustration... If you approach your manager when emotions are running high, it can easily come across as a complaint about a person rather than a genuine concern about the work,” she said. Before speaking to their manager, employees should have specific examples ready, including the tasks they have taken over, deadlines they have stepped in to meet and instances where responsibilities have fallen back on them. “Avoid sweeping statements such as ‘I’m always doing their work’ unless you can back them up,” said Koh. “Keep the conversation focused on the impact on the work and the team – once it sounds like an attack on your colleague, it becomes personal and your point gets lost.” Koh noted that it also helps to remember that employees may not know the full circumstances behind a colleague’s performance. Their role is to highlight the issue and its impact, while managing the colleague’s performance is ultimately the manager’s responsibility. “Above all, go into the conversation looking for a solution... Ask whether responsibilities can be clarified, workloads redistributed or priorities reset,” she said. Tan Weixi, managing partner at Workplace Asia, said the biggest mistake employees can make when raising concerns about a colleague is framing the issue around whether the person is “pulling their weight”. “That is a judgment, and it puts the boss in the uncomfortable position of having to referee between two employees,” he said. Employees should also avoid keeping a running scorecard of every mistake and instead focus on patterns that genuinely affect the delivery of work, Tan said. Where appropriate, they could speak to the colleague first, as there may be circumstances that they are unaware of. “Don’t make your boss the judge of your colleague. Make your boss aware of the work problem – and be clear about what you need them to help resolve,” he said. Timothy Goh is a business correspondent at The Straits Times. He covers commodities and currencies, with occasional forays into listed companies.

events.title: Trump and Marco Rubio are ‘extremely pissed off’ by U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and are considering firing her
events.summary: President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. A senior U.S. official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday’s Columbus Day holiday. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled. In a series of stories, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill. Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, although her lawyer has said she did nothing wrong and the U.S. embassy in Athens has tacitly expressed support for her. After defending Guilfoyle following the first report, Rubio has declined to comment publicly on the growing allegations. On Wednesday, Rubio said: “Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here.” But after another report appeared late Wednesday, Rubio on Thursday before leaving Athens berated journalists for asking about the allegations saying he didn’t know if they were true and that he would not respond if he could not confirm. “You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me. That’s not the way we do things,” Rubio said at the foot of his plane as Guilfoyle, who was there to see him depart, looked on. The official said that Rubio had grown increasingly frustrated as the reports multiplied. A second U.S official, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss personnel matters, said the State Department’s inspector general is looking into the allegations, which first began surfacing in the Journal late last month and have since multiplied. The second official could not say if a formal IG probe had begun. Inspectors general often conduct informal inquiries into complaints against staffers and many times those inquiries do not result in a full-on investigation, which can result in disciplinary action up to and including dismissal. The State Department has declined to comment on a potential IG investigation. The top two Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations committees, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York and Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, as well as the ranking member on the House Committee for Oversight and Government Reform, Robert Garcia, D-Calif., have already called for an investigation into Guilfoyle. Since late September, the Journal has detailed numerous accounts of questionable conduct by Guilfoyle. Its first report said that she had told guests at a reception that the U.S. could undermine the Greek government if it chose to, promoted the business interests of one particular Greek construction and energy company, and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. While Rubio was in Athens, the Journal reported — citing text messages — that Guilfoyle had asked a Trump donor and supporter to pay a $100,000 credit card bill just before her confirmation hearing, promising him access to administration officials if he did. The Journal then reported that Guilfoyle had been enraged about not being invited to a Greek-themed event at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland earlier this year and demanded to attend while boasting about luxury travel to France with energy company executives. Another report, from the British tabloid The Daily Mail, said that Guilfoyle had alienated staff at the U.S. embassy in Athens and had pushed the bounds of behavior appropriate for the top representative of the U.S. government to Greece. Guilfoyle is a former Fox News Channel host and California prosecutor who was once engaged to Trump’s son Donald Jr. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Aaron Sorkin’s ‘Social Reckoning’ is off to a weak start
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. “The Social Reckoning,” Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to “The Social Network,” is on-track to make only $5.5 million at the domestic box office this weekend, according to Sunday estimates. That’s below the already underwhelming $7 million to $8 million the studio had projected, and it means Sorkin’s new movie is unlikely to become a “Social Network”-sized hit. The earlier film had a $22 million opening weekend and made a total of $97 million domestically (and that’s at 2010 ticket prices). It also won Sorkin an Oscar and became one of most influential on-screen depictions of Silicon Valley and startup culture. Beyond the fate of a single film, the weekend box office could also offer hints about audience excitement, or lack thereof, as we kick off a fall full of movies starring villainous, real-world tech CEOs . There’s Alex Gibney’s four-hour documentary “Musk” (which also opened this weekend), Nathan Fielder’s apparently uncategorizable Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” (coming next weekend!), and the OpenAI boardroom drama “Artificial” (which has a new distributor after being dropped by Amazon). Outside of theaters, Netflix also has a series called “The Altruists” coming in November , telling the story of Sam Bankman-Fried and the collapse of FTX. As for “The Social Reckoning,” while “The Social Network” was a notable success, the theatrical landscape has changed significantly in the last 16 years. And where the first film focused on the excitement and drama of Facebook’s early days, the sequel is darker and heavier — it’s all about whistleblower Frances Haugen’s decision to leak what became known as the Facebook files. So maybe a movie about Senate hearings and algorithm changes was never going to be a big hit. Or maybe “The Social Reckoning”’s real audience is among older moviegoers who have only returned sporadically to theaters . And I wonder if critiquing Facebook feels a bit less urgent to audiences who are more likely to be losing sleep over AI. Maybe just as importantly, the new movie’s reviews just aren’t very good . (For what it’s worth, I enjoyed “The Social Reckoning” but will fully admit that it’s overloaded Sorkin’s trademark speechifying. And I couldn’t help dreaming about a version directed — like the original — by David Fincher, with a score by Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross.) “Musk,” meanwhile, made $69,000 during its opening weekend in four theaters. It will roll out more broadly in the coming weeks, but given its length and subject matter, the documentary will probably reach many more viewers once it starts streaming on HBO Max. events.title: Mildura and South Australia connected by bus service after six-year hiatus
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts New bus service re-establishes link between Mildura and South Australia The Monty Express can drop Mildura residents off in South Australia, and SA residents off in Mildura. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The Monty Express coach will re-establish a direct road transport link between Mildura, Renmark and Adelaide. The route has not been serviced in almost six years. The service will make its first interstate journey on October 12. A new bus service has launched connecting Mildura in Victoria's north-west to South Australia. From this week, a bus named The Monty Express will be travelling the Sturt Highway between Sunraysia and Adelaide via Renmark. It has been nearly six years since the route was serviced, with Greyhound Australia canning its Mildura to Adelaide coaches in 2016 , and another bus company ceasing its operations in 2020, in the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. The lone direct flight between Mildura and Adelaide also no longer exists, with Rex Airlines terminating the service in May 2023. Ever since, getting into the festival state from Mildura involved detours via Ouyen, Horsham or Broken Hill, or at greater cost, flying to Adelaide via Melbourne or Sydney. The Monty Express will start taking passengers from October 12. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) Former Sunraysia resident Stuart Saunders ran a survey six months ago to gauge interest in restoring a Mildura to Adelaide bus service. He said support was overwhelming, and he soon prepared to pivot from his information technology career to become a bus driver. He purchased a 36-seat bus, which he named The Monty Express after the family's pet Cavoodle, Monty. "There's very much a sense of community in the coach industry," he said. Stuart Saunders and his family in front of their new business venture. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The Mildura–Renmark–Adelaide service begins today. It will initially run twice a week, departing Adelaide on Mondays and Thursdays and returning on Tuesdays and Fridays. It will run as an express service with pick-ups at Mildura, Renmark, Adelaide Airport and the Adelaide Central Bus Station. Under a service agreement with the SA government, The Monty Express cannot pick up South Australian residents unless they go to Mildura. Stuart Saunders with his children, Matilda and Gabriel, wife, Melody and dog, Monty. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) The agreement exists to avoid impacting passenger numbers on the existing Stateliner coach service route between the Riverland and Adelaide. Mildura man Steven Haby describes himself as a transport enthusiast. The former Melburnian is a member of the Bus and Coach Society of Victoria and the Australian Timetable Association. He will be travelling from Mildura to Adelaide to experience the first service of The Monty Express on Monday. Steven Haby has booked his ticket on The Monty Express. ( Supplied: Steven Haby ) "I'm very much an advocate and supporter of public transport," Mr Haby says. "I thought this was a really good opportunity to support the service going forward and be one of the first passengers on the run. "You can have a sustainable public transport network in a city like Mildura … making it frequent, reliable, cheap, and to places where people want to go." Mr Saunders hopes The Monty Express will not only benefit Mildura residents, but will connect people in the Riverland with Sunraysia's V/Line bus services and flights. "Not only are we trying to give an express service into Adelaide from Mildura, but the challenges for the Riverland people trying to get into Mildura, I'm hoping we can solve some of their problems as well," he said. Tamille Hunter is a resident of Cobdogla, a South Australian town less than two hours from Mildura by car. Ms Hunter is unable to drive and has occasionally used existing transport options to get to Mildura. The journey she took involved catching a bus to Adelaide, a flight to Melbourne, a train to Swan Hill and a bus to Mildura. The Monty Express can seat as many as 36 passengers. ( ABC News: Wade Stephens ) "At the moment, for us to go to Mildura it takes us 24 hours and over $600," Ms Hunter said. She said getting The Monty Express to Mildura would open up lots of opportunities for her. "From there, I could visit my family and friends in Melbourne on the V/Line," she said.

events.title: Senators call on Trump to scrap diesel deal, saying U.S. ‘should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline’ while Russia kills Ukrainian civilians
events.summary: A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump’s administration to “immediately reverse course” on a  plan to purchase diesel  from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices. Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they wrote. The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Tillis, in an interview that aired Sunday on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” said there’s a legitimate case for saying the president is not following the law if the administration goes through with its diesel purchase plan. “We were very clear that Russia is the aggressor. Russia is the one who can end this war by backing out of territory that they occupied,” Tillis said. Trump’s announcement came just a few weeks after Congress  passed legislation  that directed Trump to impose substantial tariffs on the top importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The congressional effort was aimed at cutting the flow of money Russia receives from oil and gas sales to finance its war against Ukraine. The lawmakers also noted that Congress explicitly banned Russia energy imports in 2022 to prevent the United States from financing the war. “Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies,” the six lawmakers wrote in their statement. “President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law.” Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., said Trump is focused on reducing the cost of energy when asked whether the president’s action would be in violation of U.S. law. “The president is balancing and has to make tough decisions,” Barrasso said on CBS’s “Face the Nation.” He also encouraged Trump to enforce the sanctions law that Congress passed last month. “This is just another point of leverage for the president to use against Putin in an effort to get a long-term solution in that part of the world,” Barrasso said. Trump has recently sought to blame record U.S. diesel prices on Ukraine rather than the U.S.-led war in  Iran , which has elevated world energy prices. events.title: Ongoing Birdsville Track closure hits outback businesses
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Birdsville Track's long-term closure hurting outback businesses Cooper Creek over the Birdsville Track, in June 2025. ( Supplied: Marree Roadhouse ) The Birdsville Track has been closed for 400 days of the past two years. The road is a major freight and tourism route cutting through outback South Australia and Queensland. Part of the track is expected to reopen next week, while northern sections could remain closed for many months. One of Australia's most iconic outback roads has been closed for 400 days out of the past two years due to rain damage, with remote businesses feeling the pinch. Stretching more than 500 kilometres, the Birdsville Track connects Birdsville in south-west Queensland, to Marree in far-north South Australia. It provides access to local pastoral properties to move cattle, allows stock to flow to the South Australian market and has become increasingly popular with outback tourists. The track is largely unsealed, meaning flooding and heavy rain have periodically closed the track over the years — but never for this long. Despite the challenges, Lyall Oldfield is "very happy" living in the outback. ( Supplied: Marree Roadhouse ) Marree Roadhouse owner Lyall Oldfield said his business was "probably one third of what it normally is". "It's just dreadful what's happening with the roads. It's not even a joke." Business at the Marree Roadhouse is one third of what it normally is. ( Supplied: Marree Roadhouse ) About 230km north of Marree is the Mungerannie Hotel, which was taken over by new owners in 2023. Three years later, the business has not opened all year, with road closures stopping the daily water deliveries it relies on. Cattle coming off Clifton Hills Station on the Birdsville Track in South Australia after flooding. ( Supplied: Pete Nunn ) Co-owner Andrew Norman said it was a similar tale in 2025, when there was "no sort of season whatsoever". Mr Norman said the closure north of Mungeranie is having the biggest impact, deterring tourists from making the trip. The Birdsville Track has sustained significant damage from rain events. ( Supplied: Department for Infrastructure and Transport ) Mungerannie Hotel secures water source The owners of the Mungerannie Hotel on the Birdsville Track will now truck 13,000 litres of water to the pub each day, after being told they can no longer use a nearby bore. "Nobody's really coming up to Mungeranie to turn around and go back," Mr Norman said. "If they can get that road open just north of us and get the Birdsville Track open, next year should be fine. "If the track is open, we'll be open. But without a track, we're not open." The SA Department for Infrastructure and Transport hoped to reopen the 200km section between Marree and Mungeranie "next week", but the route north of Mungeranie is expected to remain closed for some time. Large parts of the Birdsville Track remain underwater. ( Supplied: Department of Infrastructure and Transport ) Regional north and outback road maintenance manager Juanita Chester said with some northern parts of the Birdsville Track still underwater, it would be "several more months before [the department] can even consider reopening". While the construction of a single-lane access route has been considered, Ms Chester said the local pits where materials are sourced have flooded too. The track has sustained damage from several significant rain events in the past 24 months. ( Supplied: Department for Infrastructure and Transport ) "They're like a dam when it rains, they fill with water," she said. "If we can't get in there to get material, there's very little we can do short of carting material from a long, long way away, which then impacts the roads." The department is assessing the scope and price of the remaining work, which will then require approval before it can begin, and Ms Chester said this would be unlikely in the next two months.

events.title: Senior Iranian official threatens to attack cables, data centers, and AI facilities in the region if the war escalates sharply again
events.summary: A senior Iranian official says  Tehran  finds the latest U.S. response to a proposal to end the war “insufficient” and warns of attacks on regional data centers and cables if fighting intensifies again. Meanwhile, Israel’s former attorney general took the witness stand in  corruption cases against Benjamin Netanyahu , as the political future of the country’s longest-serving prime minister hangs in the balance with elections weeks away. Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage  here . Iran says latest US response is ‘insufficient’ The head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council says Tehran finds the latest response from the United States “insufficient” as efforts at negotiations to end the war and fully open the Strait of Hormuz limp along. The comments by Mohsen Rezaei, a former Revolutionary Guard commander, were carried by Iran’s state-run IRNA news agency. Rezaei added that Iran is no longer responding to the U.S. and said Washington must clarify certain issues, without giving details. He said the U.S. has accepted some of the seven conditions but others remain unclear. Iran’s delegation to the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders last month  proposed a sped-up agreement  that echoed the memorandum of understanding that collapsed days after the U.S. and Iran signed it in June. The new proposal was rejected, but the two sides have remained in contact via mediation. Rezaei also threatened “cables, data centers, AI facilities and other sites in the region” if intense fighting breaks out again. Meanwhile, the Guard’s navy warned that any ship on the strait that turns off navigation and identification systems would be “identified as hostile,” according to an IRNA report. Attacks on ships transiting the strait have increased since Iran’s proposal was rejected. One attack was reported Sunday. Former legal adviser testifies in Netanyahu corruption case Israel’s former attorney general took the witness stand in Netanyahu’s long-running corruption trial. Avichai Mandelblit  indicted the prime minister  seven years ago for fraud, breach of trust and accepting bribes. The charges were the first-ever against a sitting Israeli prime minister. Netanyahu was in the courtroom to hear Mandelblit testify. The prime minister handpicked Mandelblit, his former Cabinet secretary, for the attorney general job. His tenure ended in 2022. Netanyahu has been accused of  offering or exchanging favors  with wealthy associates and media moguls for political gain. He denies any wrongdoing. Saudi Arabia on alert as Houthis warn of new strikes A  projectile struck  the same passenger terminal at the Riyadh international airport that was hit on Saturday. The airport had been closed after Saturday’s attack, which killed 12 people, but Saudi authorities reported injuries in the latest attack. Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen claimed responsibility for both attacks on King Khalid International Airport, which has been targeted every day since Wednesday. Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, the Houthis’ military spokesperson, urged “everyone to take our warnings seriously” about the risks of flying in Saudi airspace. The attacks have  marked a major escalation in the war  between the Houthis and the kingdom, and complicated efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war. Gaza residents return to rubble as strikes continue Residents in central Gaza returned home to assess the damage caused by Israeli strikes after they had been warned to evacuate the day before. Bassam Abed said at least 10 residences housing some 300 families were reduced to rubble, and families were not given enough time to flee. “Women slept outdoors. We did not take clothes,” Abed said. Israel’s military said it had targeted militant infrastructure, including a rocket launch site and a command center used by Hamas militants to attack soldiers. One year after  Israel and Hamas reached a ceasefire deal , Israel continues to launch near-daily strikes. Netanyahu wants probe into ‘NAZA’ documentary Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has asked the attorney general and head of the Shin Bet security service to investigate people who participated in the  new documentary “NAZA,”  in which Israeli military insiders describe what they say was the reckless killing of civilians in Gaza. Netanyahu said the film, which debuted at the Venice Film Festival to a record 25-minute standing ovation, tells “a false, misleading and biased story that slanders the State of Israel” and its military. The documentary has angered and unsettled Israelis, whose  view of the war in Gaza  differs sharply from that of much of the world, where criticism of Israel’s actions in the Palestinian territory has grown. Netanyahu is fighting to stay in power in the Oct. 27 election, in which security is a major issue. Lebanese army says retired officer killed by Israeli shelling Lebanon’s army said it had recovered the body of a retired army officer who was killed by Israeli artillery fire while checking on his property in the southern town of Yater. It said Ali Abdul Hassan Sweidan was “directly targeted by a hostile Israeli tank” and called it “a flagrant violation of existing understandings.” An Israeli military spokesperson said they were not aware of the incident. Israel has occupied a large swath of southern Lebanon since the outbreak of its latest war with the Iran-backed Lebanese militant group Hezbollah in March. events.title: Justice Department investigates TV networks as White House press-access fight escalates
events.summary: The Justice Department is investigating whether ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC violated antitrust law by jointly suspending pooled television coverage of Trump. The networks paused pooled video coverage after the White House barred CNN, MS NOW, and Politico; they later resumed coverage. A federal judge temporarily restored access to the White House on due-process grounds, but that order did not cover later Air Force One travel exclusions. The U.S. Department of Justice launched an investigation into whether the White House television press pool's decision to suspend coverage of President Donald Trump violated antitrust laws. The Justice Department said in a statement that it is examining whether the White House TV press pool — a group of broadcasters including CNN, Fox News, ABC, CBS and NBC — violated the Sherman Act by temporarily halting pooled TV coverage of Trump. The Sherman Act is a federal law that prohibits certain agreements that unreasonably restrain trade. Introduced in the 1890s, the law has rarely been applied to media organizations, particularly regarding their coverage. Members of the press pool did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment sent outside of normal business hours. The DOJ investigation follows the White House television press pool ceased its coverage of Trump on Sept. 21, shortly after he prohibited CNN, MS NOW and Politico from accessing the White House. In a Truth Social post , the president said then that those outlets "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America." A judge lifted restrictions on those reporters on Sept. 24, several days after White House staff confiscated their press passes. Despite the ruling, reporters from CNN and Politico were barred from traveling with the president on Air Force One, the New York Times reported . The Trump administration now faces a lawsuit from CNN, MS NOW and Politico over its ban of their reporters from the White House grounds. Television pool coverage of the White House has also resumed. The DOJ investigation marks another escalation in an ongoing dispute between Trump and the media over press rights. The Trump administration has moved to restrict news agencies that have produced critical coverage of its policies. Last year, Trump moved to rescind about $1.1 billion previously approved for the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, federal funding earmarked for public broadcasters NPR and PBS. Trump and his allies have also sued several media organizations, including The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal, and BBC News, over alleged biases or inaccuracies in their reporting. Seth Stern, chief of advocacy for the Freedom of the Press Foundation, called the DOJ investigation "nonsense." "Depriving Trump of the attention he craves is not a competitive harm and in any case, antitrust law has long recognized First Amendment exceptions even when there is anticompetitive impact," he said. "After all his 'fake news' rhetoric, Trump is weaponizing the DOJ to pressure the networks he calls the 'enemy of the people' to stay at the White House. It's a weird way of telling the press how much he missed them." The White House Correspondents' Association did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Disclosure: CNBC and MS NOW are divisions of Versant Media.

events.title: From crane rental to marine transport: How this third-gen leader is steering his family business up the value chain
events.summary: Led by Michael Ang, Tiong Woon Corporation, multiple award winners at the Singapore Corporate Awards 2026, is investing in talent and engineering expertise to take on haulage and large-scale projects Tiong Woon Corporation chief executive officer Michael Ang is steering the third-generation family business beyond its crane-rental roots. It is past midnight in Pasir Ris. With sections of the road closed to traffic, massive precast girders are lifted, manoeuvred into position and lowered onto their supports for a new flyover. Beam-launching work like this is usually done overnight, when there is enough space to move heavy equipment safely with minimal disruption to other road users. Behind the operation is Tiong Woon Corporation, whose role in projects like this reflects how far the business has moved beyond its beginnings in crane rental and transport. In recent years, the 48-year-old family business has expanded into engineering and marine services, allowing it to take on bigger and more complex projects. Its fleet has grown with that ambition: The company now operates several hundred cranes, with the single largest rated at 2,200 tonnes. “A lot of people still perceive Tiong Woon as purely a crane rental company,” says chief executive officer Michael Ang. “Crane rental is still our core business, but we also offer marine, transport and engineering services. We want to show our clients and stakeholders that we can provide a more integrated solution.” For Ang, who joined the company 23 years ago, the transformation is also part of his role as the third-generation leader of his family business. Tiong Woon’s first 300-tonne crane, acquired from Soon Douglas in 1987. His grandfather, the late Ang Choo Kim, founded Tiong Woon in 1978 with a single 20-tonne crane. Two years later, the business was incorporated as Tiong Woon Crane & Transport by the next generation of the family. Today, Ang represents the third generation of leadership, while his father, Ang Kah Hong, serves as executive chairman and his uncle, Ang Kha King, remains on the board as an executive director. His family’s involvement across several generations has deepened his understanding of how far the company has evolved from its beginnings as a crane and transport operator. Over the past five years, Tiong Woon has worked towards an integrated model that combines its heavy lift equipment with its haulage and marine fleet and engineering expertise. Instead of supplying a crane or vehicle, it aims to take on more parts of a project and provide customers with a more complete heavy lift solution. For contractors and project owners, that can mean dealing with one company rather than coordinating several across different stages of a job. The Tiong Woon team dismantling a 200-tonne gantry crane at PSA Singapore, an example of the more integrated heavy-lift work the company now undertakes. The company is also expanding into new sectors. Oil and gas, petrochemical and construction firms have traditionally made up the bulk of its customer base. Data centres, semiconductors and biopharmaceuticals are newer targets. In February 2026, the company announced more than $40 million worth of projects across the semiconductor, public infrastructure and biopharmaceutical sectors, ranging from crane deployment to lifting engineering and project support. But taking on more complex work requires more than a larger fleet and workforce. Today, the company has about 1,300 employees across Singapore and markets including Malaysia, Thailand, India and Saudi Arabia, and is looking to hire more crane operators, engineers and technicians as the business expands. As the company tries to move up the value chain, its next stage of growth will depend not only on adding physical assets, but on building the human expertise needed to take on bigger projects and new revenue streams. A 4,500-tonne module being loaded out at Laem Chabang, Thailand, where Tiong Woon is expanding its heavy-lift capabilities. In the last financial year ended June 2026 (FY2026), the wage bill reached $65 million, about a third of revenue. “Our single largest investment is actually our human capital,” says group chief financial officer William Tan. The challenge is particularly apparent in Singapore, where Tiong Woon has more cranes than operators, Tan says, reflecting the shortage of skilled trades workers in the built environment sector. Knowing when to move, and when to wait In December 2023, Tiong Woon formed a strategic alliance in Thailand with Netherlands-headquartered heavy lift specialist Mammoet and acquired heavy lift, haulage and transportation equipment to strengthen its capabilities and position in the market. The move reflects the broader direction of the business: using the heavy lift expertise it has built in Singapore over decades as a base to take on a larger and more complex role in overseas projects.
