events.title: This intelligence building is top secret. Here's what we know about it
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts This National Security Office Precinct will cost more than $1 billion. What do we know about it? Some details about the National Security Office Precinct were revealed to Senate estimates in May. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) A stone's throw from Parliament House, six giant cranes have been working on the biggest Commonwealth construction project in Canberra in almost 40 years. The development of a National Security Office Precinct has been heralded by the federal government as a solution to "critical accommodation and capability requirements" of several agencies. Despite the huge scale of the project, many of the details have been kept secret. We know the precinct in Barton will be utilised by a range of Commonwealth entities. That includes the Office of National Intelligence and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT). In Senate estimates in May, we heard some details and there may be more to come. Construction of the National Security Office Precinct in Canberra continues. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) "We are engaging with other agencies as part of the development for the precinct going forward," said Nick McClintock of the Department of Finance, which is leading the development. Next to the main buildings, there will also be hospitality and retail venues, servicing both the wider public and workers in the precinct. Up to 5,000 workers are expected to be based at the precinct. At the sod turning for the project, Finance Minister and ACT senator Katy Gallagher said a "purpose built" and "specifically designed" building was needed to allow the national intelligence community "to do the work they need to do in a changing world". "[It's] clearly needed in terms of our national security agencies being able to work in a facility that actually allows them to do their job properly." Katy Gallagher says the new building will be more secure. ( ABC News: Pete Garnish ) She said the precinct would be "more appropriate" and "more secure" than existing buildings, with several government agencies reaching, or at, capacity. The project's price tag has not been revealed because of "commercial-in-confidence and national security sensitivities". But, we know it will cost at least $1 billion. "It is the most significant investment we've seen in the territory in a long time," Senator Gallagher said in 2023. The total cost of the precinct is expected to be revealed publicly once it's completed. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) She also told Senate estimates "it is a very significant infrastructure spend" and she has also described it as a "multi-year billion-dollar investment". The final cost is expected to be revealed publicly, but only after construction is completed. The precinct is the biggest Commonwealth construction project in Canberra since the development of the new Parliament House, which opened in 1988. Senator Gallagher has previously rejected claims Canberra had missed out on its fair share in recent federal budgets, pointing to the precinct as an example of spending in the territory. Construction is expected to be completed by the end of 2028, with the precinct starting to be occupied from 2029. The federal government has said the project will support more than 10,000 jobs over the construction period, which commenced in late 2024. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade is consolidating its presence in the ACT into two new buildings. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) Due to the "security requirements" of the project, it was exempt from needing the green light of the public works committee, which scrutinises major public capital expenditure projects. We also haven't seen any artist impressions or plans for the precinct, which means we won't know exactly what it will look like for a while yet. The precinct is being built on the site of a former car park. What happens to the buildings after agencies move out? A Department of Finance spokesperson said as existing buildings were "privately owned commercial properties", their future use was a commercial decision for the landlords. We know DFAT is consolidating its presence in the ACT into two new buildings — the precinct and another new building also being built in Barton. The head office of the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade will be vacated. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) It means its current head office, the RG Casey building, will be vacated. The lease is due to run out in 2031, and as noted by the department, its future after that will be up to the private landlord. It was revealed in Senate estimates in June that staff will be moved into the new precinct as soon as they are "reasonably able to".

events.title: Trump bears down on Zelensky as Russia keeps up attacks on Ukraine
events.summary: President Trump's announcement Sunday about an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine referred to a potential deal that includes each side stopping attacks on oil refineries — and he expects Volodymyr Zelensky to abide by it, a White House official said. The official said if attacks on oil refineries cease, a deal to stop hitting power plants and energy grids could come next. Why it matters: Trump appears to be singlehandedly trying to will a partial ceasefire into existence. But for now Russia hasn't accepted any kind of ceasefire — and Ukraine wants one that forbids attacks on power plants. Reality check: The "refinery for refinery" proposal, as the official dubbed it, is lopsided. A Ukrainian official told Axios that the country has a single oil refinery which the Russians have attacked multiple times and isn't fully functional. Russia, by contrast, has a vast network of refineries. "We import diesel and gas. What we need is for the Russians to stop attacking our electricity grid," the Ukrainian official said. "The Russians are thinking about" it, the White House official said. "We will know soon if they are ready." Case in point: Hours after Trump's announcement, Russia conducted strikes on power plants in Ukraine, according to Ukrainian media. What he said: Trump's Truth Social post sounded at first like a major breakthrough. "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" he wrote. It appears much more tenuous than that. Zelensky said the announced ceasefire "was news for me." State of play: After reaching a deal with Russia Friday to lift diesel sanctions, Trump remains focused on stopping Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. He believes the strikes are driving up U.S. gas prices. White House officials warn that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries are hurting Zelensky's relationship with Trump more than they're damaging Russia. "Trump is really mad. He feels Zelensky is taking the U.S. for granted," the White House official said. Zoom in: Amid the crisis with Ukraine, presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have put their planned trip to Moscow on hold, at least until they get clarity on whether Ukraine and the Europeans are ready to agree to a new unified proposal for Putin. A Ukrainian official told Axios on Friday that during a meeting with U.S. negotiators in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could stop sharing U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests. A U.S. official denied that, saying Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainians that the U.S. was a strong partner, providing munitions and intelligence. Ukraine therefore shouldn't take actions that hurt American consumers, the two said. On Sunday, the Financial Times reported that the U.S. told European countries it might stop selling weapons to Ukraine through NATO if Ukraine continues to strike Russian refineries.

events.title: Insurer underpaid hundreds of NSW accident victims in 'mind-blowing' error
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts NRMA Insurance underpaid hundreds of injured motorists in NSW since 2019 NRMA Insurance initially estimated that about 700 people had been underpaid, a number later revised down to 400. ( Facebook: NRMA Insurance ) Hundreds of people injured in car accidents have been repaid by NRMA Insurance after the company miscalculated some compulsory third party benefits since 2019. The company said 700 people were affected but the number was later revised down to 400. Neither the insurer nor the State Insurance Regulatory Authority noticed the error. NRMA Insurance has been forced to repay hundreds of people who were injured in motor vehicle accidents, after failing to correctly calculate some compulsory third party (CTP) benefits since 2019. The original error was not detected by the insurer, nor was it noticed by NSW's State Insurance Regulatory Authority (SIRA), despite it having previously launched an audit of the company's practices. Instead, the mistake was spotted by a lawyer who realised their client's weekly payments did not add up. Neither the insurer nor the State Insurance Regulatory Authority picked up on the original error. ( Supplied ) Initially, NRMA Insurance estimated about 700 people who had been injured in motor vehicle accidents had been underpaid, before revising the number down to 400. However, the company told the ABC it had also identified a "further cohort" of people it believed were owed interest, after previously receiving lump sum payments. Greens MP Abigail Boyd said NRMA Insurance, a trading name of Insurance Australia Limited, should have been capable of indexing payments correctly. "It actually blows my mind," she said. Abigail Boyd says it was "extraordinary" that NRMA had not discovered the issue itself. ( Four Corners: Rob Hill ) She said it was "particularly extraordinary" that NRMA had not discovered the issue itself. "You have this massive power differential between these insurers and these injured people who are going through some of the worst times of their lives. "[Yet] it's somehow expected that [the victims] are the ones, or their lawyers … that will pick up these errors." Under the state's CTP scheme, people injured in motor vehicle accidents are entitled to income support payments if they are unable to work as a result. It starts at 95 per cent of their pre-accident weekly earnings, before dropping to a maximum of 85 per cent from 14 weeks onwards, depending on their capacity to work. The payments, made by CTP insurers like NRMA Insurance, are supposed to be adjusted twice a year, in line with average weekly earnings. The insurer markets itself as a "help company". ( Supplied: NRMA ) However, NRMA Insurance, which markets itself as "a help company", acknowledged it had incorrectly applied this principle, costing the average affected claimant $940. "We became aware in late April this year, through a customer's legal representative, that the statutory indexation may not have been correctly applied to weekly benefit payments for customers who continued receiving payments more than 78 weeks after their accident," a spokesperson said. "Our investigation confirmed an error in the application of indexation in our system, which has been corrected. We apologised to the customer, paid the amount outstanding (and interest) and notified the regulator." NRMA Insurance, which is a separate entity to the NRMA, said it had recently completed the process of repaying customers, along with the interest they were owed. "We sincerely apologised to all affected customers," the spokesperson said. This is not the first time NRMA Insurance has failed to properly pay the required weekly benefits to people who have been injured in motor vehicle accidents. In February 2023, SIRA issued a letter of censure to the company, after finding it had contravened NSW legislation and its licence conditions by underpaying more than 2,000 customers. NRMA Insurance repaid more than $735,000 to those affected, but it was not fined. In March the same year, another censure letter was issued over the late processing of weekly benefits. No fine was issued. And in June 2023, SIRA sent another censure letter to NRMA Insurance over delays in commencing weekly payments. No financial penalty was imposed. In 2023, NRMA Insurance had to repay more than $735,000 to people injured in car accidents. ( ABC News: Adriane Reardon ) Ms Boyd said SIRA's enforcement actions to date had given NRMA Insurance little incentive to raise its standards.

events.title: 'SNL' takes aim at Kevin O’Leary and his Utah data center: 'I'm going to make the future go away’
events.summary: James Austin Johnson portrayed Kevin O'Leary on "Saturday Night Live." Will Heath/NBC via Getty Images "Saturday Night Live" took on Kevin O'Leary and his data center. "These things shouldn't be anywhere. That's why I'm building one in Utah," Johnson's O'Leary said. The real O'Leary is backing a giant data center project spanning over 20,000 acres. AI data centers got the "Weekend Update" treatment on "Saturday Night Live" this week. Comedian James Austin Johnson portrayed "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary on the sketch comedy show, during which he addressed the dispute over the real O'Leary's proposed data center in Utah, known as the Stratos Project . "It's very simple. All I want is to buy up 40,000 acres of God's untouched splendor and replace it with a very loud computer that steals your job," Johnson's O'Leary said. "Is it going to take up precious water? Absolutely. Is it going to provide a necessary service? Who's to say? But on the flip side, it's going to make me a tremendous amount of money, and I think that's great." The "SNL" version of O'Leary said he understood that some Americans were concerned about data centers near their homes. (An actual May Gallup poll found that over half of American surveyors opposed constructing AI data centers in their local area.) "These things are terrible and shouldn't be anywhere. That's why I'm building one in Utah," he said. Data centers are a contentious issue in the United States. Leading tech companies rely on AI data centers to power their systems and products. Supporters say they'll create new jobs , bolster the economy, and help the US defeat China in the race to control the global AI market. Residents in the places where they are being built, however, are often much less excited about them. The Utah project, backed by O'Leary Digital, has drawn criticism from many local residents over concerns that the data center could strain local resources and worsen the environment. Some residents are also upset over what they consider a lack of transparency from O'Leary and local leaders. Critics of the Stratos Project have staged protests, created petitions, and taken legal action to stop its construction. O'Leary scaled back the data center's size from about 40,000 to just over 20,000 acres after public pushback. He has said he remains undeterred, though. "There are bumps in the road. There's litigation. There's misinformation. There's propaganda. You name it. But if you know what you're doing is right, you make it, you get there," O'Leary told Business Insider in June. "Persevere." During a May interview on Fox News, O'Leary said said some critics of the project have ties to the Chinese Communist Party, a claim he later walked back. A Utah advocacy group that has publicly opposed the project filed a defamation lawsuit against Fox News and O'Leary in July. On "Saturday Night Live," Johnson's O'Leary acknowledged the incident. "I made the mildly inflammatory claim that every single person in Utah who opposes me is a paid communist super agent from China. Was I wrong? Perhaps. But just because they're not, doesn't mean they aren't," he said. He added, "I'm going to make the future go away. And we're doing just that in Utah." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Gas shortage culprit to slip through reservation 'loopholes', say critics
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Critics say 'Santos-sized loopholes' will make gas reservation a joke Liquefied natural gas ships from Curtis Island in Queensland. ( Supplied: Photopia Studio ) Gas market players say the federal government's draft gas reservation scheme has been weakened by loopholes. They argue that changes to the policy favour the Santos-led GLNG venture, which has been blamed for rising prices on the east coast. The government is expected to release legislation for the scheme in the coming weeks. A giant LNG plant blamed by critics for driving up east coast gas prices could largely or totally escape a federal scheme designed to protect local buyers, observers have warned. The Albanese government last month released a draft plan to force gas exporters to set aside up to 20 per cent of their production for the domestic market in a bid to force prices lower. But analysts and industry players say the draft is full of loopholes that will allow some exporters to reduce or even eliminate their exposure. They point to the Gladstone LNG project, a plant on Curtis Island in Queensland that is operated by Adelaide-based Santos, as the exporter most likely to benefit. An ABC investigation revealed GLNG had sucked up and exported the equivalent of 20 per cent of eastern Australia's domestic gas demand over the past 10 years. This was because the venture built an LNG plant with a capacity of 7.8 million tonnes a year despite not having nearly enough gas of its own to fill it. By contrast, the other two LNG projects in Queensland — run by global super-major Shell and Australian company Origin along with US firm ConocoPhillips — had overwhelmingly been supplying the local market in net terms. Paul Farrow is unsympathetic to Santos. ( ABC News: Kit Mochan ) Australian Workers' Union (AWU) national secretary Paul Farrow said "Santos-sized loopholes" threatened to turn the government's reservation plans into a joke. Mr Farrow said that, compared with earlier iterations of the plan, the draft had been watered down in significant ways that appeared to favour GLNG above all others. "Australian industry and Australian consumers deserve to derive an advantage from Australia's gas because it's our sovereign wealth," Mr Farrow said. "The government is so close to getting it right. "But the exposure draft, as it stands, contains a bunch of Santos-sized loopholes. Curtis Island in Gladstone is home to three gas plants that export Australian gas. ( Supplied: Nearmap ) Under the draft policy, the Australian Energy Regulator would be able to reduce an exporter's supply obligation below 20 per cent, while the minister could cut it to zero. But critics say a raft of other provisions in the bill could enable Santos and its GLNG partners to slip the net themselves. They say the draft, unlike earlier iterations, effectively allows GLNG to count contract extensions as "existing contracts" that are exempt from consideration. Crucially, this would allow GLNG to extend a supply agreement with South Korea's KOGAS for five years from 2030. The current deal is for 3.5 million tonnes of LNG a year, an amount equivalent to about 40 per cent of annual east coast gas demand. Observers also say the draft will give rise to "take-or-pay" deals that allow Santos to generate paper sales to the domestic market without actually supplying any gas. And they argue the government has given too much ground to Santos over questions about whether the company can "reasonably" find enough gas without breaking export contracts. Mr Farrow said the provision should require Santos to explore all practical options, such as buying gas from other providers in the local market, substituting LNG cargoes from its international operations or using flexibility in its contracts to reduce overseas sales. Instead, he said the draft appeared to allow Santos itself to set those terms, which he argued the company would do so however it liked. "If a massive project like GLNG wants to claim that it simply doesn't have enough gas to share with the Australian market, it should have to prove it's actually explored all practical options to get hold of that gas," Mr Farrow said. "These options might incur a small cost for Santos' shareholders. The government hopes its reservation plans can encourage more gas wells. ( ABC News: Hamish Harty ) As well as these provisions, Mr Farrow said the draft contained other clauses that would allow GLNG off the hook. Among them was a so-called "additional gas" test. While Mr Farrow said the test was theoretically supposed to encourage new production and increase supplies, in reality he said it was likely to be gamed.

events.title: From BJ’s to Lululemon, retailers are trimming assortments to boost business
events.summary: Dollar General, BJ's Wholesale Club, Lululemon and Under Armour have said in earnings calls that they have already cut or plan to cut assortments. Analysts said that after trimming product lines, brands may focus on raising prices to get back to healthy growth. Box retailers can offer thousands of individual brands, so product cuts can help streamline assortments and stabilize their businesses. Trimming assortments comes with challenges, as retailers risk losing customers and have to answer to investors as their revenue base shrinks in the short term. Retailers are trimming assortments in an effort to clean up their balance sheets. As shoppers cut spending in the face of high gas and food prices, businesses have pulled more levers to boost profitability and appease investors. During earnings calls this year, a range of retailers have highlighted efforts to reduce the number of items they sell, commonly tracked as stock keeping units, or SKUs. In March, Dollar General said it trimmed 1,500 SKUs. In August, Under Armour said it shrunk SKUs by 25% over the past few years and plans to cut another 25%, while BJ's Wholesale Club said it plans to reduce roughly 20% of SKUs . In September, Lululemon said it cut North America SKUs by 15%. Trimming inventory can help a business stabilize its sales or even get back to growth, and can reduce the chances a company gets stuck with unwanted inventory. But the move can also leave consumers with less choice — a trade-off many retailers have been willing to make. When a brand struggles to sell certain products, it can lead to discounting, which hurts profitability. Some markdowns are expected when businesses roll the dice on new products that don't end up selling well, but too many promotions can cause problems. "If you have zero discounting, you're not taking enough fashion risk," said Guggenheim Securities senior retail analyst Simeon Siegel. "But discounting needs to be fixing mistakes. It needs to be done quickly." Under Armour and Lululemon are both facing repercussions from what investors see as too many markdowns. Under Armour's operating income, which illustrates its underlying profitability, turned negative in fiscal 2025 and 2026. The company said its problems would not be solved by chasing unhealthy sales volume or short-term revenue. "Today, we're managing for quality. Fewer products with greater purpose, tighter execution and a clear reason to buy," said Under Armour CEO Kevin Plank on the company's fiscal first-quarter earnings call in August. "We will sell so much more of so many less products at a much higher full retail price." Siegel said that when a retailer acknowledges it wants to shrink revenue, the goal is to regain pricing power. Lululemon grew its sales by more than $500 million from fiscal 2024 to 2025. Yet its operating profit fell by about $300 million in the same time span. Shares are down around 65% over the past two years. "Selling fewer options is not the same as selling fewer things," said Siegel. "Lulu has a long way to go, and simply cutting SKUs, simply saying we need to have better product is not the answer." Siegel said too much of even the best product can dilute the value of a brand. Lululemon reported $6.3 billion in U.S. sales in fiscal 2025. Siegel said $3 billion to $4 billion in domestic revenue is where companies typically hit a healthy saturation level. "It's a level where they can be large and still cool. Above that, they start cheapening what they stand for, literally cheapening the product, but also cheapening the perception," said Siegel. He noted that Nike is an exception to this rule, after posting $20 billion in North American sales in fiscal 2026. Still, the apparel and footwear giant, which has seen shares crater around 45% this year, said it is "rebalancing" its portfolio, having reduced revenue from classic footwear franchises by more than $2 billion in fiscal 2026, according to its fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter earnings call in June. For small-box stores such as Dollar General and big-box retailers like BJ's, cutting down the assortment doesn't necessarily give them the ability to raise prices. Rather, for those stores carrying thousands of brands, removing certain products can help them better manage inventory and refine their offerings to help stabilize the business. "When you shrink a box ... and say, I'm going to focus more on curation, you're getting smaller, but you're trying to reestablish why someone's walking into your box in the first place. And so it does get better, but it doesn't necessarily help your bottom line as much," said Siegel. BJ's CEO Robert Eddy said reducing choice, such as cutting the number of scents of body wash, pushes sales into the remaining products on shelves and then makes room for more product categories that weren't previously offered.

events.title: Citroen revives the 2CV for an electric age
events.summary: French carmaker Citroen has brought back its 2CV brand in a bid to boost sales of electric cars in a difficult market. The new model, unveiled at the Paris Motor Show, is a small city runabout with retro styling which harks back to one of the company's most famous designs. As a "concept car" intended to show Citroen's direction of travel, it is not yet ready to go on sale but the plan is to have a version in showrooms by 2028. As they face mounting competition from Chinese manufacturers, Citroen and other European brands are exploiting their heritage as a means of selling modern motors. Citroen chief executive Xavier Chardon described the new car as "a modern, ingenious and refreshing response to the mobility challenges of tomorrow". The original Citroen 2CV was launched in 1948, as Europe was recovering from the ravages of World War Two. It was designed as a cheap, robust way for French farmers and country folk to get around. The car had high wheel arches and soft suspension, letting it travel across a ploughed field or rough roads - as legend would have it, without breaking a tray of duck eggs. Its high roof let drivers wear a hat at the wheel. It was easy to drive and simple to repair. The car was so popular, it remained in production for more than 40 years. Over time, it went from being a utilitarian tool for the countryside to a cult classic, and a favourite of hippies and counter-culturalists. Fans of Citroën's 2CV hold annual meet-ups such as this muddy gathering in Switzerland Now, Citroen wants to draw on that heritage to sell an electric, small city car that is expected to sell for about £13,000. The look of the new 2CV may well evolve as Citroen develops its design. But as it stands, it shares plenty of styling features with its famous predecessor. The high, flared wheel arches, the tall, curved roof and the eye-like headlights are all reminders of the original "deux chevaux" or "two horses". By using memories of an old car to sell a new one, Citroen is following a well-travelled road. VW notoriously brought back the Beetle in the late 1990s, with limited success. BMW's Minis have always carried styling designed to hark back to the very British original. Fiat has been selling a retro-styled Fiat 500 for the past two decades. But the retro-nostalgia trend has accelerated recently, as carmakers have looked for ways to sell electric cars to sceptical consumers. Citroen's French rival, Renault, has led the charge. It started with the Renault 5 E-Tech, which visually echoed the distinctive boxy styling of the original Renault 5, once an ever-present sight on French streets. It has since revived the Renault 4 and Twingo brands as well. VW has the distinctive ID-Buzz minivan, a throwback to the classic T2 Transporter, while Ford is working on a new EV which is widely expected to be called the Fiesta. Rachel Burgess, senior editor of Autocar magazine, thinks it is a strategy that makes perfect sense. "It's a brilliant differentiator from all-new car brands", she says. "An older audience might remember the originals and feel warmly towards them, and a younger audience might find an appeal in the retro aspect." Finding new ways to make cars appealing has become more important than ever, at a time when European manufacturers are facing growing competition from Chinese brands. "Many in the industry believe the big automotive players in Europe…face a very serious existential threat from aggressive Chinese manufacturers," says David Leggett, automotive editor at Global Data. Back to the future: VW looked to the past when designing its ID-Buzz minivan In this hostile business environment, heritage and nostalgia could prove to be powerful weapons for more established brands, thinks automotive researcher and author Dr Paul Nieuwenhuis. "In a world where a wave of credible decent quality Chinese EVs are hitting Europe, linking European designs back to their history while using the latest powertrain technology is something the Chinese cannot do," he says. "The Chinese can establish new design trends, but there is limited history there." But Leggett thinks Citroen will need more than a heady whiff of nostalgia to turn its new car into a best-seller. "A reimagined Citroën 2CV should give a big nod to its ancestor - especially on price and design simplicity as well as visual cues," he says. "But it also needs to be a credible modern electric car in terms of functionality and features, with widespread appeal." events.title: Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic European industry
events.summary: Oliver Blume says ‘Made in Europe’ rules to counter rapid rise of lower-price Chinese brands ‘must reward real value creation’ The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals. Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week. The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries. Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs . Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”. The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU. Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China . On Friday, the EU said it had reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry. Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints. “Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said. Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Blume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.” Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin. Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”. The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes. On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.

events.title: Can the AI industry persuade data center opponents by getting rid of NDAs?
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Sean O’Kane, Rebeccan Bellan and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities. Rebecca was a bit skeptical that the recent spate of data center moratoriums will have a lasting effect, especially since the moratoriums only last for a year or two and “these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years,” though I countered that data center backers definitely seem worried. Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication. “We’ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can’t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said. Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean O’Kane: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon’s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren’t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular. There are so many things that could be said about whether or not people should be worried about the effect that data centers have on their property values, on their electricity bills, on their water usage in the area, and whether or not those things are real problems, inflated problems, etc. etc. I think so much of that just really goes back to the fact that a lot of these projects are being negotiated essentially in secret. Sometimes they’re being negotiated [with the public knowing] that it’s a data center, but just not knowing who’s actually going to use it or occupy it at any point. This is a long-standing issue with the tech industry. I always go back to the mid-2010s when Uber was expanding really fast. Uber was one of the companies that really used this tactic a ton when it came to working with local governments. In particular, I remember I was working at The Verge at the time and we had a freelancer write a story about a city outside of Orlando where Uber was trying to negotiate tax subsidies to subsidize rides for people to use public transit after the Uber trip. The whole thing was negotiated in secret. And not only that, which was frustrating on its face, but also, because of the secrecy, you could just see Uber getting really comfortable with asking for a lot of other stuff, too. So there needs to be more of this. I’m glad Amazon’s doing this. We’ll see if it actually does have any positive effect, but people are pretty entrenched right now. Rebecca Bellan: Yeah, I’m curious about what effect this will have and whether it will lead to communities successfully delaying or or killing any infrastructure that the companies need to build. What I’ve heard from some people I’ve spoken to, who deal with data centers every day, a lot of these moratoriums that are getting passed — and there are a significant number of them, including one recently in San Francisco , which is pretty ironic — but they’re only for like a year or two years. But these data centers aren’t coming online for the next two, three, four, five years. All of the buildouts are going to be massively delayed for a number of reasons from zoning to funding. Of course, if the pushback keeps going, then it might have an effect, but I often wonder just how much of an effect this political pushback is having on this. Anthony Ha: The moratorium I’m most familiar with is the one in New York . I believe it’s a one year moratorium, and that’s on permits for large projects. [Technically, it’s until the state finalizes an environmental review process, which is expected to take a year.] So already, there’s some wiggle room within that. And often, they’re framed as: “It’s not like we think [data centers are] bad, let’s not do this. It’s [that] we need to take the time to study this.” Which gives them a lot of room to say later on, “Actually, we’ve decided this is great. We love it.” But you can tell that the people trying to build these data centers are worried, which is why you have these unhinged tweets from people like Trump or David Sacks. Only time will tell in terms how long and how deep that [community] resistance is, but I do think they are worried.

events.title: Alexandr Wang wanted to make Meta 'cool again' — and memes were part of his plan
events.summary: Alexandr Wang's wild X feed seemed to lack any rhyme or reason, but the 29-year-old said it helped serve a broader purpose. Bloomberg/Getty Images Alexandr Wang said his prolific X posting is part of a broader effort to make Meta cool again. The 29-year-old has filled his feed with memes about Muse, the company's AI agent. Wang said his posts "made an impact" on the growth of Muse. Alexandr Wang said he had trouble focusing during recent Meta meetings. On his mind: New memes to post about the company's popular new AI assistant. "I would just like think of a meme and I'd be like 'Oh God, I have to get this out,'" Wang said in a recent interview with podcaster David Senra, adding that his coworkers were "somewhat surprised" at the buzz his posts were generating. "It actually made an impact on growth," he said of the posts, "which is kind of hilarious." Much has been said about Meta's chief AI officer and his chaotic X feed, which the 29-year-old has crammed with occasionally off-color yet invariably eccentric references to Muse, Meta's personal AI assistant that sent the company's stock soaring and redefined the market for AI tools. https://t.co/TXOR8iI4MK pic.twitter.com/NnBHKMdj8X — Alexandr Wang (@alexandr_wang) October 9, 2026 In his interview with Senra, though, Wang said that his often spur-of-the-moment posts served a broader goal — to make Meta "cool again." "Despite having like these incredible pieces of cultural software like Instagram and Facebook, historically, Meta was not cool," he said. "I remembered that the internet rewards risk." After launching on September 8, Muse shot to the top of Apple's app store 10 days later, surpassing ChatGPT. Meta says Muse can help users research , fill out forms, buy items online, book restaurant reservations, find a dog sitter, and connect with services such as email, calendars, Spotify, Instagram, and OpenTable. The app marked Meta's first successful breakthrough in AI tech, after its Llama and Spark LLM models failed to find niches already filled by widely used models from OpenAI and Anthropic. With Muse, Meta found a largely untapped gold mine — though competing AI agents from OpenClaw and Instinct already existed in Silicon Valley circles. Muse, however, had the advantage of coming from a popular company with several billion potential customers already signed up on Instagram and Facebook. And the internet, weary of staid pronouncements from CEOs who were perhaps once cool but are now entering their 40s (Mark Zuckerberg is 42), welcomed the boundless energy of a young executive newly endowed with power in the AI era . "It was a lot of fun," Wang said. "There were like a few tweets where I just didn't think that much about it and just said, 'Fuck it, post.'" events.title: Trump sticks with tariffs even as US voters turn against them before the midterms
events.summary: President Donald Trump shows no signs of budging from a trade policy that many Americans don't like as the midterm elections loom NEW YORK -- Maybe President Donald Trump really does believe that “tariff” is the most beautiful word in the dictionary . Despite higher prices, criticism from trade experts and displeasure among voters, Trump holds fast to his belief that imposing the highest import duties on U.S. trading partners since the Great Depression is a winner . A recent poll suggests that is a big gamble with less than a month before the Nov. 3 midterms. Most U.S. adults disapprove of his trade policies, with more than 64% saying he has gone too far with his latest tariffs, compared with 58% in January. A look at the political, legal and economic challenges to the Republican president's approach to trade. The United States has set taxes on imports from most countries in the low double digits, although the rates have gone up and down because of legal setbacks as well as Trump's habit of changing them seemingly on a whim . In the biggest round last year, Trump levied what he called “reciprocal” tariffs and other duties on dozens of countries. He cited a 1977 law that he said allowed him to act without congressional approval in an economic emergency. After the Supreme Court struck that down in February, Trump turned to an array of other trade laws to accomplish his goals. The primary one he is using now, Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 , allows him to impose tariffs on countries that he believes are engaging in unfair trade practices, such as not adequately enforcing a ban on forced labor. The new duties range from 10% to 12.5% on imports from 60 economies, including big U.S. trading partners such as the European Union, India, Japan, Canada and Mexico. Trump is taking a sledgehammer to a relatively open global trading system that many mainstream economists think has benefited the U.S. enormously. It has helped boost growth, keep prices low and make U.S. businesses more competitive and often dominant in global industries. The U.S. is the second-largest exporter in the world, after China. It exported $3.4 trillion in goods and services last year, far ahead of third place Germany’s $2.3 trillion. Although Trump claims foreign exporters are paying tariffs, it is mostly Americans who are footing the bill. Studies, including ones from New York Fed and Harvard , have shown that overseas companies have largely not lowered their prices to offset the tariffs that U.S. businesses pay at the border. Those businesses are absorbing the added costs or passing them along to consumers through higher prices. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer The White House responds that the factory boom is already underway and points to statistics showing that manufacturing jobs, after falling last year, are on the upswing and work in certain nonresidential construction trades is rising, too. “Factory construction jobs of today mean more manufacturing jobs down the road once those factories come online,” said White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers. In the four years after China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, nearly 3 million U.S. manufacturing jobs were lost, accelerating a shift away from factory work. Even global trade enthusiasts recognize the damage. Many U.S. companies struggled to compete with an influx of discounted products from China, which has suppressed consumption to encourage exports It also is true that some countries have higher tariffs than the U.S., manipulate their currencies lower to ensure to make their exports to the U.S. cheaper and help industries with subsidies. But tariffs among U.S. major trading partners are low, often comparable to U.S. rates and sometimes lower. Before the trade war, the U.S. rate averaged 1.47% for goods from the European Union, slightly above the average 1.35% imposed by the EU on American products , according to the Brussels think tank Bruegel. Europeans are big buyers of what America wants to sell. About 30% of European imports are from U.S.-owned companies, according to the European Central Bank. The relationship with Canada, America's big trading partner to the north, was also similar before trade talks broke down this summer. Canada's effective tariff rate on U.S. imports was about 2.4%, less than half the 5% that the U.S. had on Canadian imports, according to calculations by Oxford Economics. Now the countries are mired in a tit-for-tat dispute, with both countries escalating tariffs on each other. Self-driving truck companies Aurora Innovation and Kodiak AI received a federal exemption this week that removes a massive barrier to commercialization. Under federal regulations, if a traditional big rig runs into trouble, the human driver must pull over, activate the hazard lights, and then physically place reflective warning triangles on the road within 10 minutes to alert other road users. But if a mechanical problem forces a self-driving truck to pull over, there’s no human driver to deploy those warning devices. It was a big enough hurdle that Aurora took federal safety regulators to court over the requirement. After the court denied its request for an exemption, the company escalated the fight to the District of Columbia Court of Appeals. (Companies did have a temporary waiver as it awaited a decision.) Now Aurora and other self-driving truck developers have been given the green light from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration . The agency has granted a five-year exemption allowing companies to replace roadside warning devices, such as reflective warning triangles, with cab-mounted warning beacons. Check out Aurora’s first responders page to see how it works. Daniel Goff , vice president of external affairs at Kodiak AI, said the exemption will help the industry “usher in an autonomous era of freight movement on U.S. roads, one that can save lives and improve the efficiency of goods delivery.” Gerardo Interiano , Aurora’s head of government relations and public affairs, echoed that sentiment, saying the decision underscores the government’s recognition of the economic and community benefits of autonomous trucking. He described the high-visibility, cab-mounted warning beacons as a “critical, 21st-century solution that enhances roadside safety by immediately alerting other road users without ever needing to put a person in harm’s way.” One question I’m left with: Could these cab-mounted warning beacons eventually become standard equipment across the entire trucking industry? events.title: Dawn Myers is making it easier to style, detangle, and care for curly hair
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Normally, Dawn Myers wears her hair up in a big old afro, and anyone with an afro can attest that wash days — the routine of washing and styling textured hair — are often tedious. They take a lot of detangling, product, styling, and, well, time. “I was watching ‘Shark Tank,’ and there was another curly girl idea,” she recalled of a day around eight years ago, when a pitch for a hair product aired. She started thinking about all the hair tools on the market, like blow dryers and curling irons, “things that straighten and change the chemistry of our naturally curly hair,” she told TechCrunch, adding that it takes around an hour and 20 minutes to wash and style her own hair. None of those tools help with that, and for Myers, it highlighted a gap that has always existed in the beauty hardware space — a lack of tooling for textured hair. It’s a space that’s complex, expensive, and just overlooked . “If you think back to slavery, we were mandated to cover our hair. That’s where do-rags come from. You had to cover your hair. Why? Because our hair was seen as ugly and unkempt and unacceptable,” she said. Later came hot combs, chemical relaxers, and flat irons, all of which straighten textured hair. “It’s only been the past 15 years or so where women of color and Black women in particular and, quite frankly, white women as well have really felt comfortable exposing their naturally curly hair and really just embracing it.” Soon after that episode aired, she whipped out a legal pad and sketched out a business idea, then went to Ace Hardware and CVS and put together a “Frankenstein-looking prototype.” Her idea eventually became the company Richualist , which is known for its product Mint, a hair tool that helps detangle, condition, gel, and style in a single stroke using refillable product pods. It even has warming technology to gently heat the product before it’s applied. “We get that styling time down to about seven to 10 minutes,” she said. “It’s a massive game changer for the customer really stressed out by wash day.” She said her product, which also comes in travel size, helps make hair a bit healthier, reducing shedding and breakage by up to 70% since people no longer need to tug endlessly on their strands as they wash and style. She built it with the materials science company Dow, after an early prototype caught the company’s attention during a startup accelerator program. “It just so happens that Dow had identified this white space recently as well, and they were starting a textured hair care unit,” she said. “So they ended up collaborating with us and giving us a lot of engineering help and manufacturing guidance.” Even though she eventually became one of the first 100 Black women to raise more than $1 million in venture funding, the early days were rough. “It’s really impossible to get hardware funded,” she continued. “It’s even more impossible to get it funded when we’re talking about such a niche problem.” She recalled the early meetings with executives in the beauty industry. “There are no people who look like me in those R&D suites.” In fact, she said, when she described wash days, “these people didn’t know what a wash day was. They didn’t understand that there’s this whole process that their customers have to go through.” She would tell them how painful and arduous the process is. “And the powers that be, up until this point, did not know,” she continued. “Even the bonds in our hair are totally different than other technology types. We really do need bespoke technology.” Myers sold her home and liquidated her 401(k) retirement account to fund the initial development of this product. “That was a crazy bet, but it paid off,” she said. “We were able to get about $1.4 million in the door to commercialize the product and just validate it.” Overall, it took about five years of development to get the product to “a place where it made sense to the customer,” she said, adding that her team also had to conduct their own research in the space since what they needed — like how much product the average person with textured hair uses — didn’t yet exist. Then, in 2022, just as she was about to expand and go to market, she was diagnosed with stage three colorectal cancer. “We ended up closing our round while I was still going through treatment,” she recalled, saying the round took “forever” to close. She remembers sitting in the chemo chair at Johns Hopkins, on her laptop, trying to close deals. She applied to Shark Tank in 2023 and appeared on the show later that year, though the episode aired in 2024. “I was still wearing a binder around my abdomen [a compression wrap] under the dress I wore for my ‘Shark Tank’ experience,” she said.

events.title: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agree to energy ceasefire
events.summary: President Trump claimed Sunday that Russia and Ukraine agreed to an " energy ceasefire " and will halt attacks on each other's energy facilities. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky tells Axios the announcement "was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree." Why it matters: An "energy ceasefire" would be a dramatic diplomatic breakthrough ahead of the winter. It remains unclear if Russia indeed agreed to stop the strikes. Trump made a similar announcement last month, but neither party confirmed that there was a deal. Both Russia and Ukraine continued attacking energy infrastructure. What they're saying: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on Truth Social. In a short interview after Trump's announcement, Zelensky told Axios, "If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it." Catch up quick: The announcement follows days of escalating tensions between Trump and Zelensky over Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries. On Friday, Trump announced a deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel exports in an effort to lower soaring fuel prices, infuriating Ukraine. On Saturday, Trump called for Ukraine to replace Zelensky , accusing him of refusing opportunities to end the war. Zelensky responded Sunday on ABC's "This Week," saying Ukraine would hold elections if Russia agreed to a 60-day ceasefire. He also said Ukraine was prepared to stop attacking Russian refineries if Moscow halted strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The big picture: The war with Iran has driven up global fuel prices, intensifying pressure on Trump to deliver relief for American consumers. "It's more difficult to stop Putin than to pressure others," Zelensky told ABC on Sunday. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: My parents made me take music lessons as a kid. I refused to do the same to my own children.
events.summary: The author (not shown) said she started piano lessons in fourth grade, but didn't always enjoy them. Hakase_/Getty Images I loved being in the marching band in high school. I didn't love the practice that was forced on me from a young age, and neither did my husband. We waited until our three kids asked about music lessons instead of forcing them on them. Some of my favorite high school memories involve music. I played flute in the marching band , and I still remember traveling with my friends to p erform at Disneyland in our senior year. Those trips were fun, and the friends I made in band class are the only high school friends I still keep in touch with. But getting there involved years of music lessons that I didn't exactly choose. I started piano lessons in fourth grade, which meant giving up after-school hours when I'd much rather have been doing almost anything else. Eventually, I switched to flute and continued playing through high school. By then, I was good enough to enjoy being in the marching band, but years of being told to practice left me with mixed feelings about music. My husband had a similar experience with the viola. He spent countless hours practicing an instrument because his parents wanted him to. Today, decades later, he doesn't play it. Neither of us wanted to repeat that experience with our own kids. The author said she and her husband were forced to play instruments when they were growing up. As parents, they chose a different path for their kids. Courtesy of Kate Loweth. We decided not to sign them up When our kids reached the age when many of their friends were starting piano, violin, or other music lessons, we took a different approach. We didn't say no to music. We simply didn't volunteer them for it. Do you have a hot take on a common parenting belief? Email Jennifer Beck Goldblatt at jgoldblatt@insider.com to share your experience with Business Insider. If they wanted to learn an instrument , we told them we would support them. But we weren't going to spend hundreds of dollars on lessons and then spend the next several years nagging them to practice something they never asked to do. It wasn't always easy to stick to that philosophy. As a parent, it's tempting to look at all the activities other kids are doing and wonder whether you're supposed to be signing your kids up, too. Music seemed particularly important. I knew firsthand how much kids could get out of being part of a band or orchestra. I also knew that learning an instrument can teach discipline and give kids an outlet for creativity. I didn't think those benefits required us to force it on them. Eventually, they came to us Then something interesting happened: They asked about music lessons. The author said all of her children now enjoy playing musical instruments. Courtesy of Kate Loweth. My daughter eventually decided she wanted to take acoustic guitar lessons. Later, my sons got interested in music, too, signing up for electric guitar and drumming. Because they chose these activities themselves, the dynamic was completely different from what I remembered from childhood. I'm not hovering over a piano bench telling someone to practice scales. I'm not threatening to take away screen time because someone hasn't picked up a guitar. They know they have to practice to get better, and they're more invested because the decision to play was theirs. I get to enjoy the show The biggest surprise has been how much more enjoyable music is for me as a parent. Instead of being the kid who is being told to practice, I'm the mom sitting in the audience with my phone out, waiting for the performance to start so I can record them. I get to cheer when they nail a song and encourage them when they don't. I get to listen to them practice "Johnny B. Goode" in their bedrooms and watch their confidence grow. The author said she's glad she waited until her kids were older and had their own appreciation and interest in music before signing them up for formal lessons. Courtesy of Kate Loweth. And because they chose this for themselves, their accomplishments feel like theirs. Maybe that's what I was really trying to give my kids by taking music lessons off the parental to-do list: not necessarily a childhood without instruments, but one where they get to decide what they want to become good at. After spending my childhood being told to practice, I've found that one of my favorite parts of parenting is not having to be the practice police. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Efferon wants to eradicate the devastating toll of pediatric sepsis
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Sepsis, an acute inflammation triggered by infection, is a leading cause of childhood mortality, claiming roughly 3 million children under the age of five annually. Efferon , a startup selected as one of TechCrunch Disrupt 2026’s Startup Battlefield 200 , is on a mission to drastically lower that number. The company has developed a medical device that it says lowers organ failure rates and significantly accelerates recovery in children. When standard treatments like antibiotics cannot stop the immune system’s overreaction, a patient’s blood must be filtered to remove deadly toxins. That is where Efferon’s devices, of absorbers of dangerous cytokines and toxins, step in to make a critical difference. Dima Romashin, Efferon’s co-founder and CEO, compares what happens in the body during sepsis to a fire, where an immune response overwhelms the body rapidly. “In a fire, there are two things: the flame itself and smoke that it produces,” he told TechCrunch. In sepsis, endotoxins are the flames and cytokines are the smoke. Efferon, unlike other devices on the market, has developed a mechanism that can absorb both at once, according to Romashin. Although Efferon makes absorbers for adults, Efferon NEO, its pediatric device developed specifically for young kids, is proving especially effective. Since children have a significantly lower circulating blood volume, they require medical devices engineered specifically for their physiology, according to Romashin. In April, Efferon NEO received a CE mark , Europe’s equivalent to FDA approval, making it the first multimodal blood purification device specifically engineered for pediatric sepsis. Efferon NEO is used in intensive care units across 30 countries, including European hospitals, Saudi Arabia, and Thailand. The company is now preparing to file for FDA approval and is on track to hit $2 million in annualized revenue by the end of 2026. The startup’s technology was originally developed by scientists at Moscow State University, including co-founder Ivan Bessonov. Recognizing its potential, Romashin, a serial entrepreneur, stepped in earlier this year as CEO to help commercialize it. Although Romashin admits that Efferon isn’t growing at the breakneck pace of today’s AI startups, true success for the company is measured by something else entirely: every child who gets to go home. events.title: Ukraine strikes Yandex data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant
events.summary: Yandex's data centres have been targeted three times this week - like this one in Sasovo on Thursday Yandex has been forced to pause its operations at a data centre near Moscow after the facility was damaged in a Ukrainian drone strike - the third attack on the Russian tech giant's sites this week. The company - dubbed "Russia's Google" - said no one was injured at the centre in Vladimir, east of the capital, but some of its services were unavailable to users. Earlier this week, Yandex said it was struggling to maintain its services after two of its five data centres were hit in Ukrainian strikes. Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between them continues in its fifth year following Russia's full-scale invasion. Kyiv said it was targeting places that provide revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the attacks could force Russia to divert its resources to repair the damage at Yandex. Sunday's attack came hours after US President Donald Trump warned that Ukraine should "damn well stop" attacking Russia's oil refineries so Moscow could release more diesel to the global market - a deal that has drawn criticism from Europe and sparked a diplomatic row with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky. 'Time for Ukraine to get new president,' says Trump after Zelensky condemns diesel deal Published 1 day ago Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices Published 2 days ago Yandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said it was working to restore connectivity. The other strikes against Yandex facilities were on Thursday in Sasovo and Friday in Kaluga, south-west of Moscow, causing problems for some of its services, such as its AI chatbot and smart home devices. The tech company - which also runs a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people - said at the time that its data centres were critical for the normal operation of its services, and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online. Meanwhile, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued through the weekend. The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said six people were injured in Russian attacks overnight on four districts in its south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region. On Saturday, at least 20 people including four children were killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, local officials confirmed. Russia has previously also struck Ukrainian data centres, causing internet outages and prompting some firms to move their servers abroad. events.title: Only 33 albums in history have yielded 3 or more No. 1 songs — here they all are
events.summary: Taylor Swift performs the "1989" set during the Eras Tour. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management Taylor Swift's "The Life of a Showgirl" has yielded three No. 1 songs on the Billboard Hot 100. It's the first female album since Swift's own "1989" to achieve the feat. The Beatles, Whitney Houston, Mariah Carey, and Rihanna also have multiple albums on the list. Thanks to "The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore," Taylor Swift has added another rare achievement to her resumé. The deluxe edition of Swift's 12th album added four new songs to the tracklist, including "Patient Zero," which debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 — becoming the album's third song to reach the chart's summit, following " The Fate of Ophelia " and "Opalite." Since Billboard launched the Hot 100 in 1958 as the definitive all-genre singles chart in the US, only 33 albums have spawned three or more No. 1 hits (not counting greatest-hits compilations). Counting songs that were released later on deluxe editions and reissues, Katy Perry's "Teenage Dream" holds the all-time record with six No. 1 songs, followed by Michael Jackson's "Bad" with five. This elite group of musical blockbusters seems to be getting more exclusive over time: Only 12 of the qualifying albums were released in the 21st century. events.title: Trump's AI rebrand is catching on with tech leaders like Elon Musk and Satya Nadella
events.summary: Marc Benioff said Salesforce's AIForce platform will be renamed SIForce. Bloomberg/Getty Images Trump called those who don't adopt the term Super Intelligence "the enemy." Marc Benioff said Salesforce's AIForce platform is becoming SIForce. Elon Musk also pledged to rename SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI. Donald Trump wants two letters scrubbed from the tech industry’s vocabulary, and some executives are already reaching for replacements. Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said Friday that his company’s AIForce platform is getting a new name. “The era of Super Intelligence is here. AIForce is officially SIForce,” Benioff wrote on X. The announcement follows Elon Musk’s pledge Sunday to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, giving Trump’s campaign to replace “artificial intelligence” with “ super intelligence ” traction beyond Washington. The company's X account has already been changed. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has also made the switch, referring to the tech as "Super Intelligence" in an X post about AI model containment and governance on Saturday. While Nadella has used the term "superintelligence" in the past, this was the first time he used it as two words — and capitalized. Salesforce’s change concerns its agent platform, rather than the company’s corporate name. Trump, meanwhile, is turning his terminology preference into a test. “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday. The warning escalates a push Trump formalized in a September 29 executive order directing federal agencies to substitute “Super Intelligence” and “SI” for “ Artificial Intelligence ” and “AI” in official communications, websites, reports, and policy documents, to the extent permitted by law. Private companies aren’t required by the order to follow suit. But Benioff’s announcement and Musk’s proposed rebrand show how the president’s preferred language is making its way into corporate branding. The administration’s argument is that AI has outgrown its name. The executive order says today’s systems increasingly amplify human creativity and that “Super Intelligence” better captures their potential. The rebranding push complicates matters for companies whose names include AI, and raises questions over what counts as superintelligence. The term generally describes systems far more capable than humans across a broad range of tasks, and renaming existing products doesn’t establish that they meet that threshold. OpenAI, Scale AI, Character AI, and Resolve AI did not respond to requests for comment. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: My parents spent 25 years celebrating me. For their 30th anniversary, I finally got to celebrate them.
events.summary: The author's parents have been married for 30 years. Courtesy of the author My parents met as teenagers and celebrated their 30th wedding anniversary this year. My twin brother and I surprised them with more than 40 friends and relatives. Planning the party reminded me that my parents have a story beyond raising us. My parents met in May 1986, when they were just 14 and 15 years old, and started dating in September that same year. Just a month later, my mom turned 15. She can't remember exactly what their first date was. Maybe a movie, she says, or something simple, like hanging out with friends. But when she first saw my dad — a quiet yet funny guy — playing catch with his best friend while she babysat across the street, neither of them could have known what kind of journey they were about to take together. They were married in June 1996, at Alex & Henry's, a then-popular catering hall that closed a few years later. This year, the day before their official 30th anniversary , my twin brother and I pulled off what I'd argue was one of the best surprises of our adult lives: a party with more than 40 of their closest friends and family members. They deserved to be celebrated My grandma traveled from Delaware to our hometown in Westchester County to help bring the surprise together. For months, she fielded my frantic calls about table arrangements, centerpieces, and cake flavors, while I dodged my parents at home. Trying to surprise the people you live with is no small feat. The author and her twin brother threw their parents a party for their 30th anniversary. Courtesy of the author I quietly texted out invitations, made decorations, including "Back in 1996" cards for each place setting, and coordinated with vendors and the restaurant to make sure every detail was just right. I was flooded with butterflies. I wanted so badly for them to be completely stunned — they deserved it. And because I had dropped off the decorations beforehand, the final setup was in the hands of my grandma and my best friend since kindergarten, who I tasked with bringing my vision to life. My brother and his girlfriend needed a believable reason to come home from Austin for the weekend. He told my parents they'd visit to celebrate their pearl anniversary , which made sense before a major work trip. He fibbed. There was no work trip . We surprised them Several weeks before they arrived, my brother "made a reservation" at one of our favorite restaurants — where he had worked in high school— for six people on June 7. We'd have a late lunch to celebrate our parents' anniversary with our partners and us. Since we'd be together, I convinced them we should take family pictures. My plan was solid. That afternoon, my boyfriend and I left the house first — racing to the restaurant just a few minutes away, leaving my brother with the coveted task of escorting my parents inside without them noticing the familiar cars belonging to friends and family in the parking lot. They turned the corner expecting to sit down at a table for six, but instead were met with a roar of "Surprise!" in a room full of their favorite people. They were shocked. The author invited friends and family to celebrate her parents. Courtesy of the author As they bounced between tables, they embraced, laughed, caught up, and reminisced while admiring the several photo boards my grandma had made, which captured decades of their love story in still moments. To me, the process, the surprise, and the aftermath — how it has remained a dinner-table discussion months later, and how the joy and love they felt that day still radiated from them whenever they talked about it — were a joy in themselves. It filled me with so much happiness. This joy has lingered in conversations, in the photo boards my mom kept displayed around the house, and the cake-table decorations draped over the piano. The pieces of that day scattered throughout our home became reminders that our parents are more than the people who raised us — they are people with their own stories, memories, and milestones worth celebrating. As we marked a milestone in their marriage — a stretch of time longer than my 25 years on this earth —I found myself thinking about the lives my parents had lived before they became my parents. They had already spent years together before my brother and I were born in 2000. They had been teenagers, friends, boyfriend and girlfriend, and eventually husband and wife. They had memories and inside jokes, losses and milestones, dreams and disappointments that belonged entirely to them. Their lives did not stop when they became parents. They are still living, experiencing, learning, loving, and losing things for the first time, just like my brother and I are as young adults. Read the original article on Business Insider
