events.title: I got divorced abroad and decided to stay in Europe. My $900 pension goes so much further in a tiny French village.
events.summary: Karen Anderson moved to a small village in Northwestern France. Courtesy of Karen Anderson/ Getty Images After divorcing her European husband, Karen Anderson decided to remain in France. She says she'd love to move back to the US, but the higher cost of living makes that unrealistic. She says affordable housing and healthcare have made life in France far less stressful. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Karen Anderson, 57, a Californian who moved to the UK in 2011 and now lives in a small village in northwestern France. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. I was working as a 911 dispatcher for a California police department when I met my ex-husband, who is English. After dating for a year, we got married in 2011 and eventually moved to his home country, the United Kingdom. I wanted a different life and the chance to experience more of the world. For years, we split our time between the UK, where he worked, and France. And in 2016, we bought a house in France for €45,000 ($50,450), far less than anything we could have afforded in the UK. At closing, I remember being handed more than 100 pages of paperwork. We were foreigners buying a home in a language we didn't understand, so it was very scary. But our hands were held during the process. After my divorce, I decided to remain in France In 2021, I returned to the US to care for my mom, who had been diagnosed with cancer. After getting screened myself, I was also diagnosed, so I ended up staying in the States for about a year while undergoing treatment. During that time, I got a job at Amazon , which helped me get health coverage. I eventually returned to Europe, but by 2023, my ex-husband and I decided to divorce. Although we were married in California, we had to divorce under French law. The process was difficult and took three years to finalize. While the divorce was still underway, I returned to the US to see whether I could make a life there again. It took me about six months to find work, and I eventually became a flight attendant with Frontier Airlines. Unfortunately, I could only afford a twin bed in a house I shared with 13 other women, so I decided to move back to Europe. Once our divorce was finalized, my ex-husband bought out my share of the house. This year, I bought a home of my own in France for €59,100 ($66,159). The process couldn't have been more different from the first time around. I only had to sign three documents electronically, and that was it. The system has changed so much in less than 10 years. For me, staying in France is really about affordability. My $900 monthly pension from my former job as a dispatcher is enough to cover my mortgage, utilities, home insurance, and car insurance. If I were living in the US, I would still need to work just to support myself, but there aren't many job opportunities at my age. I live in a small, idyllic village in northwestern France I live in Saint-Servais, a village of about 400 people in Brittany, in northwestern France , mostly known as the birthplace of crêpes. Breton has a distinct identity, and its people have their own language and traditions. What I love most about living here is that there just aren't as many temptations. You don't feel the same pressure to buy material things. The lifestyle is easy and tranquil. Saint-Servais is surrounded by farmland, with fields of maize grown for cattle feed, as well as sheep, pigs, and chickens. Despite being so small, the village has a restaurant and a church dating back to the 14th or 15th century. There aren't many everyday conveniences. There's no bakery, butcher, or grocery store, so I drive about two and a half miles whenever I need to pick up groceries or fresh bread, which is important to me. A village in Brittany, France. Andrea Pistolesi/Getty Images There's no light pollution or traffic noise in Saint-Servais. I can look outside and see the stars every night of the year, which amazes me. There aren't police sirens or much crime, either. Like many homes in the village, mine is made of stone and, to be honest, it's been a bit of a money pit. It's about 732 square feet. It's small but very cute. The ground floor is underground, and the two bedrooms are upstairs, one of which has an ensuite bathroom. Altogether, I have three bathrooms, which is very unusual for a house this size. Because the ground floor is underground, I have a great deal of humidity. Dampness is a real problem across Europe because of the cool, rainy climate. We get about six months of rain each year, which is very different from California. There isn't central heating or air conditioning in most homes here. I heat mine with a wood-burning stove, and I cut my own firewood. I could install a heat pump, which also provides cool air; it's still relatively new. France is behind the times in some ways — we only got fiber internet in my area in the last few years. My quality of life is better in France In America, we live to work. In France, people work to live. The standard workweek is 35 hours, and many businesses close from noon to 2 p.m. for lunch — they take it very seriously. I came from the US, where I worked 80 to 100 hours a week at the police department. I absolutely loved my job, but it owned me. I recently got a job as a real estate agent. I'm relatively new, and right now my hours are scattered. I'm not quite there yet on understanding how to curtail self-employment. A town in Brittany, France. Clement LEONARD/Getty Images Europe has great healthcare . In the UK, our healthcare was covered regardless of whether you worked because of the National Health Service. France is a little different. Everyone — citizens and legal residents alike — is reimbursed for about 70% of most healthcare costs. Then you buy a top-up, or what the French call a "mutuelle," to cover the rest. How much you pay depends on the coverage you choose. Because I previously had cancer, I receive full coverage, and I've always been looked after. The challenge, though, is access. Doctors and dentists are few and far between. My doctor is two hours away, but my local pharmacy now has a Telebox where I can have a video consultation and get advice or a prescription. I don't see myself moving back to the US Living in France on my own has been a big transition — it's not exactly the life I envisioned. It may look like a dream to other people, but Americans don't always see the sacrifices you make to live abroad. I don't have my children or grandchildren nearby, and I really miss that. At this point, I can't imagine moving back to America. I wouldn't be able to afford the healthcare or housing. I'd love to have a partner again someday. Will some man whisk me away? Maybe. Maybe not. But I don't pin my hopes on that. For now, I have a great circle of friends, and I'm happy with the life I've built. France has given me the ability to enjoy life without worrying about the next paycheck or what it will afford me. Read the original art

events.title: US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy
events.summary: ‘Even if AI supercharged the economy, its impact on the government’s finances would be muted’ Back through political history to the age of Ronald Reagan , Republicans have repeatedly promised the US public that tax cuts would pay for themselves, firing up economic growth and filling the government’s coffers. The promise never really panned out. From the Gipper’s day on, the Republicans’ tax cuts inevitably increased the budget deficit. Despite its failure, though, the promise is back, coated in a fine new layer of artificial intelligence pixie dust. It will fail again. The treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, is relying on an AI-laced economy when he promises to deliver annual economic growth of 3% – a rate that, except for the rebound from the Covid pandemic, has been achieved only twice this century. Dreams of AI inflect Donald Trump’s fantasy that “we’re growing at a faster rate than we’ve ever grown before,” which will allow the government to “take care of the 40 trillion ” in federal debt “over a period of time”. Financial markets, however, are not buying. Last week, the yield on the 10-year treasury bond surged to its highest in almost a quarter century, more than a full percentage point higher than when Trump launched his misbegotten war against Iran. The war’s inflationary impact is the most immediate cause of rising bond yields. It already persuaded the Fed to raise short-term interest rates. But the treasury market is also being walloped by the US’s unbalanced finances. There is no realistic path for economic growth to generate the tax revenues needed to fix the US’s enormous and growing budget deficit. Investors are demanding more to cover the growing funding gap. Borrowing is likely to become more expensive still. Foreign central banks, which once reliably bought treasuries to build up foreign reserves and manage their exchange rates, have cut back on their exposure to US government debt. The treasury now relies largely on private investors seeking to turn a profit. It finds itself competing for their money with the very AI superscalers on which it is pinning its future hopes, which are borrowing hand over fist to fund the buildout of datacenters to train their agents. Indeed, the US’s finances find themselves in a bit of a negative spiral, as rising bond yields put additional pressure on the budget. Interest payments on the federal debt alone are consuming 3.3% of GDP, up from an average of 2.1% over the preceding 50 years. And Trump’s fiscal management – his One Big Beautiful Bill Act is estimated to add $4.7tn to the federal debt through 2035 – is not making the budget math easier. The deficit already hit 6% of GDP – twice the size Bessent once promised. The Congressional Budget Office projected it will close in on 7% of GDP by 2033. And that was before Trump promised a $5,000 “dividend” to every US adult if the GOP kept control of Congress in the midterms. There is no realistic amount of growth that can fill the fiscal hole that Trump keeps digging. The Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFPB) sketched out a few scenarios . Assuming the temporary tax cuts in Trump’s 2025 law are made permanent by a future Congress – an assumption that fits the historical pattern – and that the government does not recover the revenue lost when the supreme court struck down its national security tariffs, achieving a budget deficit of 3% of GDP by 2036 would require annual growth of 4.4% over the next decade. Achieving a balanced budget by then would require the economy to expand 7.2% per year. It is not impossible for AI to deliver this kind of growth. Some economists are willing to contemplate scenarios in which artificial intelligence boosts economic growth to 15% per year, by taking over much of the cognitive work usually performed by humans. But these scenarios do not appear likely. According to the CFRB, stabilizing the federal debt would require average growth in total factor productivity – a measure of how efficiently economic inputs are converted into goods and services – to hit 2.5% per year over the next decade. The US has only hit that once since 1959. And that is despite massive productivity gains over the period from electrification, the completion of the federal highway system, the telecommunications revolution and the first wave of IT and automation. Even if AI supercharged the economy, its impact on the government’s finances would be muted, for it would massively shift the fruits of growth from labor to capital, and the tax rate on capital today is only about half the tax rate on labor. Moreover, such a shift in the distribution of economic spoils would probably call for massive government spending to sustain the livelihoods of the many workers left behind. What can we expect from the AI-pixie dust? At the moment people seem particularly worried about AI agents slipping their enclosures and killing us all.

events.title: ‘Some aren’t going to make it’: how pressure on farmers threatens UK food security
events.summary: Food producers are adding their voices to the chorus of warnings about the vulnerability of British supply chains “There are so many decent, capable, productive, efficient arable farmers out there, asking how they are supposed to finance the crop they are meant to be putting in the ground,” Jamie Burrows says. Sitting in his tractor at his arable farm in Norfolk, Burrows is listing the multiple challenges facing him and other food producers. Crop growers such as Burrows are ploughing and cultivating their fields, preparing the ground – hardened and dried out during the long, hot summer – for their next crop. But machinery requires fuel, and the cost of red diesel – used for agricultural vehicles and machinery that is taxed at a lower rate than standard diesel – has almost doubled since the conflict in Iran began in late February. The cost of most fertilisers used to grow crops and feed for animals has also soared by about 20% over the same period. “Some of these businesses aren’t going to make it,” concludes Burrows, who is also the chair of the crops board at the National Farmers’ Union (NFU). “It is very, very difficult.” These are among the latest worries for Britain’s food producers, who also faced a succession of heatwaves and drought conditions during the UK’s hottest summer on record , which resulted in England’s worst recorded cereals harvest, according to official production estimates . Farmers, the first link in the food production chain, are adding their voices to the chorus of warnings about the vulnerability and precarity of the UK’s food supply. Food experts, academics, businesses and the public spending watchdog , the National Audit Office (NAO), have in recent weeks called on the government to work on making the UK’s food system more resilient. The climate crisis, this year’s huge El Niño weather pattern , geopolitical shocks, energy outages and cyber-attacks are all considered threats to food chain security. Amid calls for ministers to treat food as a national security issue, parliament’s influential public accounts committee is to begin a series of hearings on Monday as part of its inquiry into the resilience of the UK’s food supply. MPs on the committee will look at the NAO’s findings on the shortcomings of the last catastrophe planning exercise by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), which largely excluded food supply chain businesses. Britain produces about 60% of the food it needs to feed itself, but is more dependent on imports than many European peers. The government’s own research has shown Britons are less prepared for potential future emergencies than several European neighbours. Some in the food industry believe there are signs Andy Burnham’s government is beginning to take the threats to Britain’s food system more seriously. The Cabinet Office will launch a campaign telling households to stock up on tinned foods alongside preparations for possible future emergencies. The government’s Prepare website outlines steps it says people should take, which include storing items at home, including bottles of water and nonperishable food, such as tinned meat, fruit and vegetables that do not require cooking. Despite this, a recent warning from more than 150 food experts and academics accused ministers of being “complacent” about food security and not having a plan to feed people in an emergency. “Historically we have done pretty well coping with specific events such as Covid and we’ve managed to ride through them, but we’re moving into a period where we’re having multiple crises impact at the same time,” says Prof Paul Behrens of the Oxford Martin School, University of Oxford, who signed the letter. These include the worsening climate crisis and increased water scarcity in regions that now provide some of the fresh produce UK households rely on, including the Mediterranean and north Africa. Meanwhile, Behrens and other experts, including Prof Tim Lang of the Centre for Food Policy, City St George’s, University of London, have been warning for some time that the UK’s food distribution network is concentrated, leaving it exposed to potential disruption or targeting by bad actors. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Lang has previously stated that the UK’s supermarket network is supplied by just 131 distribution hubs – serving 12,300 stores – while the industry body the Cold Chain Federation has warned that most of Britain’s food imports enter the country through four ports – Dover, Felixstowe, Southampton and London Gateway. The UK government wound up the strategic food stockpile that had been in place since the second world war in the 1990s. Behrens says other nations, particularly Scandinavian countries, now have “far greater national preparedness”. He says: “They’re looking at community responses and how much households can have on hand.

events.title: I left my $200K Microsoft job to bet on my startup. Work became less fun, and AI made me feel ready to build it alone.
events.summary: Junead Khan left Microsoft in 2025 to focus on building his AI startup, Treasury, without a cofounder or venture capital funding. Junead Khan Junead Khan earned over $200,000 his at Microsoft, but he decided to leave the company anyway. He said the job had become less fun and that he wanted to go all in on his side business. He resigned with no customers or VC funding and has since grown his social-media following to around 30,000. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Junead Khan, a 25-year-old entrepreneur in Seattle. He worked at Microsoft before resigning last year to focus on his startup, Treasury. The following has been edited for length and clarity. I had a really good experience at Microsoft when I first joined full-time in 2023. It was my first job out of college, and I joined right in the middle of the AI boom . I was involved in the rollout of data centers across the world. It was a great opportunity. Then Microsoft experienced some service outages , and by early 2025, I saw a greater emphasis on security and service stability. It felt like shipping things got slower. That started to take some of the fun out of the job for me. At the same time, I was watching new AI coding tools emerge. I wanted to experiment with them and get access to them faster. I was making very good money at Microsoft : I earned more than $200,000 in 2024, including stock and bonuses. But I didn't feel like I was learning all the AI skills I wanted to learn. I started to think more seriously about leaving the company and pursuing an AI startup I'd been working on on the side. Still, I wasn't ready to quit immediately. I built my startup on the side of my full-time job My business idea came to me during my senior year of college. I was born and raised in the UK but came to the US in 2019 to pursue a bachelor's degree in computer science at the University of North Carolina. I had money to manage in both countries, and I felt like the existing financial tools weren't working well for me. Around the same time, AI models were getting much better. I started wondering if I could use the technology to build a financial advisor tool for the average person who might not have access to one or want to pay thousands of dollars a year for one. So after graduating from college and before starting at Microsoft later that summer, I started building Treasury, which I describe as an AI money coach. For roughly the next two years, I worked on the business at night and on the weekends alongside my day job. Eventually, I started thinking seriously about leaving Microsoft . Jacob Zinkula writes about how workers in tech and other industries are navigating their careers. Share your story with him by filling out this form , emailing him , or reaching out via Signal at jzinkula.29. Follow his work by clicking here . I waited for my Microsoft stock and bonus before leaving Last year, I applied to a few startup accelerators, including Y Combinator . My thinking was that if I got accepted, I'd quit Microsoft and work on Treasury full time. But I didn't get accepted. At that point, I decided I didn't want to wait for somebody else to give me permission to go all in on Treasury. So, I started thinking of the money I'd earned at Microsoft as my own seed funding. Junead Khan said AI coding tools helped give him the confidence to leave Microsoft and build his startup without a cofounder. Junead Khan I also wanted to be strategic about when I left. I waited for some of my stock to vest and until I'd been at Microsoft long enough that I wouldn't have to repay part of my sign-on bonus. Last August, after about two years at Microsoft, I resigned and officially launched my company two months later. I built an audience by sharing the highs and lows When I left Microsoft, I started documenting what I was building on social media, primarily on TikTok and Instagram, but I also posted on LinkedIn and X. Part of the calculation was practical. If I wasn't going to raise venture funding and spend money on paid advertising, I needed to find another way to help people discover the product. I also thought that, as AI made software engineering more accessible, having a personal brand and an audience would become increasingly important to my career. Even if Treasury didn't succeed, I thought documenting my journey could put me in a better position if I decide to look for another job one day. The problem was that I had basically no social media following at the time, but I had to start somewhere. I began sharing my whole business journey on social media: the highs, the lows, and even failed product launches. I wanted to show what it was actually like to build a startup by myself without VC funding . I think that approach resonated with people. Over the past year, my following has grown to around 30,000 across platforms. About a year ago, I had fewer than 500 followers on TikTok. Today, I have more than 9,000. My advice for growing your social media presence is to focus on telling your story in the way that suits you best. People might assume that means making TikTok or Instagram videos, but that won't be the best fit for everyone. For some people, it might be writing articles or making long-form videos. Find the platform and content that work best for you and your style. AI made me think I could build the company solo One reason I felt comfortable trying this on my own was how much AI had changed software development. A few years earlier, I think I might have needed a cofounder to help me build the product behind the business. But today, Claude Code and Codex allow me to code so much faster. Building a basic version of a software product without a cofounder or VC funding felt achievable. If I eventually decide to raise money, I'd rather do it after I've had a chance to validate the idea with an audience on my own terms than give up equity before I've really tried. Today, I'm still the only person working on Treasury. I'm still living off my savings Treasury now has paying customers and has generated more than $6,000 in revenue. It's still very early. I don't pay myself a salary. The money the business makes stays in the company, and I've been living off the savings I accumulated before leaving Microsoft. When I initially quit, I told myself I'd give the company a year and then see where things stood. I've continued because I believe I've built a good product and have an audience that wants the company to succeed. Now I'm focused on figuring out how to reach more people and grow the business. Leaving a well-paying job without paying customers or outside funding was a risk. But one thing I've learned through the process is not to wait for somebody else to give you permission to pursue something. I used to think: If I get into this accelerator, then I'll quit. If this happens, then I'll do the next thing. Sometimes we look for those things as validation. I've learned that sometimes the only permission you need is your own.

events.title: British Airways is launching the world's largest business-class cabin on its Airbus A380s. Take a look inside.
events.summary: British Airways is re-fitting its Airbus A380s with 106 business-class suites. Courtesy of British Airways British Airways is updating its Airbus A380s with plush first-class suites. This week, it unveiled new designs, including what it says is the world's largest business-class cabin. The new A380 was expected to debut earlier this year and is now set for the coming months. Airlines love business class, and  British Airways'  latest updates to its  Airbus A380s  are proof. This week, the airline unveiled a major overhaul to the interiors of its superjumbos, including what it says is the world's largest business-class cabin, with over 100 suites spanning the double-decker jet's upper floor. "This is the largest single investment that any airline has ever made in reconfiguring an aircraft, stretching from nose to tail and touching every single aspect of the experience on board," CEO Sean Doyle said at a media event, which Business Insider attended. Over 35,000 individual parts are installed on each aircraft as part of the retrofit, which includes new galleys and staircases, British Airways said. While the A380 has fallen out of favor with many airlines since the pandemic, it still plays a key role in British Airways' fleet. The flag carrier has 12 such airplanes — the second most behind Emirates. "You're going to see a glimpse into the future of long-haul air travel on British Airways, and it represents the investment we've been making in our premium experience, and the A380 is one of our flagships in demonstrating our commitment to that mission," Doyle said. British Airways is making a rare bet on the A380. A British Airways Airbus A380. Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto via Getty Images Airbus stopped making the A380 in 2021, as many carriers retired their superjumbo jets to save costs during the pandemic. However, its enormous size allows space for extra features and plush first-class suites. Although the aircraft type is expected to stop flying by 2040, British Airways is spending millions retrofitting its A380s as its most opulent offering. British Airways previously unveiled its luxurious first-class suite in 2024. Pete Syme/Business Insider "Our ambition throughout this whole transformation journey is to take British Airways to the next level and to make it really special," Calum Laming, chief customer officer, said during British Airways' first-class suite reveal in 2024. While most US airlines have cut first class , European carriers have been investing in extra luxury. At the time, British Airways said it was set to debut in mid-2026, but this has been pushed back and could slip into next year. The airline says its retrofitted A380 is expected to debut "in the coming months." First-class passengers have their own selection of snacks inside their suite. Pete Syme/Business Insider This includes peppermints, chips, chocolate bars, and hydration sachets from ViDrate. And they get amenity kits made by Swaine, a luxury British brand established in 1750. The amenity kit on display at Monday's event. Pete Syme/Business Insider The kits are available in blue or cream, and contain a selection of skincare products from Wildsmith, including a face mist, hand and body lotion, ceramide multi-balm, lip balm, and face cream. It launched in early October for first-class passengers on all British Airways' outbound long-haul flights. The new business-class suites match the same modern color palette. Courtesy of British Airways British Airways also said it includes added storage space, informed by customer feedback. Business class, or Club World, will occupy the entire upper deck, with 106 seats. Courtesy of British Airways It reflects travelers' growing willingness to pay extra for luxury experiences since the pandemic — especially among wealthy American passengers. The cabin also has its own snack station, called the Club Kitchen. Courtesy of British Airways Passengers will be able to get drinks and snacks, like popcorn and chips. British Airways also said there will be "dedicated dwell areas" to encourage people to move freely throughout the airplane. Downstairs, the updated A380 will include 84 premium-economy seats. Courtesy of British Airways They will come with brand-new bedding and pillows. The seats feature privacy wings, too. Courtesy of British Airways Passengers will receive a reusable amenity kit that's designed as a tote bag for onward travel, featuring a Dr.PAWPAW moisturizing balm and more. Plus, there are bigger screens in coach. Courtesy of British Airways British Airways says economy passengers will also get upgraded bedding and pillows with more filling than before. The seats are wider as well. Courtesy of British Airways Passengers will also get blankets designed for added warmth and comfort. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Pope Leo to have "nodule" removed from lung
events.summary: Pope Leo said Sunday tests had discovered a nodule in his lung , which he will have removed surgically this week. The big picture: The first American pontiff, aged 71, is less than 18 months into a papacy that has been defined by public stances at odds with the White House , including clashes over immigration and deep skepticism about AI. What he's saying: "Dear friends, during some recent medical examinations, doctors found a localized nodule in my lung. It was detected at a very early stage and is well localized. The doctors believe surgery is appropriate," the pope said during public remarks, per a translation from the Vatican. "Following their advice, I have therefore decided to undergo an operation to remove it. The operation is already scheduled for the coming days. I thank you for your spiritual closeness and entrust myself to your prayers." The pope did not explicitly say the nodule was malignant. Vatican officials later said the operation would be in the next few days and the recovery would take about a week. This is breaking news.

events.title: Fujairah shows why resilience is the Gulf’s greatest energy asset
events.summary: For a city sometimes unfairly described as “sleepy”, Fujairah is keeping the global energy industry awake these days. The Indian Ocean port has emerged as a crucial hub for the world economy, sustaining the UAE ’s energy exports despite the Hormuz crisis. Last week, Fujairah’s importance was highlighted when Dr Sultan Al Jaber , Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology, and chief executive of Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc), attended the UAE Energy Markets Forum in the city. This continued a hectic run of conferences as the global energy industry emerges from a sticky summer and tries to find a way through conflict and disruption. The biennial WPC Energy Congress takes place in Riyadh this week, its first time in the kingdom and only the second time it has taken place in the Middle East , after Doha in 2011. The event has gone ahead despite the fatal attacks on the Saudi capital’s airport . Then, at the start of next month, executives take on the final boss, at Adipec, the world’s biggest energy event. Probably the most popular word in Fujairah last week was “resilience”. The UAE has managed to sustain, and possibly even increase, its oil exports through the conflict, as well as maintaining its essential imports. The Indian Ocean ports of Fujairah, Khor Fakkan and the others have been crucial. Rather than hasty workarounds, this rapid shift builds on years of preparation. The Habshan-Fujairah oil pipeline, with capacity up to 1.8 million barrels per day, was opened in 2012. Preparation for a second line had begun before the war, with the announcement in May and planned completion next year. Massive oil storage in caverns hewn out of Fujairah’s rugged brown mountains began construction in 2018. Adnoc Logistics and Services has amassed a large fleet of tankers and other ships, which has proved essential for moving oil. Supertankers are now in desperately short supply – it costs more to hire one, $80 million, than to launch SpaceX, a bargain at $74 million. Work on the impressive, modern new railway to Fujairah started in early 2020. The Barakah Nuclear Power Plant, an important part of assuring electricity even when gas facilities came under attack, began splitting atoms in August of that year. Regional preparedness Beyond the UAE, we could highlight similar regional examples of preparedness, such as the Gulf Co-operation Council electricity grid, Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline , and the new port, refinery and oil storage facility at Duqm on Oman’s south-east coast. Like Adnoc, Saudi Arabia – with Bahri – Kuwait and Qatar have their own sizeable tanker fleets. Physical assets are only one part of resilience. Adnoc has over several years built a strong trading capability. That was profitable in the years of peace. In months of war, it has been even more important by salvaging supply to customers, and seizing attractive commercial opportunities. These assets were not accumulated with precise foreknowledge of the current conflict. Of course, blockade of Hormuz, or general trouble in the Gulf, has been a known risk since the Tanker War of the 1980s, if not before. In general, though, having a broad set of deployable national assets, whether in one company or several, whether in state or private hands, enables a country to cope with crises of all kinds. That could be regional political unrest as in 2011, a price crash such as that of 2014, a pandemic such as 2020, or a far-off war as in 2022. We do not know what the next challenge may be: a natural disaster, a big climatic upset, an energy technology breakthrough, an international market meltdown over AI or government debt. But combining physical, institutional and human capabilities with a flexible and proactive mindset is the best way to come through such storms. Resilience alone, though, is not enough. When the bombers thundered through the sky on February 28, politicians and observers alike thought it would be a short war. It has now ground on for more than seven months, though most direct strikes on Gulf and Iranian territory have stopped. Other theatres – Yemen, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq – have become entwined. Every regional country, even the non-involved such as Turkey, Egypt and Cyprus, have seen some unwelcome visitor land on their soil, and have suffered disruption to their airspace and trade routes. On Friday, US President Donald Trump announced proudly that Russia’s Vladimir Putin had promised to provide some diesel to ease the growing global fuel crisis, a product of the wars in the Gulf and Ukraine. Handling future crises The Gulf energy industry must build on the resilience established so far, establish new options to respond to future crises, and accelerate creating value. Of course, that is not easy to do while the spectre of renewed violence hovers over the region, and while shipping routes are still not functioning freely. The regional countries were, overall, investing heavily and sensibly in their energy industries before this year. They were solidifying their oil upstream, making the downstream more sophisticated, accessing gas for the domestic economy and for export, generating more value from commercial ingenuity, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, electrifying their economies and seizing on transformational new technology in the AI space. Those remain excellent aims, even if specific projects have to be reprioritised for the new regional reality. Regional energy companies can do more. Becoming true international players fills a capital gap, builds their capabilities and somewhat reduces their near-total reliance on the Gulf. They can do more in inventing and deploying truly game-changing hard technologies. These often struggle in the rest of the world because of lack of visionary capital, overregulation and difficulty in co-ordinating diverse interests. Regional energy companies can work together more. Huge gains are possible from networking physical infrastructure – pipelines, ports, electricity grids and data cables. Greater achievements can come from soft integration, such as commercial joint ventures, cross-border investments and technology partnerships. The energy industry, one of the first truly globalised businesses, needs more than most to reimagine or construct institutions that govern its world by laws and not by the missile. The power to convene the world’s leading energy doers and thinkers, as at Adipec in Abu Dhabi, brings positive influence. Finally, at recent events elsewhere, the energy business has sometimes given the impression of being relieved the issue of climate change has been dethroned by that of war. That is a mistake. Conflicts will, by some smart application of strength and diplomacy, be resolved. Climate change, bad or worse, will be with us for the rest of the century and beyond. It will reshape everything we do in energy and itself can inflame war.

events.title: Labour has got the message – developing nations suffer most from bond market turmoil | Heather Stewart
events.summary: Labour has got the message – it’s developing nations suffering most from bond market turmoil Just as Brown and Blair did in 2005, Andy Burnham aims to champion debt relief to help developing countries Developing nations face triple shock, UN warns F rom Washington to Paris, London to Tokyo, policymakers in every large economy have been counting the costs of bond market turmoil in recent weeks. But the brunt of the pain is being borne by heavily indebted developing countries that have little hope of influencing the whims of global investors, but pay the price regardless. Markets have responded to the war in the Middle East, and a spendthrift White House, by dumping government bonds – driving up borrowing costs just about everywhere. Finance ministers and central bankers gathering in Bangkok this week for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank may be loth to point the finger at Donald Trump’s regime, but all are at least in part hostage to the US president’s war plans. That has made what was already a perilous situation even worse – just as the world is battling an energy crisis, and as developing countries urgently need to invest in adapting to the climate emergency. Even before the latest market gyrations, experts calculated that debt servicing costs absorbed 45% of government revenues in the global south , and 70% in low-income countries. That crowds out desperately needed spending on public services and investing for the future. There have been growing demands for reform of the framework for international debt in recent years, including from African Union heads of state , and under the G20 chairs of Brazil and South Africa. The G20 – the forum in which Gordon Brown coordinated a global fiscal stimulus package in the depths of the financial crisis in spring 2009 – is meant to be an important body for discussing international economic issues. With a much wider membership than the G7, it has coordinated previous efforts on debt, including establishing the IMF-administered Common Framework, to which struggling countries can apply, and suspending repayments for hard-hit borrowers during the Covid crisis. However, this year’s chair has been Trump’s US, which has placed much more emphasis on other aspects of the G20’s remit, including promoting global economic growth – somewhat ironically, given the main obstacle to achieving it is the war on Iran. Next year, the presidency falls to the UK, and Labour has made clear it will have different priorities. These will include seeking a global agreement on AI regulation, which seems a faint hope but is clearly worth pursuing. The UK also intends to put unsustainable debt on the agenda. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, who will be in Bangkok, told Labour conference delegates last month: “Friends, I promise this. We will use our G20 presidency next year to meet our responsibilities and mobilise the world, building on the great achievements on debt and development of the last Labour government.” He was referring to 2005, when Brown and Tony Blair rode the vociferous Make Poverty History movement to the Gleneagles G8 summit and beyond, securing significant debt relief for more than 30 countries . As the development minister, Kirsty McNeill, herself a veteran of that campaign, said recently, the circumstances now are very different, for two reasons. First, she said, “we’re now dealing with private creditors – the debt isn’t held by us. So that is quite a big shift.” And second, she suggested it was harder now to delineate a group of countries clearly deserving of support. “There isn’t this really clear demarcation between the very poor world and the very rich world that was true when I was starting out, and it was just a much starker and therefore more readily told story because the antagonists and the protagonists were just much clearer,” she told an event at the Labour conference. Yet she and other ministers have made clear they are open to proposals – and ready to throw the UK’s diplomatic weight behind making progress on this formidable challenge. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning One ambitious plan drawn up by the thinktank Development Finance International (DFI) and shared with the government would involve 27 of the most heavily burdened countries being given a 10-year “holiday” during which their debt service costs would be slashed to below 10% of their revenues. Implemented by cutting interest rates and extending loan terms rather than writing off debt altogether, the $13bn-a-year cost would fall primarily on private creditors – which might have to be coaxed, cajoled, perhaps even legislated into taking part, as in previous debt relief initiatives.

events.title: As youth sports booms, churches compete for American families' Sundays
events.summary: America's youth sports boom is quietly rewriting Sunday mornings, turning the family calendar into a competition between the pews and the playing fields. Why it matters: For generations, churches helped organize American family life around a shared weekly ritual. Youth sports are increasingly filling that role on Sundays — reshaping what families treat as sacred time. The U.S. has undergone one of its fastest religious shifts in modern history, marked by a rapid increase in the religiously unaffiliated and in church closures . Youth sports are one of the less visible forces driving that broader cultural change. As it's boomed into a multi-billion-dollar industry , more games are moving to Sundays, something less common a generation ago. "The idea of missing church for sports is just assumed," Linda Flanagan, author of " Take Back the Game : How Money and Mania Are Ruining Kids' Sports — and Why It Matters," tells Axios. "It's just not even a consideration anymore." By the numbers: Among parents of children ages 5-17, Sunday religious participation fell from 26.8% in 2003-07 to 16.7% in 2021-24, an Axios analysis of American Time Use Survey data found. Meanwhile, youth sports participation climbed to 58% in 2024, up from 53.8% in 2022 and marking a third consecutive annual increase, according to the Aspen Institute's Project Play . Another measure found 65% tried a sport at least once — the highest share in Sports & Fitness Industry Association data dating to at least 2012, the Aspen Institute's Project Play found. State of play: The youth-sports industrial complex is rapidly commercializing, fueled by private equity , massive tournament complexes and the normalization of out-of-state travel teams. Parents are increasingly treating sports not just as recreation, but as a primary identity and community anchor. How it works: Youth sports often start in local rec leagues, then move into club and travel teams that play weekend tournaments across a wider region. Across basketball, baseball, softball, volleyball and soccer, many weekend tournaments use Saturday for pool or preliminary play and Sunday for elimination rounds and championships. That fuels cities' and towns' investments in sports complexes built to draw traveling families and their hotel and restaurant spending. Zoom in: The average sports parent spends 3 hours, 23 minutes every day their child has a practice or game, including driving, attending activities, washing uniforms, preparing meals and communicating with coaches. Families are spending heavily, too: The average sports family spent an average of $1,016 on a child's primary sport in 2024, up 46% from 2019, Aspen found. What they're saying: Tim Morey, lead pastor at Life Covenant Church in Torrance, Calif., tells Axios that sports don't necessarily sever families from church, but they make attendance "more spotty" at times. "If we inadvertently teach our kids that sports (are) more important than weekly worship, then everything is more important than weekly worship." Yes, but: Religious institutions are attempting to adapt rather than surrender. Morey said some families "divide and conquer," sending one parent to church and the other to the field. Others have kids attend the first 10 minutes of service in their sports uniforms or stream services live from team hotels. Between the lines: Youth sports can create the same sense of community that mirrors what church did — to a point, Flanagan said. Parents form tight bonds because they spend so much time together, but competition for positions and playing time can also strain those relationships, Flanagan said. The bottom line: For generations, Sunday was about getting the family closer to heaven. For many families today, Sunday can also be about getting a daughter closer to UCLA's softball team.

events.title: Musk vows affordable Starlink in India days before Ambani’s record Jio IPO
events.summary: Elon Musk has previously accused India of stalling Starlink’s entrance into the country’s market. Musk said Starlink will be priced affordably in India to challenge Reliance Jio, as Jio’s parent prepares for India’s biggest-ever IPO. He said competition would help Indian users, while Ambani’s profits would fall. He did not give prices, but noted India’s data costs are already very low. Musk accused Modi’s government and Ambani of delaying Starlink’s entry. India denied bias, saying Starlink and Jio satellite ventures still await final security clearance. BENGALURU, India – Elon Musk said he would price Starlink’s satellite internet service affordably in India to take on Mukesh Ambani’s low-cost Reliance Jio, escalating his attacks on the rival billionaire days before Jio’s parent launches India’s largest-ever initial public offering. Jio Platforms, which owns the telecom arm, is targeting a valuation of US$106 billion ( S$135.62 billion ) in the offering. Much like SpaceX-owned Starlink , Jio’s own satellite venture is also awaiting final security clearance to launch. Cheap data is the playbook that built Jio in India, and the one Musk has used in markets like Kenya to unsettle local telecom players. SpaceX now plans to enter the mobile carrier market itself, starting in the US. Musk did not specify prices for India, where mobile data costs about eight cents per gigabyte, among the lowest in the world. “Obviously, if Starlink is too expensive in India, no one will buy it, so SpaceX will need to make pricing affordable,” he said in a post on his social media platform X on Oct 10 . “The reality is that competition would greatly benefit the average citizen in India by giving them more choices, as it always does. Ambani’s profits will be lower, but he is not going out of business,” Musk added. The billionaire’s remarks were the latest in a series of X posts where he accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government and Ambani of stalling Starlink’s entry into one of the world’s biggest internet markets to favour market leader Jio . The posts have marked a sharp turn for Musk, who has long enjoyed a warm public rapport with Modi. India’s government has denied any bias in its approval process, noting that the three satellite ventures seeking to launch, including Starlink’s and Jio’s, are all awaiting final security clearance. Late on Oct 9 , Musk taunted Ambani directly, addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and asking whether he would “consider allowing Starlink to compete”. Reliance has not responded to requests for comment on Musk’s remarks. REUTERS

events.title: Saudi Arabia presses on with global energy summit after deadly Riyadh airport attack
events.summary: Saudi Arabia pressed ahead with a major gathering of global energy ministers and industry executives on Sunday, hours after an attack by Yemen's Houthis on Riyadh's international airport killed 12 people and injured 309. The International Energy Forum's 17th ministerial meeting, hosted by Saudi Arabia and co-hosted by Italy and Nigeria, is being held alongside the WPC Energy Congress, bringing together policymakers and industry leaders. Media access to the ministerial meeting will be restricted, with only journalists invited directly by the IEF permitted to cover the opening remarks, according to a Saudi Energy Ministry spokeswoman. “As you are aware, the ministerial plenary will be held behind closed doors,” she said. No live broadcast pool arrangements were in place, she added. The event is proceeding despite mounting security concerns after repeated attacks on King Khalid International Airport , which have forced airlines to cancel flights and complicated travel arrangements for delegates. Italian Energy Minister Gilberto Pichetto Fratin said on Friday that he would participate in the IEF meeting by video link rather than travel to Riyadh. The WPC Energy Congress, which runs from Sunday until Thursday, is also proceeding as scheduled. Organisers have directed delegates to alternative routes into the Saudi capital, including by road from Dammam on the kingdom's east coast. A projectile landed near King Fahd Airport in Dammam on Saturday, a representative for the Saudi coalition said. Saturday's strike was the third on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport in a week and the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack, which killed four Saudis and eight foreign citizens, including one from the US. Two attacks on the airport this week killed four people and caused extensive damage to a Saudi commercial aircraft parked on the tarmac. The latest strike caused widespread disruption to aviation, with about 260 flights cancelled and another 219 delayed on Saturday, according to flight-tracking data from Flightradar24. The attacks have heightened security concerns, as Saudi Arabia seeks to maintain its calendar of high-profile international gatherings despite the war's growing regional spillover. Riyadh is scheduled to host the Future Investment Initiative from October 26 to 29, with organisers saying the event will proceed as planned, with additional security arrangements put in place.

events.title: ‘Halloweenmas’: how the spooky one-nighter turned into a month-long spectacular
events.summary: Welcome to Halloweenmas, weeks of themed fun and gifts – from costume parties to decorating trees – without the stress, rules or cost of Christmas The tree is up, the wreath is hanging on the front door and you’ve just opened your advent calendar . All told, it’s beginning to feel a lot like … Halloween . If it sounds like the stuff of nightmares then that’s the point: Britons are increasingly decorating their homes with ghoulish versions of Christmas traditions. Think of it as Halloweenmas. “What was traditionally a single-night celebration has turned into a month-long event mirroring many of Christmas’s traditions, but without the same level of expectation,” said Charlotte Broadbent, the UK general manager for the online wholesale platform Faire. Analysis of thousands of sales transactions on the platform revealed a huge rise in the number of Halloweenmas products available – up more than 500% in the past four years, from 425 in 2021 to 2,632 in 2025. The biggest areas of growth are trees, wreaths and ornaments. According to the budget retailer Wilko, Halloween trees are one of the biggest decorating trends of 2026. It said sales of artificial trees were 200% higher in September than a year ago. “There really aren’t any rules with a Halloween tree,” says Wilko. “You can go all-out or keep it simple with a smaller tree and a few spooky accessories.” The lack of rules is clear from social media, where the looks span student party – black tinsel tree shaped like a witch’s hat – to child-friendly cuteness. The arts and crafts retailer Hobbycraft’s website offers “five ways to decorate a twig tree” that include DIY spiderwebs made out of lolly sticks and felt pumpkins. Libby Ewart, who runs the online partyware and gift retailer The Box Party, has bought 40% more stock this year. “Houses are decorated earlier and with way more thought than before,” she said. “Also, this year it falls on a Saturday, so there has never been a better excuse for a party.” Emily Viberg, a senior retail analyst at the research group Mintel, said Halloween was “no longer just about costumes and sweets, it’s about a full season of engagement, gifting and themed activities”. Mintel’s research shows young Britons, in particular, see it as an opportunity to express themselves and experiment with fashion and makeup, with 16- to 34-year-olds over-indexing in purchases of fancy dress, cosmetics and decorations. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning “Consumers are increasingly buying into the atmosphere and social moments Halloween creates,” Viberg said. “Younger adults are at the heart of this shift, transforming Halloween from a one-night celebration into a broader season of self-expression and experience-led spending.” Viberg said social media had accelerated this shift, with 40% of Halloween buyers using the platforms to buy products directly. “Viral costume trends, makeup tutorials, home decor inspiration and content tapping into popular culture are shaping consumer spending and helping to extend the season well beyond October,” she said. While some people might complain it is all over the top, Broadbent said: “What we’re seeing is people investing into Halloween as a reason to share quality time together ahead of Christmas, with lots of fun and creativity at its heart and without the need to spend big.”

events.title: Charities and businesses wrestle with diesel cost
events.summary: Cancer charity Daft as a Brush's Scott Jobson said funds raised by donations were being lost at the pump Charities and businesses across the North East have said they are struggling with the rising cost of diesel. The average price of diesel has risen above £2 a litre in the UK for the first time, according to the RAC motoring group . Over the past seven months, the Iran war has severely disrupted the production and transportation of wholesale oil and refined products from the region, causing prices to surge worldwide. The North East cancer charity Daft as a Brush said it could no longer afford to upgrade its diesel vehicles to electric as they grappled with filling them up, whilst Teesside Minibus Hire said soaring prices were "not sustainable". Daft as a Brush, which provides cancer patients with transport to their hospital appointments, said it was shelling out £15,000 a month on diesel - £5,000 more than last year. The Newcastle-based charity - which drives 600,000 miles every year in its 30 vans - said it had planned on replacing them with electric vehicles, but now could not afford to because the money was being swallowed up at the pump. Volunteer driver Davey Hall said: "Before the big hikes, we used to maybe fill up and it would take £40-45. "Last week, it was £94 to fill the tank from half full." Head of income generation Scott Jobson said the money was being taken from funds raised by donations, and they were not eligible for any kind of discount. "At the pump, what you see is what we pay," he said. "It stunts our growth and development." In Middlesbrough, Teesside Minibus Hire director Billy Johnson said they often signed contracts with schools and businesses which could span multiple years - and were based on the cost of fuel when they were written. "We're not running at a loss yet, but we're running close it to it not being worthwhile or sustainable," he said. Johnson said they were having to pass the cost on to customers using services such as day hires, but because those customers were struggling with inflation themselves, they were not always prepared to pay the increased price. Instead, people were turning towards cheaper, unlicensed hire services which did not pay the same overheads, he said. Asked whether the business could survive if fuel prices did not drop, he said: "Long term, probably not." In May , the government announced it would extend a fuel duty (tax) freeze until the end of the year. It caps the tax at 5p per litre for petrol and diesel, and was introduced by the previous Conservative government after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine pushed prices up in 2022. The government has stressed that there is no cause for concern about potential diesel shortages over the Iran War and has said the country has a "diverse and resilient supply". events.title: ‘You have a meeting’: the calendar phishing scam growing exponentially
events.summary: Appointment or renewal reminder appears in victims’ calendar to lure them into logging in to fake Google, Microsoft or PayPal page Y ou’re preparing for the week ahead and take a look at your Google calendar. There’s an entry for a meeting that you must have completely forgotten. The note that pops up when you click on it says you’ll be reviewing a project and includes a link to more details. Confused, you follow it to find out more; the website you land on asks for logon details, and you provide them. Unfortunately, this was not a failure of your memory but a calendar phishing scam. You have handed your name and password to fraudsters who will sell it on in a batch with other people’s details, use it to break into your work email, or to persuade you that they are contacting you from your bank , or another institution. Luke Wescott, a threat detection engineer at Sublime Security, says calendar phishing is still relatively new but the company has seen “exponential growth”. The scam takes several forms, including a fake meeting, or a prompt to renew a service you pay for. In all, an entry appears in your electronic calendar. It ends up there after scammers send an email to your work, or personal address, with a calendar request. It doesn’t matter if you miss it, or it ends up in your spam folder. “Calendar apps, such as Google Calendar, can add invitations automatically without users even accepting them,” Wescott says. “So scammers don’t even need you to open an email.” And while you may not look twice at one from someone whose name you do not recognise, when something turns up in your calendar you may treat it differently. “It can create a borrowed credibility by showing up in the same place as your dentist appointment or a weekly 1:1 with your boss,” he says. Max Gannon, an intelligence analysis manager at the cybersecurity company Cofense, says some scammers are using legitimate platforms such as Zoom to send the invitations, making them look more convincing to the recipients, and to security software. “That makes it really hard to block,” he says. “Even AI-backed blockers struggle.” If you set up something to filter out invitations from these platforms, he says “that would also block any legitimate meeting invitations”. You will receive an email and see an entry in your calendar. The titles vary: examples seen by the Guardian include fake meetings, notifications of voicemail messages, and software renewals. Wescott says this is standard. “We typically see stuff like ‘New voicemail received’, ‘Payment receipt confirmation – $298.99’, ‘PayPal unusual activity’ warnings, ‘Your auto-payment will be processed within 24 hours’, and invitations to bid on a contract,” he says. Gannon says the invitation could look like it has come from within your company. “If they want to they could make it look like an internal invitation,” he says. “They can customise the content, may be adding the logo of your company.” The event description will typically contain a link, or a phone number. Wescott adds: “Either they want you to click a link to a fake login page like Microsoft, Google or PayPal, and enter your password, or to call a ‘support’ number to cancel a charge that never actually happened.” Until you click on this, or make a call, you are not compromised. The scammers do not have access to everything in your calendar – they are just trying to lure you to a place where you will hand over your details. As Wescott says, “it sounds familiar to typical phishing, it’s the same technique, just using a different delivery method”. Don’t panic if you see an unexpected meeting or reminder in your calendar. Treat it as you would an unexpected email and don’t click on the link. “My number one advice is people just need to be paranoid,” Gannon says. “It doesn’t matter if the invitation has come from someone two desks down, you’ve got to be suspicious of everything.” Wescott advises turning off automatic accepting. In Google Calendar you can go into settings and opt to only accept invitations from known senders, or when you have accepted. He adds: “Don’t click ‘decline’ on suspicious invites as it can tell the sender that your address is ‘live’. Instead, delete or report it as spam/junk.”

events.title: ‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action
events.summary: Tories plan to scrap low-carbon housebuilding, Greens back new nuclear reactors, and Labour put oil-drilling decisions on hold New homes could be built without solar panels, heat pumps and high-grade insulation, leading to higher household bills if the Conservative party wins the next general election. Kemi Badenoch made scrapping the future homes standard (FHS) one of the central planks of her bid to become the next prime minister at the Tory party conference this week. The announcement gained little attention compared to her inheritance tax bombshell , but it would have more far-reaching impacts on a greater number of people. The UK is in need of approximately 6m new homes and failing to equip them with efficient and low-carbon energy sources would doom households to higher bills for decades to come . The Tories quoted estimates of £30,000 for new-build houses, but the real cost is likely to be much less. Installing heat pumps, solar panels, batteries and insulation costs about £5,000 to £8,000 at the point of building – a figure estimated in 2024 when energy prices were much lower – to save more than £1,300 a year on bills , a saving likely to be substantially higher now. To retrofit homes after building would cost more than £20,000. Jan Rosenow, a professor of climate and energy policy at the University of Oxford, said: “Every home constructed today that runs on fossil fuels is a liability for the occupants. It also results in investor uncertainty and disrupts the supply chain that has been gearing up for this. What we need is less political point scoring and more long-term clarity.” Housebuilders have been among the biggest donors to the Conservative party , though this has fallen off in recent years. And according to the UK Green Building Council (UKGBC), the construction industry is well prepared for the FHS and will have to implement the policy before the next general election, so scrapping it is of little benefit. Simon McWhirter, the chief executive of UKGBC, said: “The housebuilding industry has spent years preparing for the introduction of the FHS, investing in skills, supply chains and new products. Reversing course would … risk slowing progress towards building the homes that people want and need.” Badenoch’s housebuilding plans are only part of a torching of the Tories’ green policies. Despite the crisis of sewage and farm pollution in the UK’s rivers and beaches, and the dramatic drop in wildlife, the party would abolish the Environment Agency and Natural England. The party’s U-turn on environmental issues and net zero was contrary to what voters wanted, said Robbie MacPherson, Kennedy scholar at Harvard University and the former head of the UK’s all-party parliamentary group on climate. “No winning political strategy, after years of fossil fuel-driven energy price spikes and a summer of climate breakdown, can include environmental regression. “Voters won’t reward politicians who want to kill employment opportunities, spurn economic growth and fail to keep Britain safe.” While the Conservatives spent their party conference burning their green credentials, an equally unexpected U-turn came from the Green party, which resolved last weekend to abandon its long-held opposition to nuclear power . Although the party would still prioritise renewable energy, Green MPs could now support new reactors, in recognition of their potential role in low-carbon generation. Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Paul Dorfman, Bennett scholar at the University of Sussex and the chair of the Nuclear Consulting Group thinktank, said: “The Green party has taken a wrong turn on nuclear and this will lose them significant grassroot support and votes. “With 20-plus-year construction times, repeated delays and huge cost overruns, new nuclear diverts scarce resources from faster options. Renewables, storage, efficiency and stronger grids can deliver much more for every pound spent.” The battle between the Green party and the Labour party in this week’s Holborn and St Pancras byelection is likely to be repeated during the general election, where the Greens could be the main challengers in urban Labour strongholds. Responding to Sagal Abdi-Wali’s win for Labour, Greenpeace UK’s head of politics, Ami McCarthy, said: “Abdi-Wali has shown that voters are putting their trust in Labour, but the Green party increased its share of the vote and remains a serious challenger. As extreme heat becomes a regular threat and droughts extend for much of the year, concern about climate change is on the rise and cannot be ignored.” At Labour’s conference, Andy Burnham made only passing references to the climate, pollution crises and nature. He announced a publicly owned body to invest in the energy grid , alongside the privatised National Grid, which has been criticised for slow progress on upgrades.

events.title: UAE IPOs and credit markets primed for growth once war ends, Morgan Stanley executive says
events.summary: The UAE is expected to see a rebound in initial public offerings once the US-Iran conflict ends, and the country’s credit market is also set to boom, according to a senior Morgan Stanley executive. While there have been no listings in the UAE so far this year, the investment bank is bullish about the capital market prospects despite the uncertainty caused by the war. UAE companies raised a total of $1.1 billion through three IPOs in 2025, Dealogic data shows. “I think long term, as the conflicts get resolved or hits some level of stabilisation, you will definitely see a rebound in the IPO marketplace in the UAE,” Dan Simkowitz, co-president of Morgan Stanley told The National . “So, we are investing in and have high confidence in that. And we've been so impressed with the leadership on the sort of financial infrastructure in the country all the way around,” he said. The Iran war, which began on February 28, has led to increased uncertainty across the Middle East. After the US-Israeli bombing of Iran and Tehran’s retaliatory strikes on its Arab neighbours halted in early April, peace in the region has teetered on a fragile ceasefire. A report from the World Bank released last week said Gulf economies will contract by an average of 4.3 per cent this year, a downward revision of 5.7 percentage points from its April forecast. While the International Monetary Fund also anticipates that the Gulf economy will contract this year, the region is expected to face a strong recovery next year, conditional on the normalisation of shipping, the fund’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, said. "I think it [the war] clearly creates a slightly higher and hopefully temporary risk premium in the region, but not so much that it changes long-term investment perspectives and investor interest," Mr Simkowitz said. The investment bank's commitment to the region is "as strong as it's ever been". "We continue to be thinking about how to invest in growth. Our corporate clients, FDI clients, are still very focused on the demographics in the region, the potential for GDP growth, the diversification that is coming in the marketplace,” he added. There is extreme resilience that has been built in the region, the Morgan Stanley executive said. “There is also real capital strength in the region, and so as they need to either rebuild or redirect energy infrastructure, for example, there is the capability to do so. And … there is international capital ready to help do that,” he explained. Morgan Stanley, which is headquartered in the US and has more than $10 trillion in assets, has been present in the region for the past 20 years. It also opened a new office in Abu Dhabi in 2024. But I would argue most of it that was on is underway." Credit market boom The Morgan Stanley executive is also bullish about growth in credit markets in the UAE and across the region, with global trends also positive. Credit markets cover bonds, government debt, private credit and bank loans. Globally, asset managers and owners, including sovereign wealth funds and pension funds, are playing a key role in the credit market, he said. “The credit market has become more important because we're entering into a period where high capex manufacturing is back ... and in that context, you need to spend money, and you need to bridge this ‘build to revenue, build to profitability’ gap … and it is not just banks or governments.” Economic tailwinds from the AI buildout and "surprisingly enduring demand" have bolstered credit conditions in many major economies this year, S&P Global Ratings said in a report this month. But the positive momentum of overall credit stability seen over the past few years will become more difficult to sustain, it said. Heading into the fourth quarter, "risks are building amid the sharp rise in benchmark borrowing costs, including yields on government debt, as investors bet that major central banks have a complex challenge in their fight against inflation", the ratings agency said. In the UAE and the Gulf, the credit market “is coming, and I think that's encouraging”, Mr Simkowitz said. Gulf debt capital markets reached $1.2 trillion outstanding at the end of the first half of this year, according to Fitch Ratings. Even in mature markets like the US, the credit market is evolving and building, Mr Simkowitz said, adding that the growth of a fixed income market or a bond market is "incredibly important”. “Over the last several years, the conversations we've had throughout the Gulf with finance ministries, stock exchanges, and other leadership … has been skewing more and more towards bond markets and credit markets, as we've had some great success with ADX [Abu Dhabi Securities Exchange] and with other exchanges in the Gulf around equities, it's a natural progression,” he said. More than $100 billion has been raised in debt markets in the region this year, he said. "That is really important to continue to satisfy the growth, diversification and resiliency ambitions, it can't all be done with equity, and so you need some element of credit and bond markets.” AI, midterms and outlook The big economic theme is AI, which is "incredibly transformational", Mr Simkowitz said. events.title: Mary Chia admits disclosure lapses over CPF arrears at four subsidiaries after SGX queries
events.summary: Mary Chia Holdings has admitted that it failed to disclose CPF arrears and court proceedings involving four of its five subsidiaries. Mary Chia admitted it failed to disclose CPF arrears and court cases at four subsidiaries. SGX RegCo queried the Sept 11 filing, and the group blamed weak internal checks. The CPF Board revised total arrears to $103,727, down from about $153,000. The company said its chief executive knew of the notices, while independent directors learnt later. Mary Chia is reviewing reporting controls and plans instalment payments for the debts. The disclosure issue comes as it faces loan disputes, weak cash flow, and a planned $1 million share issue. SINGAPORE – Cash-strapped beauty and wellness group Mary Chia Holdings has admitted that it failed to disclose CPF arrears and court proceedings involving four of its five subsidiaries, despite its chief executive being aware of the court notices earlier on. The admission came in an Oct 9 response to queries from Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo), which questioned why the four subsidiaries and their involvement in court proceedings were not disclosed in the company’s Sept 11 announcement, and when the company first became aware of these matters. Mary Chia’s Sept 11 announcement disclosed $50,208 in outstanding CPF contributions at one subsidiary but omitted arrears and court proceedings involving four others. All five subsidiaries’ cases had already been heard together on Sept 10, and the CEO knew of their court notices. The Catalist-listed company attributed this omission to shortcomings in its internal information consolidation and disclosure assessment processes, saying it failed to sufficiently consolidate information across its human resources, finance and management functions when preparing its Sept 11 announcement. The group said its earlier disclosure assessment had focused primarily on Mary Chia Beauty & Slimming Specialist, whose CPF arrears and court appearance were the subject of SGX RegCo’s initial query. It said it had not undertaken a comprehensive assessment of similar issues involving other group entities, resulting in the omission of four other subsidiaries from the announcement. These were Masego, Organica International Holdings, Spa Menu and Urban Homme Face & Body Studio for Men. Mary Chia also revealed that the outstanding CPF contributions across the five subsidiaries had been revised to $103,727 as at Oct 9, down from approximately $153,000 stated during a court hearing a day earlier. The revised figure was provided by the CPF Board following a reconciliation of outstanding contributions, taking into account payments made by the subsidiaries towards their arrears. The latest filing also shed light on when the group’s management and independent directors became aware of the CPF issues. Mary Chia said its CEO Ho Yow Ping and the group’s human resources manager were aware of the respective notices to attend court upon receiving them. Ho also attended an interview with the CPF Board on July 22 concerning the outstanding contributions of the five subsidiaries. The group’s independent directors, meanwhile, first became aware of CPF contribution discrepancies within the group at an internal audit meeting on May 25. At that meeting, management informed them of the discrepancies uncovered through an internal review, rectification reports submitted to the CPF Board and efforts to settle the arrears. However, the court notices and related proceedings were not brought to their attention. Mary Chia said its two current independent directors, Chay Yiowmin and Foo Say Tun, learnt of the outstanding contributions and court proceedings involving the four other subsidiaries only on Oct 8, when management updated the board following that day’s hearing. The company disclosed that nine separate notices to attend court had been issued by the CPF Board across the five subsidiaries. Although the matters were initially handled separately, the CPF Board requested in August that the court mentions be consolidated. All five companies subsequently appeared together in court on Sept 10 and Oct 8, with their cases adjourned to Nov 12. According to the CPF Board’s updated computation provided on Oct 9, Mary Chia Beauty & Slimming Specialist owed the largest amount, at $52,266, for outstanding contributions covering November 2025 to May. Organica International Holdings owed $25,248 for contributions covering November 2025 to May 2026, while Masego had $11,341 outstanding for the period from November 2025 to April. Urban Homme Face & Body Studio for Men owed $9,847 for contributions covering September 2025 to March, while Spa Menu had $5,025 outstanding for February. The periods refer only to months for which CPF contributions remain unpaid, rather than every month within the stated date ranges. The revised aggregate amount of $103,727 excludes late-payment interest and composition sums.
