events.title: How de-extincting dire wolves and woolly mammoths may extend human life
events.summary: To join the CNBC Technology Executive Council, go to cnbccouncils.com/tec Colossal Biosciences is on a mission to revive extinct species. The company has created three genetically engineered dire wolf pups and is working on the woolly mammoth. The science of de-extinction has implications for the environment, medicine and research on evolution. Colossal Biosciences' efforts to bring back extinct animals like the woolly mammoth and dire wolves have drawn comparisons to Jurassic Park. CEO and co-founder Ben Lamm told CNBC's Julia Boorstin at the CNBC AI Forum last week that he understands those comparisons. "I think anyone that saw Jurassic Park in the 90s and didn't say it was cool, like I don't think they're probably very fun at parties," Lamm joked. "But yes, I saw the movies. I love them. They entertained us. They scared us." However, Lamm said, "I constantly have to remind people on X that, you know, they were movies," he said. "I don't think Jurassic Park had any conservation or general human benefit models to it, so we've tried to take a slightly different perspective." Since viable dinosaur DNA is no longer available, bringing back dinosaurs is, in fact, impossible. But what is underway at Colossal, besides the dire wolf and woolly mammoth projects, is work to genetically engineer the dodo bird, the Tasmanian tiger, and a giant bird called a moa, among others. "It's highly likely in the next coming year or two, people will continue to see us deliver extinct species back to Earth, and we could even have more dire wolves, too," Lamm told Boorstin. The process of creating the wolf pups involved taking genetic material from a skull and a tooth that were tens of hundreds of years old. Using AI models, Colossal used the ancient DNA to reconstruct the dire wolf genome and map it to its closest living relative, the gray wolf. The team then created embryos by editing the cells of modern gray wolves. Three pups, named Romulus, Remus, and Khaleesi, have been born to domestic dogs used as surrogate mothers. Skeptics, Boorstin pointed out, say that they didn't really de-extinct a dire wolf, rather, they created a genetically modified gray wolf. Lamm called this a "semantic argument" that "misses the forest for the trees." "Gray wolves are just genetically modified dire wolves. They were just done by nature or God or however you want to classify it," he said. Colossal is undertaking a similar process in their woolly mammoth project – that involves genetically modifying an Asian elephant. Lamm told Time in August that the company is aiming to have a woolly mammoth birth in the 2030s. "We call it a woolly mammoth," he said. "Because if it looks like a duck, it quacks like a duck, it serves ecological functions of a duck, it's a duck, in our perspective." Lamm became interested in this work after a 2019 meeting with renowned Harvard geneticist George Church, who Lamm called "arguably the father of synthetic biology." Church, who initiated the Personal Genome Project, had been dreaming about bringing back the woolly mammoth for decades, he told CNBC in 2021. However, the vision to revive animals like the woolly mammoth goes far beyond creating a real-life Jurassic Park with previously extinct creatures. "[Church] had this vision that we could leverage CRISPR and all these tools and technologies to bring back extinct species, use some of those technologies for human healthcare, and then build this programmable life model that we could apply to so many different use cases on Earth," Lamm said. Those use cases include those aforementioned conservation-focused benefits that de-extinction promises. For example, the engineered woolly mammoths could help fight climate change by stomping down snow cover in high-altitude arctic regions, which keeps soil frozen, and knocking down trees, thereby converting heat-absorbing forests into grasslands. But the processes around de-extinction are also opening new doors in genome engineering and developmental biology, Lamm said. That could have implications on "everything from microbes to plastic in the oceans to gene therapies and targeted delivery for humans to eradicating genetic diseases," he said. Lamm theorized that these efforts around DNA synthesis could even lead to developing crops or trees that grow faster. "We're pushing the bounds of DNA synthesis to synthesize the largest cargos of DNA," he said. "That will be massively transformative for how we think about programmable life." A company spun off from Colossal, called Astromech, is pushing into what Lamm called "convergent evolution," studying what causes species that are similar in nearly every way to have different immunities or other health issues, such as why elephants get cancer at a fraction of the rate humans do. That research could be leveraged to solve human healthcare challengers or pandemic responses, Lamm said. Astromech was valued at $2 billion in March, according to D Magazine .

events.title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
events.summary: Last day to exhibit your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders at Disrupt is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished. Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps. It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls. Comma is free to start and open source. Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription. Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations. One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally. Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background. Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account.

events.title: United Auto Workers president Shawn Fain easily wins re-election
events.summary: Fain was dogged by investigation but still decisively beat challenger Rich Boyer, who received just 13% of vote The president of the United Auto Workers, Shawn Fain, has easily won his re-election bid after an campaign period marred by accusations of corruption and election interference. The union’s election of leadership for a four-year term began with mail-in ballots being sent out in late August 2026, with vote tabulating commencing on 6 October. Fain won with over 68% of the vote as of Friday evening, with additional 13 candidates on his slate, United UAW, winning their elections. The closest opponent to Fain, Rich Boyer, received just over 13% of the vote. “The membership has spoken. UAW members are united and want us to keep fighting and building on what we’ve done,” said Shawn Fain in a statement on his re-election win, citing upcoming contract negotiations at John Deere, Volvo and General Dynamics Land Systems in 2027, and the big three automaker contracts expiring on May Day in 2028. “These results are about taking on corporate America and reversing the worst out-of-control wealth inequality in America’s history,” added Fain. “We are fighting for the entire working class, whether that’s at the bargaining table, organizing new members or in the political arena.” In July 2026, the Department of Justice announced it was investigating Fain over allegations he pressured Boyer, another union official, to provide benefits to his fiancee and sister and then retaliated against him when Broyer refused to cooperate. Fain denied the allegations and characterized them as an attempt to interfere in the election. Fain won his first election to serve as the union’s president as a reform candidate in March 2023. He has clashed with the union’s independent monitor, Neil Barofsky, claiming the monitor was weaponized by his re-election opponent. The monitor was also accused of pressuring Fain over the UAW’s passing of a resolution calling for a ceasefire in Gaza. Fain led the union during a roughly six-week strike in September 2023 through October 2023 at the big three automakers, General Motors, Ford and Stellantis, highlighting corporate greed through the strike and citing the companies’ stock buy-backs and record profits. Joe Biden joined the union on the picket line, the first sitting president to ever join a strike picket line.

events.title: Putin relayed Iran war proposal to Trump, Kremlin says
events.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Tehran's view on a possible resolution of the Iran conflict to U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian state media reported. The report comes a day after Trump said Russia will supply diesel to the global market amid a surge in energy prices caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Trump said Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under an arrangement Trump said he agreed with Putin. Russian President Vladimir Putin conveyed Tehran's vision for a possible end to the war in Iran to U.S. President Donald Trump , Russian state media reported Saturday. Russia's Interfax news agency quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as saying Putin sent the message to Trump "in agreement with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian," according to a Google translation. Other Russian media reports said Putin spoke to Trump by phone after the Russian leader met Pezeshkian on the sidelines of a summit in Turkmenistan. Interfax didn't elaborate on the specifics of how Iran sees the war — which began on Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli airstrikes on Iranian targets — coming to an end. The White House didn't immediately respond to CNBC's emailed request to confirm the reported conversation between Putin and Trump. Trump said Friday that Russia will supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market under an arrangement the U.S. president said he agreed with Putin during a phone call. Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons immediately thereafter, Trump said in a post on Truth Social . Moscow will then deliver another 3 million tons of diesel based on the condition of Russia's refineries, Trump said. The Treasury Department temporarily waived sanctions on Russian diesel through April 2027 under a general license issued Friday. Iran has stepped up its attacks on oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, with vessels coming under fire almost daily as Tehran tries to choke off a rebound in crude exports. A senior Iranian Revolutionary Guard official said Wednesday that Iran will block all "illicit routes" through Hormuz, according to the Fars News Agency , an outlet considered close to the Guard. The surge in attacks on tankers comes as crude oil exports from the Middle East rebounded in September to prewar levels, largely because the U.S. military escorted ships through Hormuz along Oman's coast. An interim deal signed in June between the U.S. and Iran to pause hostilities to allow for negotiations quickly broke down. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediately condemned Trump's diesel deal with Putin. Ukraine's leader warned that easing sanctions without a commitment from Russia to de-escalate the war will only prolong it. "Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Zelenskyy said in a social media post . "Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged." Diesel prices have surged worldwide as Ukraine has pounded Russian refineries, forcing Moscow to ban diesel exports to global markets. Iran and its Houthi allies have also attacked refineries in the Middle East, further constraining fuel supplies. Trump is under growing political pressure to lower fuel prices ahead of the November midterm elections. Republicans face competitive elections in conservative strongholds like Iowa, where farmers feel the pinch of high diesel prices.

events.title: UAW tries to reassert political power in Michigan despite internal divisions
events.summary: Membership is divided over which party best represents working-class interests. SHELBY TOWNSHIP, Mich. -- Walter Usakowski was mowing his lawn in a northern suburb of Detroit when three canvassers from the United Auto Workers approached. “I don’t even need to talk to you,” Usakowski said. As a retired member, he was already supporting the union’s slate of Democratic candidates in the Nov. 3 midterms. But he is not sure how many of the other “guys in the shop” will vote for Democrats. He worked at Ford Motor Co.’s Sterling Axle Plant for more than 45 years, and he knows many members who backed Republican President Donald Trump . The election-year canvassing was one part of the UAW’s efforts to reassert its political power in Michigan, a premier political battleground. Although the union generally backs Democrats, its membership is more divided over which party best represents working-class interests. It also is reckoning with past corruption scandals , a drop in membership and a lack of transparency that has eroded trust within its ranks. “It’s not going to be an overnight thing,” said JJ Jewell, who is part of the UAW’s Community Action Program executive committee. “Even if this election goes fantastically, that’s not mission accomplished. That means we’re 1% of the way done.” Jewell and others made the rounds on a recent sunny Saturday in Macomb County, where Trump won by nearly 14 percentage points in 2024. Many of the union members they met in a neighborhood of well-kept suburban houses were retirees, and while most said the cost of living was their top concern , they did not agree on whether Democrats or Republicans would better address it . One resident, who said she blamed billionaires for the country’s problems, planned to vote for Democrats. Another street over, a couple said they both supported Trump and declined to take a flyer of the UAW-endorsed candidates. In a microcosm of broader political rifts , union voters remain politically divided. Union voters have traditionally been seen as a Democratic-leaning constituency, but Trump made direct appeals to them with his anti-elite rhetoric and promises to overhaul international trade agreements that sapped factory jobs. In 2024, voters who were union members or were in a household with a union member split between Trump and Democratic nominee Kamala Harris , with more than half voting for the then-vice president and 44% for Trump. Betty Anderson, a UAW member, thinks the organization is on the right track, but she is not confident about bridging internal political divisions. She said she is angry with members who voted for Trump, whom she sees as selling out the working class. “I don’t think those people are ever going to be on our side,” Anderson said. “They think they have an opportunity to be in an elite class.” Since 2017, more than 10 UAW officials have pleaded guilty in a corruption investigation that found millions of dollars of union dues were stolen. Members also faulted leaders for closed-door contract negotiations that they said destroyed trust in the UAW. Shawn Fain was elected UAW president in 2023 on a platform of transparency, and victories in labor disputes with Detroit's three major automakers bolstered member support. Leaders hope this will translate into votes for its candidates. “I think the UAW members now are starting to fall a little more in line,” said Usakowski, the retired axle plant worker. On Friday, Fain said he won reelection to lead the union for four more years. The results have not yet been certified. Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Fort Hood survivors speak out on Pentagon's decision to livestream Hasan's execution Christa Pike asked 'Where am I?' after waking up following botched execution: Lawyer Mark DePaoli, director for one of the UAW’s southeast Michigan regions, said the union hosted forums with candidates where any member could ask questions. The UAW endorsed progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the U.S. Senate primary even though rival Haley Stevens , a four-term congresswoman, worked as chief of staff on an auto bailout task force during the Great Recession, a position she frequently cited while campaigning. “I don’t think anybody expected us to endorse him,” DePaoli said. In its announcement, the union referenced El-Sayed’s support for universal healthcare and criticism of corporate money in politics. El-Sayed wore a UAW pin during the first Senate debate with his Republican opponent, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers . “The UAW’s backing of Abdul was critical in winning a historic primary despite being outspent by tens of millions of dollars, and will be just as critical in winning" next month, El-Sayed spokesperson Cole Wozniak said in a statement. Rogers is emphasizing his opposition to controversial federal regulations under Democratic President Joe Biden that would have required automakers to ramp up production of electric vehicles, which some feared would lead to factory closures.

events.title: Pokémon card values are soaring. What collectors should know before buying or selling
events.summary: What is driving interest? Pokémon and other trading-card games are drawing strong collector demand, while sources say high sports-card prices are pushing some buyers toward non-sports cards. What determines value? Authenticity, condition, graded population, liquidity and verified transaction history can sharply affect what a card sells for. What is the biggest risk? Counterfeits are rising, especially in Pokémon submissions, making authentication and careful price research critical before buying. In 2022, a rare Topps 1952 Mickey Mantle baseball card — one of sports-card collectors' holiest grails — sold for $12.6 million. Wow, you say, that's a lot of dough for a thin piece of cardboard, slab of bubblegum not included. Well, what do you say about a 1998 Pikachu Illustrator Pokémon card going for $16.5 million earlier this year? If you're pro wrestler and social media influencer Logan Paul, seller of the item, you say, Not a bad return on the $5.3 million (plus a trade) I paid for it in 2021. Those are extreme examples, but a vivid illustration of how TCGs — shorthand for competitive trading card games, led by Pokémon, Magic: The Gathering and Yu-Gi-Oh! — are encroaching on an over-saturated sports-card market as an enticing investment opportunity. Throw in vintage and modern-day non-sports trading cards, depicting historical events and fictional characters ranging from the Civil War to Luke Skywalker, and it's a whole new ballgame. The record $16.5 million Pokémon card sale is drawing fresh attention to a collectibles market where grading, scarcity and authentication can determine whether a card is worth dollars or hundreds of thousands. "It is one of our fastest-growing categories that we've seen and one of the largest contributors to [our] growth over the last number of quarters," said Adam Ireland, vice president and general manager of collectibles at online marketplace eBay , which also provides authentication and price guides for TCGs and non-sports cards. "From an investment point of view, you start with Pokémon," he said. "It was the most searchable term within the eBay collectibles environment through the first half of the year." Heritage Auctions, which deals in art, jewelry, coins and many other collectibles, launched a dedicated TCG department six years ago. "Now it's a $50-million category," said executive vice president Joe Maddalena. "That's just TCGs. I'm not talking about Star Wars and any of that stuff," he said, though he added that non-sports stuff contributed around $10 million to Heritage's overall sales in 2025, which topped $2.1 billion. While buyers can find myriad non-sports cards for less than $10 — almost like investing in penny stocks in hopes of eventually striking gold — Maddalena and Ireland cited some eye-popping sales on their respective platforms. A first-edition Pokémon Charizard card worth $20,000 pre-Covid is now valued by Heritage at $500,000. A Tyler the Great Warrior Yu-Gi-Oh! card shattered records when it was auctioned on eBay for $311,211, while Magic's Black Lotus card has gone for $500,000 on the site. Heritage sold a 1977 Luke Skywalker card for $687,500 in May. Whereas collectability, value and investability of sports cards can rise and fall on the real-world performance of athletes, both trading-card genres share common factors. For instance, rookie cards of superstar athletes are highly coveted; the non-sports counterpart is referred to as first appearance. Especially critical are the authenticity, physical condition, total graded population, liquidity and pricing of specific cards, criteria determined by professional grading services such as PSA and CGC Cards. How cards are graded for monetary value PSA (Professional Sports Authenticator), founded in 1991, is the most recognizable grading service. Its process begins when a trained grader examines a card to verify its originality or genuineness, then assesses the quality and condition of the card using PSA's grading scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the most pristine, aka gem mint. There generally are very limited populations of PSA 10s of highly sought-after cards, thus their astronomical values. PSA has been grading non-sports cards since its inception, "but with more people viewing it as a potential asset class or thing they want to potentially invest in or speculate in, you're seeing more demand for grading services in the last seven years," said PSA president Ryan Hoge. Indeed, PSA graded more than 19 million cards in 2025, up from two million in 2020. The company had already graded more than eight million cards as of last May, with output from January through April up 39% year-over-year. Much of that uptick, Hoge said, is attributable to TCGs. "Collectively, TCGs [account for] 50% of our current business, more than all the sports cards combined.

events.title: The big unknown behind Democrats' polling leads
events.summary: Poll after poll spells trouble for GOP candidates — in purple states and deep-red ones alike — but while Democrats see a blue wave coming, some Republicans see a polling mirage. Why it matters: Pollsters worry they're flying partly blind. Even a modest polling error could mean the difference between Republicans retaining control of Congress and President Trump facing Democratic majorities in both chambers. The big picture: Polling Trump voters has long been notoriously difficult. The polls underestimated Trump's support in 2016, 2020 and 2024. Midterm polling has been more accurate, though some still underestimated Republican support in 2022, notes Scott Keeter, senior survey adviser at Pew Research Center. Catch up quick: With less than a month until the midterms, the polls paint a bleak picture for Republicans. The House: Democrats lead Republicans 49.8%-41.9% in the RealClearPolling generic congressional ballot average. Cook Political Report projects Democrats will gain nine to 19 seats, enough to win a narrow majority. The Senate: Cook now sees a potential Democratic net gain of two to six seats. Democrats need four to take control, and Cook just moved the Kansas Senate race into its toss-up column. Trump: The president's approval rating stands at 37.6% in Cook's polling tracker . A recent Economist/YouGov poll found 35% approving and 60% disapproving of his performance. State of play: Research suggests Republicans have become somewhat less likely than Democrats to participate in telephone surveys, and response rates overall have plummeted since the late 1990s, per Pew . "We definitely have more people answering surveys who voted for [former Vice President Kamala] Harris than who voted for President Trump," says Brent Buchanan, a Republican pollster and founder of Cygnal. "But if you're a good pollster, you still get the other people." Pollsters can compensate by giving greater weight to Trump voters or adjusting samples to better reflect the Republican electorate, which skews male, white and working class. Advanced statistical modeling tools can also take a poor sample and make it look like the true electorate, though results may be inaccurate for subgroups like young people or Hispanic voters, Pew's Keeter says. But that has risks: "The adjustment assumes that the Republicans who respond to a poll are similar to the Republicans who don't respond to the poll," Rice University political science assistant professor Matthew Tyler tells Axios. Tyler said weighting GOP respondents more heavily can backfire if those willing to answer polls are also more willing to vote Democratic than the Republicans who never respond. That could inflate the apparent size of a Democratic wave. Between the lines: Predicting who will actually vote can dramatically change the results. YouGov chief scientist Douglas Rivers found Democratic leads ranging from six to 16 points depending on how likely voters were identified in a September survey — and called the 16-point margin "almost certainly an overstatement." The bottom line: Even with the questions about the accuracy of recent polls, most pollsters believe Democrats have the edge heading into Election Day. " I think it's telling that we're hanging our hopes on, 'The polls are wrong,'" Buchanan says. "That's not very strong."

events.title: Hegseth's public execution plan meets the age of viral violence
events.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's announcement that the Fort Hood shooter's execution will be livestreamed reflects a shift toward putting raw, real-world violence on display for unlimited audiences. Why it matters: The Trump administration has made a show of flexing American power, sometimes with grisly footage. Now, it's preparing to make the government's ultimate punishment available for all to see. The big picture: Americans are increasingly encountering shocking images on their phones, often without warning. Graphic footage of Charlie Kirk's assassination spread widely across social media, searing in the brains of social media users — often young ones. Since Oct. 7, 2023, footage from the Hamas attacks and Israel's military campaign in Gaza has circulated online. Some videos have spread from Telegram to social platforms like X , where clips are easy to find. Footage of the August 2025 killing of Ukrainian refugee Iryna Zarutska on a Charlotte train went viral across X, stirring debate about crime and public safety. President Trump later said he had watched the video and wished he hadn't. A livestream of Nidal Hasan's execution would be the first known public broadcast of a lawful execution, according to death penalty experts interviewed by Reuters. Public executions are increasingly rare worldwide. In recent years, most have taken place in Iran and Taliban-run Afghanistan, according to Amnesty International. Friction point: Tech companies are now facing the question of whether they would allow the Pentagon to livestream the execution on their platforms. Hasan, who killed 13 people in 2009 at the Fort Hood Army base in Texas, is scheduled to be executed on Dec. 3. TikTok and Kick said that livestreaming the event would violate their policies, The Verge reported. YouTube, Meta, X and Twitch did not respond to The Verge's requests for comment. Yes, but: Elon Musk has positioned X, in particular, as a bulwark against internet censorship in the name of free speech. Hegseth's plan is putting the limits of that free-speech philosophy to a new test. The platform defended its decision to keep graphic content of the Kirk shooting on the platform, saying: "We will continue to stand against violence and censorship, ensuring this platform amplifies truth and open dialogue for everyone." After a bishop was stabbed during a livestreamed church service in Australia in 2024, X defied government demands to remove footage of the attack worldwide. Zoom out: Hegseth's announcement raises the prospect of reversing America's nearly century-long retreat from public executions. He justified making the execution public, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." The 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky, which drew 20,000 spectators, is widely considered America's last public execution. A modern-day livestreamed execution could reach billions. The intrigue: Vice President JD Vance questioned Friday whether the execution would actually be livestreamed and said he wouldn't watch if it were. Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) posted : "A civilization erodes when it cultivates an appetite for executions as a form of entertainment. ... Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent." Trump told reporters he had approved the decision to livestream the execution. The bottom line: America spent nearly a century moving away from public executions. Now, with real-world violence just a click away, the U.S. government is preparing to show one to the world.

events.title: FDA may allow some toxic chemicals to be added to food without safety review. Experts are alarmed
events.summary: Regulator looks to expand loophole to allow dangerous compounds in food as long as they’re not carcinogenic The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is proposing to expand a controversial loophole to allow some of the world’s most toxic chemicals to be added directly to food without a safety review. The “threshold of regulation” (TOR) exemption currently allows dangerous compounds to be used without review in food contact materials, such as packaging or processing equipment, if they are not carcinogenic, and are added at levels below 0.5 parts per billion (ppb). But campaigners say many chemicals, especially hormone disruptors linked to brain damage and reproductive harm in children, are considered dangerous at levels far below 0.5ppb. Even in its limited form, the loophole has already raised alarm. One TOR exemption that allows the rocket fuel chemical perchlorate to be used in grain bags dramatically increased the amount of the compound found in kids’ cereal, which advocates say could cause brain damage . The new proposed TOR expansion would allow companies to use the chemicals as an ingredient added directly to food, as flavorings, preservatives, emulsifiers, processing aids, enzymes, stabilizers and binders, and for myriad other uses, in ultra-processing. The revelation comes after Robert F Kennedy Jr and the FDA claimed victory and declared “ promises kept ” in August for “closing” a different controversial regulatory loophole called “generally regarded as safe” (Gras), which over the decades was used to send ingredients to the market that campaigners said could sicken , injure or kill people. But Kennedy and the FDA did not mention in their public relations material that the proposed Gras rule submitted quietly to the Federal Register includes the TOR expansion, which public health advocates warn will also send alarming levels of toxic chemicals to grocery store shelves. Some advocates have accused Kennedy of deception. Regardless, the proposal represents a major win for big food, advocates say, and is based on flawed science. “The FDA and industry have this position that if there’s only a little bit of something in the diet, then it’s not going to be problematic, but that isn’t supported by science of any kind,” said Maricel Maffini, an independent food consultant who worked on TOR issues. “I don’t know how they’re going to square that circle because there are many ingredients that at very low levels also cause serious issues in the body,” Maffini added. The FDA did not respond to a request for comment. The proposed rule states that “any substance used in food (both directly or indirectly added) will be exempted from regulation as a food additive” if there is “no appreciable risk to human health”. Advocates say the problem lies in the definition of “appreciable risk”. Chemicals like perchlorate, some phthalates, some bisphenols, some Pfas “forever chemicals” and some flame retardants are not classified as carcinogenic, but they can cause harm at doses far lower than 0.5ppb. These could in theory be used as TOR ingredients, as could chemicals that are neurotoxic, cause brain damage, attack the immune system, harm the microbiota or give rise to any number of other adverse health impacts. Maffini said she was particularly concerned about flavorings because ultra-processed food companies use chemicals that “play around with the nervous system and receptors in your mouth to try to make us eat more and more of something”. Advocates say the rule also does not take into account cumulative effects – one small dose of a TOR-exempted chemical may not be harmful, but many small doses of multiple toxic chemicals could be a problem. It also creates a secondary loophole in allowing carcinogens if the substance is created as an impurity. Meanwhile, there is no way for consumers to know if a product contains a TOR-exempted chemical. “They’re widening another loophole, but trying to say they made our food safer,” said Maria Doa, a scientist with the Environmental Defense Fund (EDF) non-profit. “They did not make our food safer.” How TOR led to children eating rocket fuel chemicals The problems with perchlorate in kids’ cereal are a warning about TOR’s risks, advocates say. In 2005, German chemical giant BASF used TOR to exempt perchlorate from regulations for use in “super sacks”, which are one-ton polypropylene plastic storage bags used on farms to move grains, including rice, flour and oats. Perchlorate stops grains from sticking to super sacks. But the grains are loaded into and emptied from the sacks at high velocity, which can cause perchlorate and microplastics to break off. The FDA’s own data published in 2017 showed the number of samples of kids’ cereal with perchlorate increased after the 2005 TOR exemption. The agency similarly detailed a broad increase in the levels in each sample.

events.title: S&P lifts UK GDP growth view on resilient consumer spending and services sector
events.summary: S&P Global Ratings has upgraded its growth outlook for the UK, citing “reasonably resilient” consumer spending and services that have helped shield the economy from the conflict in the Middle East. Real gross domestic product in Europe's second-biggest economy is now expected to climb by 1.3 per cent, from a previous lowered prediction of 1.1 per cent , the New York-based agency said on Friday. S&P analysts noted that hospitality and professional services underpinned economic growth in the second quarter. GDP growth is seen to average 1.4 per cent from 2027 to 2029, expecting the economy to improve if the situation in the Middle East is “contained”. The agency also maintained the UK's long and short-term foreign and local currency sovereign credit ratings at AA, two notches below the top prime grade. An investment grade makes it easier to access capital markets and raise funding when the need to borrow arises. “The stable outlook reflects our view that the UK economy has remained, and will remain, resilient in the face of the energy shock emanating from the Middle East conflict, with growth remaining reasonably robust,” analysts at S&P wrote. “This is balanced against risks from the UK's constrained fiscal position, elevated public debt levels, and high government spending, including on debt servicing.” S&P also noted the UK's policy direction under Andy Burnham, the UK's sixth prime minister in the past decade. The start of his tenure in July was marked by questions about how he would handle the economy, including how to ensure fiscal discipline. Mr Burnham's government has “focused on devolution, industrial renewal, social care and closer ties with the EU, with simultaneous pledges to respect fiscal prudence”, S&P said. UK inflation was pegged at 3.1 per cent in August, the highest in five months, according to the Office of National Statistics, and well above the Bank of England's 2 per cent threshold. S&P said this has risen on domestic price pressures and energy and transport costs, underpinned by higher hydrocarbon costs. The agency expects the Bank of England to raise interest rates by 0.25 basis points at its November meeting after maintaining them last month, “then hold that level until the second half of 2027 because the current policy rate level of 3.75 per cent and soft labour market conditions suggest the UK may require less additional policy tightening than the eurozone”. Egypt's growth accelerates Meanwhile, S&P said Egypt's economy accelerated at its fastest pace in three years, but cautioned the North African nation remains vulnerable to shocks stemming from the conflicts in the Middle East. Real GDP in the Arab world's most populous nation jumped by 5.1 per cent in fiscal 2026, buoyed by non-oil sectors including manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade, information and communication technology, and tourism, it said in a separate report. That compares to a 4.7 per cent reading in its previous estimate . Household consumption emerged as a primary factor, boosted by record remittances, easing inflation and stable labour market conditions, it added. S&P, however, projects this growth to ease to 4.5 per cent in the fiscal year 2027, as shipping disruptions related to the war are expected to further pressure trade, logistics and import prices. Consumption and investment activities are also predicted to soften amid persistent uncertainty and rising inflation. Higher energy costs kept inflation elevated at 13.9 per cent in September, according to Capmas data. S&P expects inflation to average 12.9 per cent in fiscal 2027. This might result in a policy reversal from the Central Bank of Egypt, which has resisted increasing interest rates. S&P also kept its B sovereign credit rating on Egypt, which is six levels below investment grade, with a stable outlook. “Nevertheless, we expect the continued implementation of the reform agenda, including the commitment to exchange rate liberalisation, to enhance structural economic competitiveness over the medium term,” the S&P analysts said.

events.title: Trump rages over Nobel Peace Prize loss
events.summary: President Trump lashed out late Friday night after he once again did not win the Nobel Peace Prize he has openly coveted . Why it matters: The award is Trump's white whale, an honor he talks about frequently and believes he deserves. This year's prize went instead to a former judge of a court Trump has sanctioned and called "rogue" and "evil." Navi Pillay, the winner, reacted to the award by saying world leaders have a "legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war," according to the AP . What he's saying: " I know nothing about this woman, and neither does anyone else! In fact, to the best of my knowledge, no one ever heard of her other than the fact that she, very obviously, hates Israel. I don't know what the woman has done," Trump said in a Truth Social post of nearly 600 words that went up just before midnight on Friday. "I settled 8 Wars, with letters being sent from every President and Prime Minister from the countries that I helped to the Norwegian Nobel Committee, and I'm about to settle, or win, two more, Iran and, Russia/Ukraine," Trump wrote. "They're both happening at breakneck speed but, forget them, it's the 8 that I've already settled, any one of which, in particular, Pakistan and India, would be far more than necessary to win the Nobel Prize. In actuality, I should have won 8 Nobel Peace Prizes, not just 1." Between the lines: Pillay, this year's winner, is a former judge of the International Criminal Court and also the former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights. Nobel officials said she received the honor "for her efforts to promote peace and international law." Originally from South Africa, Pillay, 85, also served as chair of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. Zoom in: Trump took aim at that UN association as well. "In all of the Wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations—they were of no help. The United States of America, represented by me, as your President, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn't," he said. The intrigue: Trump also blasted Norway, as he's previously done over Nobel snubs, though the country doesn't award the prize. "This is an indelible stain on Norway, one that will never be forgotten. The Nobel 'Peace' Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of Radical Ideologues who are Anti-Democracy, and Enemies of Civilization!" The bottom line: The president didn't hold back making his case for why he should have won — and why his loss was a personal snub.

events.title: As Trump’s Wall Closes in, DHS Intimidates a Border Tribe With Surveillance, Masked Agents and Drones
events.summary: A border patrol vehicle drives past the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on the Tohono O’odham nation on Sept. 5. Cam Mackey At 4:59 a.m. on Aug. 25, Verlon Jose, the chairman of the Tohono O’odham Nation in Southern Arizona, received an email from the head of the U.S. Border Patrol’s Tucson Sector. Government contractors were en route to conduct soil tests for construction of a 62-mile wall along the Nation’s southern boundary, wrote acting chief patrol agent Henry N. Laxdal. If the tribe wished to have cultural monitors observe the work, they were welcome to, but they could not interfere with the government’s operations. The work would begin in exactly one minute. Jose, 59, was already aware of the contractors’ arrival. An hour earlier, a tribal member had called to report a caravan heading south through the reservation, and Facebook was lighting up with similar accounts. The convoy included not only work trucks and drilling rigs, but Border Patrol vehicles as well. Dozens of border wall contractor and Border Patrol vehicles pass the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on the morning of Aug. 27. Nate Sosa For months, the O’odham had maneuvered to avoid such a scene, taking their case to federal court. Their homeland straddles the border, and thousands of tribal members live in Mexico. A wall would disrupt routine border crossings for ceremonies and family visits and destroy landscapes they consider their duty to protect, members and leaders say. Their lawsuit argued that the Trump administration’s efforts to build it despite their opposition constituted an historic attack on tribal sovereignty. But administration attorneys gave assurances that the government was engaging with the O’odham in good faith, and a judge in Washington, D.C., denied the tribe’s request for a preliminary injunction. In his Aug. 25 email providing Jose a 60-second heads up, the Border Patrol chief said his agency’s willingness to accommodate cultural monitors underscored its “commitment to ongoing coordination” with the Nation. As daylight broke, Jose learned the contractors were guarded by federal agents in masks and tactical gear, drawn from a special operations cadre that participated in citywide sweeps in Minneapolis and Chicago the previous year, which left three people dead, including two U.S. citizens. When the tribe’s chief of police tried to reach the worksite, he was stopped at a roadblock set up by the agents. Merrian Felix Davy Cross Border Patrol tactical team members amass around the Tadai Me:i prayer camp on Aug. 26. Jose issued a statement on the Nation’s website declaring the incursion illegal and revealing that the Department of Homeland Security had deployed a surveillance blimp and enlisted Mexican security forces to help protect the work crews. For a quarter-century, Tohono O’odham leaders have staved off a border wall by allowing DHS to use the reservation as a testing ground for some of the government’s most aggressive homeland security measures — from vehicle barriers on the reservation’s southern boundary, to state-of-the-art surveillance towers , to law enforcement partnerships with the Border Patrol and Immigration and Customs Enforcement . Despite the collaborations, and assurances from the Trump administration, ProPublica found that DHS has turned its vast apparatus on tribal members, with 24-hour surveillance directed at an ongoing border prayer ceremony and tribal members being questioned outside the reservation about their ceremonial activities. ProPublica’s account is based on photos, videos, court filings, interviews with tribal leadership, firsthand observations and more than 1,000 contemporaneously written observations compiled by tribal members. The battle over a border wall on the Nation has broken along familiar partisan lines in Arizona. While GOP legislative leaders have filed briefs in support of the project, Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs has done the same in support of the tribe. Progressive U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, whose district includes the reservation, has said she is crafting legislation to rein in the Department of Homeland Security’s sweeping powers to waive federal laws in order to expedite wall construction. The Trump administration has used those authorities to circumvent environmental and cultural preservation statutes on 60 occasions across its two terms. For Deshane Gregg, whose vehicle was forced off the road by a convoy of contractors and federal agents, the recent show of force on the reservation has felt like a government siege, not cooperation. “You just feel helpless. You see these people, and they’re just so aggressive. They want you to react. They want you to show them that we could be ugly too,” she said. “We’re just here doing prayer. We’re just here, not trying to bother them, but it gets to you when it’s constantly being like that.” “The drones flying over us all day,” she added, “it’s a lot.” A drone hovers over the Tadai Me:i camp during morning prayer songs on Aug. 27. Ryan Devereaux/ProPublica ProPublica sent DHS, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, and the Border Patrol nearly 30 questions about the government’s surveillance and interactions with tribal members and leaders. The agencies answered none of those questions. Instead, CBP pointed to a statement Commissioner Rodney Scott made in August, in which he described the reservation’s southern boundary as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border” and a “remote desert that has facilitated decades of drug loads, migrant deaths, and cartel activity.” Regarding construction of a wall, Scott said, “Congress funded this work, a Federal court has affirmed it, and CBP is carrying it out under the legal authorities that apply. Under President Trump’s leadership, we are securing the border and giving our agents the tools and support they need to protect the American people.” A post on X from James Percival, general counsel of the Department of Homeland Security, celebrates the denial of a request for an emergency injunction against border wall construction filed by Tohono O’odham leadership in August. Screenshot of X With no sign the White House or the O’odham government is backing down, DHS has cast off any pretense that the agency will work cooperatively with the Nation. Within hours of the judge’s denial of the emergency injunction, on Aug. 14, the department’s general counsel, James Percival, posted a celebratory meme depicting one of the cybernetic Star Trek supervillains known as “the Borg.” “RESISTANCE IS FUTILE,” it read. “We respect tribal sovereignty but not to the detriment of border security,” he wrote. “This wall is getting built. Our authority is beyond dispute.” The O’odham have inhabited the Sonoran Desert, from what is now Southern Arizona to Mexico’s Sea of Cortez, for thousands of years . events.title: US-Russia energy deal opens up diesel can of worms
events.summary: US President Donald Trump's announcement that Russia will be supplying diesel to global markets has opened up a can of worms, says analysts. Washington agreed to lift sanctions on the Kremlin in a bid to bring down energy prices, especially for diesel, which is vital to many economic sectors. Analysts, however, have raised alarm bells, saying the numbers Mr Trump has touted will not add up, and highlighting double standards over Russia's conflict with Ukraine and the International Criminal Court. 'Happy birthday Putin' The first fallout came from Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy immediately after Mr Trump announced the deal. Mr Zelenskyy said allowing Russia to sell its petroleum products “is an investment in war that needs to end, not continue”, and that the Kremlin “will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy”. In a subsequent interview with Axios , Mr Zelenskyy likened the deal to a “birthday present” to Russian President Vladimir Putin, who turned 74 on October 7. Peace never comes through weakness. Today, representatives of the U.S. Congress were in Kyiv – a bipartisan delegation – and I am grateful to them for visiting Ukraine at such a difficult time. They asked: what is needed to end the war? The answer must be strong. There must be… — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 9, 2026 Mr Zelenskyy apparently also felt betrayed. Last week, the Ukrainian President met Steve Witkoff, the US special envoy to the Middle East, and Jared Kushner, the US envoy for peace (and Mr Trump's son-in-law), to discuss a potential peace breakthrough before the US midterm elections. But nothing was discussed about a potential diesel deal with the Russians. “It looks like that they used this opportunity to meet us from one side, and from the other side called Putin and negotiate this,” Mr Zelenskyy said in the Axios interview. “If the price is energy ceasefire, this negotiation is good … what did [Trump] get? That he will have more diesel? For whom? More Russian diesel for Americans? It shows weakness of the world.” 'Fantasy arithmetic' Mr Trump, in a social media post, said that under the deal, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel fuel to the US and global market, in addition to 500,000 tonnes in November, followed by one million more tonnes “immediately thereafter”. In total, and “based on the condition of their diesel refineries”, Russia will deliver three million tonnes of diesel fuel “within a short period of time”, he added. Those numbers “will not work”, according to analysts at Quantum Strategy and Geonomics, which said the figures above are, respectively, 60 per cent, 100 per cent and 200 per cent of Russia's diesel exports. Furthermore, Russia needs to import 80,000 and 140,000 barrels per day of diesel, petrol and other refined products just to run its domestic refineries and make up for the shortages of refined products, Singapore-based Quantum said. Its analysts also pointed out that Ukrainian strikes have taken out more than half of Russia's refining capacity, according to Kyiv's defence ministry. The International Energy Agency estimates that Russia's diesel production capacity has been cut by nearly a third as a result of the attacks. In addition, Russia's exports of diesel and gasoil fell to a decade low of about 144,000 barrels per day in September, down from as high as 270,000 bpd in August and a peak of 820,000 in April, according to Quantum data. “Russia cannot supply the diesel Trump claims it will … technically, the balance [between diesel and other refined product exports and imports] needed to run domestic refineries cannot be switched into supplying Trump without endangering Russian domestic refinery supply in other areas,” the Quantum analysts said. “So Trump's simple fantasy arithmetic is nothing but that … we expect this deal to fail economically.” "Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and… pic.twitter.com/tZMCfT95ru — The White House (@WhiteHouse) October 9, 2026 Double standard The US-Russia diesel deal also poses as a double standard. On Friday, Washington imposed more sanctions on the International Criminal Court, on the same day that former ICC judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. The move was seen as retaliation for Mr Trump not being awarded the honour, which he claimed he deserved. “The contrast is striking. Sanctions against an institution pursuing accountability for war crimes; sanctions relaxed on energy exports from a country waging a war of aggression against Ukraine,” said Nicolai Kiskalt, a Germany-based partner at global consultancy KPMG. “The US administration has its own arguments: protecting American sovereignty from the ICC’s jurisdiction and bringing down energy prices for American consumers. But from a European perspective, these decisions raise fundamental questions that go far beyond trade, energy or diplomacy.” Riku Huttunen, director general of the energy department at Finland's Economy and Employment Ministry, also called this a “stark contrast” to the US sanctions law aimed at clamping down on the oil and gas revenue that fuels Russia’s war against Ukraine. “At the same time, there are doubts concerning Russian supplies. Russian oil refining capacities have been destroyed by Ukrainian drone attacks, causing fuel shortages,” he said. “The deal's effects on diesel markets might remain small. The agreed amounts are relatively modest and it is still unclear how the deliveries would be made in practice.” The timing of the US-Russia deal may also be bad, especially for Ukrainians, as winter approaches. Any further attacks on energy infrastructure would prove to be a serious challenge for both the economy and society. “An energy ceasefire was one of the few practical ideas that could have directly protected Ukrainian civilians this winter,” said Robert Potter, founding partner of Washington-based Cyber Activities Group, who is also an expert in geopolitics and security. “The negotiating logic was straightforward: if Moscow wanted sanctions relief or economic concessions, those could potentially be exchanged for something tangible, stopping attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Instead, Trump has handed Putin the economic benefit first,” he said. “That pulls the rug from under one of the few areas where western leverage could have been converted into immediate civilian protection. Worse, the signal to Moscow is really dangerous. Putin can escalate attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, refuse to commit to renewed peace talks, and still receive access to western-linked energy markets because US diesel prices are politically painful ahead of the midterms.”

events.title: Watch: Inside Our $22K Sports Betting Experiment
events.summary: Illustration by Mauricio Rodríguez Pons/ProPublica. Source images by Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images. Earlier this year, we heard that reporter Jake Pearson planned to ask our editors at ProPublica for more than $20,000 so he could spend the NBA playoffs betting like a problem gambler .  We told him we wanted in on the action.  For 10 weeks, our documentary team at ProPublica filmed Jake as he dove ball-cap-first into DraftKings and FanDuel, the country’s largest online sportsbooks. Jake bet early, late and often, ramping up the amounts and frequency of his wagers, chasing his losses with even bigger bets.  He wanted to flagrantly wave the red flags of a gambler descending into addiction. Would the apps serve up speed bumps as he careened into the red, or would they push him to keep betting?  Since 2018, the year the Supreme Court opened the door for states to legalize sports betting, the number of people staking money on games has exploded. It’s now legal in 39 states and Washington, D.C. The apps don’t just offer straight action on the outcome of a “Sunday Night Football” game — you can put money on myriad sports events and outcomes, including who will score the next point in a tense contest of Czech table tennis. Every month, millions do.  More than $600 billion has sloshed through the legal sportsbooks in wagers — and brought billions in state tax revenue — in the last eight years. But between the ever-present ads featuring celebrities from LeBron James and Charles Barkley to Kevin Hart and Kendall Jenner, cracks in the system have started to show.  About a quarter of active sportsbook account holders surveyed by the Siena Research Institute this year said that they’d lost enough on a bet that they’d have trouble meeting their financial obligations . Other studies and public health experts warn of rising cases of bankruptcy, addiction and self-harm. ProPublica reporter Jake Pearson at a Manhattan bar this spring, testing DraftKings’ and FanDuel’s guardrails. More than a quarter of people in the U.S. say they have an active account with an online sportsbook, according to a poll by the Siena Research Institute. Gerardo del Valle/ProPublica DraftKings and FanDuel say that they don’t want to profit off bettors who can’t control themselves, and they provide a range of what the industry calls “responsible gaming” tools to help users stay in check.  Jake received pop-up notices, reminders and emails noting his time on the app and nudging him to “take a beat” after a loss. He opted into some of the tools DraftKings makes available. But he was struck by user design choices and promotions that encouraged him to keep betting, some of which he was served right after setting limits on his play.  In a statement, DraftKings told ProPublica that it trains its more than 5,000 employees on responsible gaming and has more than 50 full-time staff dedicated to its “responsible engagement” program. A FanDuel spokesperson wrote that the company’s program is “designed to identify potential risk early and empower customers with real-time information about their play.”  Even so, regulators and lawmakers from Colorado to Massachusetts have begun to question whether sportsbooks have sufficient protections in place. Those concerns have risen with the popularization of prediction markets, which are even less regulated than sports betting apps like DraftKings.  We were behind the camera back in April when Jake opened his DraftKings account to place his first bet, a $100 Hail Mary wager for the New York Knicks to win the chip. We had no idea what a ride it would be.   Watch our new documentary that follows Jake as he intentionally descends into problem gambling — and see how the apps react.  Have you used apps like DraftKings or FanDuel to place sports bets? ProPublica is looking for at least 250 people who use these apps to share their data with us. Your transaction history will help us better understand how the apps respond to user behavior. You can also reach Jake Pearson and the reporting team at 917-512-0276 or sportsbetting@propublica.org . The post Watch: Inside Our $22K Sports Betting Experiment appeared first on ProPublica .

events.title: 2 Inflation reports, retail sales and big bank profits all arrive in the coming week
events.summary: The upcoming week promises to deliver notable updates on inflation, a topic sure to dominate the U.S. midterm elections now less than a month away NEW YORK -- The upcoming week promises to deliver notable updates on inflation, a topic sure to dominate the U.S. midterm elections now less than a month away. A separate report will show how retailers are faring in an inflationary environment, while the nation's biggest banks roll out financials details from the most recent quarter. The price of oil will be front and center as the U.S. war with Iran drags into its eighth month. Renewed violence has sent oil prices back above $100 per barrel and average gasoline prices remain well above $4 per gallon, while diesel remains just below the record high prices reached in September. That has all fueled inflation, putting more pressure on household budgets and businesses. Here's a look at some of the events that will be front and center in the week ahead. No news is good news lately in the U.S. housing market. On Tuesday, the National Association of Realtors reports existing home sales for September, and economists believe sales held steady from August. But August was awful , with sales declining to their slowest annual pace in more than a year. Prospective home buyers are being thwarted by rising mortgage rates which, as Freddie Mac reported Thursday , marched higher for the seventh consecutive week. The average long-term U.S. home loan rate is now higher than it's been in nearly three years. The housing sector has been in a slump since 2022 and sales of previously occupied homes were essentially flat last year, stuck at a 30-year low. The U.S. reported last month that inflation accelerated in August as gas prices spiked in the wake of renewed fighting in the Middle East. More of the same is expected for September with all sides in the Iranian conflict unwilling to concede ground. The Labor Department is expected to report Wednesday that its consumer price index rose by two-tenths of a percent month over month and rose 3.6% compared with a year ago at this time. A day later, the department will release its producer price index — which captures inflation before it reaches consumers. Same story there. Economists expect an increase from the 5.4% registered in August , which was up from 4.8% in July . Last week, PepsiCo said it was raising prices on Doritos and other favorites, citing rising costs for fuel, aluminum and commodities. Economists believe that Americans pulled back on shopping in September with the holiday shopping season just around the corner. Most expect a 0.65% bump. That said, consumers surprised just about everyone in August . As they griped about higher prices at the pump and at the grocery store, Americans spent heartily, expanding retail sales by 1.2%, nearly twice what forecasters had expected. Also next week, the National Retail Federation releases its forecast for the holidays. UN human rights office slams racist abuse of Coco Gauff Park service could remove more than 500 trees at historic golf course Trump wants to redesign Pakistan provides fuel aid to 9 million low-income people as Middle East war drives up prices Banks have notched record profits this year as their trading desks benefit from a volatile stock market while the U.S. war with Iran drags on. Big swings in markets tend to increase activity on trading desks, leading to higher commissions and fee revenue for the banks. Meanwhile, consumers keep spending despite pressure from high prices, and that helps boost fee and lending revenue. Wall Street expects more of the same from the third-quarter updates. Analysts expect JPMorgan Chase to report a 47% boost in profits and Citigroup to report a 61% profit jump when both release earnings Tuesday. Bank of America is expected to tally a profit gain of 36% when it announces results Wednesday. Several other banks and financial institutions, including Morgan Stanley, will also report results during the week. Households and businesses are also facing high interest rates that allow banks to charge more for loans and that won't likely change anytime soon. events.title: Opal Tower declared defect-free eight years after evacuations
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Sydney's Opal Tower officially declared defect-free eight years after mass evacuations Topic: Housing Construction Industry Thousands of residents were forced to evacuate on Christmas Eve in 2018 after cracks were found in the building. ( ABC News: Liam Patrick ) The Opal Tower apartment complex in Sydney's west has been declared defect-free at a ceremony. Residents were forced to evacuate the complex on Christmas Eve in 2018 after cracks were found in the building. The process of fixing the high-rise and securing compensation for owners has involved a class action, two legal cases, and has cost millions of dollars. A ribbon-cutting ceremony has taken place at the once-plagued Opal Tower in Sydney's west to mark the building officially being declared defect-free. The celebration brings an end to a saga, spanning close to eight years, that involved a class action, two legal cases, ongoing rectification work and relocations after cracks appeared on level 10 of the complex on Christmas Eve in 2018. Fearing a collapse, thousands of people were forced to evacuate with the emergency response also shutting down the nearby train station and surrounding roads at Sydney Olympic Park. Opal Tower was officially declared defect-free on Saturday. ( ABC News ) At the time, police said the tower had moved "1 to 2 millimetres". Days later, more cracks were discovered on other levels of the 36-storey high-rise. Opal Tower Owners Corporation chairman Shady Eskander has been at the forefront of the fight to get the complex made up of 392 units repaired, and secure compensation for those affected. "It's fantastic to announce that Opal Tower is defect-free." Shady Eskander says the impact of the defects has been devastating for residents. ( ABC News: Liam Patrick ) Mr Eskander told the ABC that a lot of work had taken place and millions of dollars had been spent to be able to declare "this building is the safest and best residential building in Australia". "Everything that was done was done with the consultants, with the builder, with all of those involved in the design and construction of Opal Tower. "We came alongside each other in a very collaborative manner." Developer Ecove, backed by Japanese firm Kajina Corporation, engineers WSP, and builder Icon have been the other parties involved in the process. An engineer's report commissioned by the NSW government concluded in 2019 that the cracks had been caused by a combination of "design and construction matters, in particular changes made after the original design". In what Mr Eskander described as an Australian-first, the high-rise is now protected by a 20-year structural warranty. A report concluded the defects were caused by a combination of "design and construction matters". ( Supplied ) All owners have been fairly compensated, and all legal matters have been resolved. "This is the greatest property comeback story in Australian history," Mr Eskander said in a statement. Nutan Borkar was out of her unit for 11 months after the incident, and was glad there was finally "light at the end of the tunnel after a big struggle". "It's great because a lot of time has been invested in getting the building back to the way it should've been," she said. "I love being here. I wouldn't think of being anywhere else but here now. It's home." Nutan Borkar says she "wouldn't think of being anywhere else". ( ABC News: Liam Patrick ) Building standards were lifted across the state, with the Coalition government at the time introducing the role of building commissioner and a suite of other reforms. "The lesson that can be learnt from Opal Tower … is that quality needs to be there so that defects aren't," Mr Eskander said. "And we need to ensure that defects don't occur in the towers that are being constructed over Sydney because builders and contractors will spend more on fixing the defect than building it right the first time." 100 preschools set to open in NSW, but how many will be accepting children?

events.title: Old Bendigo gold mine hosts underground piano concert
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Piano taken down gold mine for unique underground concert in Bendigo A 300kg piano has been transported 61 metres underground in a 'world-first' piano concert in a Bendigo gold mine. The concert was held in the mine to celebrate the 175th anniversary of the discovery of gold in the central Victorian city. Bendigo Fine Music says it's the first time they know of that a concert has been held underground in such a unique venue. A unique piano concert 61 metres underground in an old gold mine. That was the brainwave of Bendigo Fine Music chair Thomas Heywood. And yesterday that brainwave became reality, with a piano descending into the Central Deborah Gold Mine in Bendigo for a one-off evening performance. The 300kg piano was formerly owned by Mr Heywood's mother, who was a renowned concert pianist. "It's one of those classic 'don't drop the piano' scenarios," Mr Heywood said. "We couldn't find any evidence that this has been done before. "It's really quite emotional; it sounds fantastic in here. It is an amazing room for sound. There's a timber ceiling and hardstone walls, and they're ideal for musical performance." Thomas Heywood came up with the idea of holding the concert in a gold mine to mark 175 years since gold was discovered in Bendigo. ( ABC News: Tyrone Dalton ) The Bendigo Fine Music event celebrated 175 years since gold was first discovered in the central Victorian city. "We were always taught in school that basically the riches that followed from gold made possible what would have taken 500 years in European history to be achieved in a mere 50 years to Federation." Friday's concert was limited to 60 attendees, who were allowed to remove their hard hats once in the concert room. Pianist Yasmin Rowe said performing this rare and unusual concert was exciting. "I've never played underground before, and this is just so special. When I entered this room, I thought it was so, so beautiful," Ms Rowe said. "You've got this millions-of-years-old rock there right behind the piano; the light, the colour, the atmosphere is wonderful." Yasmin Rowe and Ian Munro played before an audience of 60 people. ( ABC News: Tyrone Dalton ) Ms Rowe and fellow pianist Ian Munro said the underground concert made playing the piano interesting again. Mr Munro said the rare and unusual concert brought back the memory of a conversation with his piano teacher at the age of 14, who questioned whether he would continue to love playing the piano as an adult. "When I was 30 [and still loved playing piano], and now I'm very much older than 30, I'm still very interested; it's still got that magic for me." The main body of the piano was covered with a blanket to protect from moisture in the tunnels. ( ABC News: Anna McGuinness ) The operation to get the instrument underground was a family affair by Joshua McPherson, his wife Jo and son Sam. Mr McPherson said it was "definitely the most unusual" place he had ever taken a piano. The disassembled instrument was wheeled on a trolley into a lift and rolled along the rocky tunnels of the mine. "We were worried about moisture dropping from the ceiling — that was our main concern. [It was] a little bit rough underfoot but nothing scary really," he said. Nic Hamilton was tasked with making sure the piano stayed in tune. ( ABC News: Anna McGuinness ) Once in place, it was over to piano technician Nic Hamilton to ensure nothing had gone awry on the journey and to tune the piano before the concert. "It's a fun thing to do, and it's very typical of Thomas [Heywood] to come up with projects that are interesting and exciting." The piano is moved into the entrance to Central Deborah Gold Mine.
